items.title: Welcome
items.text: This is your one-stop shop for lab notes, slides and other content for this course. Slides are available to view directly in your browser and PDF versions of the same are available to download.

items.title: About this course
items.text:
This course is aimed at introducing you to core networking concepts and implementations through a blend of theory and hands-on practical activities.

The course assumes basic computer literacy, some familiarity with file system and operating system concepts. Familiarity with the Linux operating system is not strictly expected, but the ability to run simple bash commands and edit text files in a command line interface will come in handy.

items.title: Course Goals
items.text:
• Explore key networking concepts through hands-on practical activities
  • Learn to use networking tools to configure network devices and services for basic inter-network connectivity and analyse network traffic moving across the network

items.title: Methodology
items.text: Learning in this course is lab-led. Each topic is introduced through a series of exploratory practical activities and this is followed by a discussion of relevant concepts and protocols.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
The course relies on GNS3, a network emulation software, to design and configure network topologies of increasing complexity.

See the GNS3 section for details on how to set up your lab environment.

The following tools are required:

  • a GNS3 server: either provisioned in the cloud or installed locally on your machine
  • a GNS3 GUI: a.k.a GNS3 client. It can talk to both local and remote GNS3 servers.
  • Wireshark: a network analysis and debugging tool
  • Python3: for generating lab reports

items.title: README
items.text:
Import these appliances into GNS3.

They are all based on the same Oracle Linux 9 base image, so you only need to download the disk image once.

However, each appliance has its own settings (symbol, interface count, RAM, ...) according to its intended use and capabilities.

  • OL9 PC
  • OL9 Switch
  • OL9 Router
  • OL9 Server
  • OL9 Firewall

items.title: GNS3 Overview
items.text:
GNS3 is a network emulation software used to simulate, design and test network topologies of varying degrees of complexity.

  • It lets you create topologies by dragging different types of devices on a canvas and connecting them with virtual cables.
  • It uses Dynamips to emulate a subset of Cisco devices such as switches and routers
  • It integrates with QEMU (Quick Emulator), allowing you to virtualize your own custom devices such as servers and PCs.
  • It integrates with Wireshark letting you capture and inspect live traffic data moving across your virtual cables
  • You can connect your virtual network topologies to real physical network equipment, enabling you to test your virtual networks under real world conditions.

GNS3 has two parts: a client (the GUI your interact with) and a server responsible for running the simulations. The server can run either on your local machine or on a remote server for enhanced performance.

Recommended

This course recommends running GNS3 on a cloud server for enhanced performance. It is also easier to set up.

If you choose to run it on your machine, ensure you have sufficient memory to spare, and enable nested virtualization

Match versions

The client and server versions must match, otherwise you may experience behaviors that are hard to troubleshoot.

This course uses v2.2.61

On Linux, GNS3 server runs natively on your machine. On Windows and macOS it runs inside a virtual machine called GNS3 VM, which needs a hypervisor to host it. 

Windows11 | macOS
  └── hypervisor (Hyper-V, VMware, or VirtualBox)
        └── GNS3 VM
            └── emulated devices

Not supported on ARM

Apple Silicon and ARM machines cannot run GNS3 server locally. The emulated devices are x86_64 images, and an ARM machine has no way to virtualize them - only slow emulation.

Use the cloud server option if you are on ARM.

Because the emulated devices are virtual machines running inside another virtual machine, the hypervisor must support nested virtualization. Without it, devices still run but performance takes a big hit, which makes multi-device topologies practically unusable.

Note

The cloud server option is not a remote desktop. You still run the GNS3 client on your own machine; only emulated devices run elsewhere.

items.title: 1. Google Cloud account
items.text:
1. Create a Google Cloud account and (optionally) redeem the $300 / 90-day free trial: https://cloud.google.com/free

    $300 credit

    • The 90 days runs from signup, not from first use.
    • Eligibility requires never having had a Google Cloud trial before.

  2. Install the Google Cloud CLI.

  3. Initialize and authorize the gcloud CLI: 
    gcloud init
  4. Create a project if you haven't yet: 
    gcloud projects create acit-2620-lab
    If you would like a human-readable name for your project, do this: 
    gcloud projects update acit-2620-lab --name="ACIT 2620 Networking Lab"

  5. Create a named gcloud configuration and log in: 

    gcloud config configurations create acit-2620 
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project acit-2620-lab
gcloud config set compute/zone us-west1-b

    Configuration bundle

    A configuration bundles account + project + zone under one name, so this won't interfere with any other Google Cloud projects you may have.

    Naming resources

    You don't necessarily have to use the names acit-2620-lab and acit-2620 for your project and configuration respectively. You are free to use any names you like. That being said, it is good engineering practice to choose names that clearly express the purpose of the things being named.

items.title: 2. Install the wrapper
items.text:
This will allow you to easily create, provision and manage a Google Cloud VM with a simple user interface.

The wrapper's primary value proposition lies in provisioning and configuring your cloud GNS3 server, but it has other useful features:

  • it handles configuration for you
  • it lets you turn off you VM when you're not using it, saving you unnecessary costs
  • it makes it easy to refresh you connection when you move into a different network
git clone https://github.com/yveshema/gns3-cloud-lab.git
cd gns3-cloud-lab
python install.py

install.py bootstraps uv automatically if it isn't already on your machine, then installs the gns3-cloud-lab command with five subcommands: scan, create, enroll, start/refresh, upgrade, stop, status. To uninstall later, run python uninstall.py from the same checkout.

If nothing on your machine is already called gclab, install also sets it up as a shorter alias for gns3-cloud-lab — same command, less typing. (If something's already using that name, it's left alone and only the full gns3-cloud-lab command is installed.)

items.title: 3. Create your cloud GNS3 server
items.text:
gns3-cloud-lab create

This creates a firewall rule scoped to your current public IP address and a n2-standard-4 VM (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM) then installs and configures GNS3 on first boot. It takes a few minutes to finish booting and provisioning — gns3-cloud-lab status will show you where it's at. You only need to do this once ; re-running it later is safe and just confirms the VM is already there.

Naming resources

The VM created by gns3-cloud-lab create is named gns3-lab by default. If you would like to name it something different, run it like this: 

gns3-cloud-lab --instance <your_vm_name> create

items.title: 4. Install the GNS3 desktop client
items.text: See Install GNS3 Client

items.title: 5. Start your lab, each session
items.text:
gns3-cloud-lab start

Every time you start, both your VM's address and your own public IP may have changed since last time — this command refreshes both: it starts the VM if it's stopped, updates the firewall rule to allow your current location, and writes the connection details into your GNS3 client config. It prints a summary block with the server IP and other connection details.

items.title: 7. Stop when you're done
items.text:
gns3-cloud-lab stop

Always stop the VM when you're finished for the session. You're only billed for compute time while it's running; the disk keeps a small charge either way (~$3/month), but leaving the VM running unnecessarily will end up costing you more that it should.

items.title: Checking on things
items.text:
gns3-cloud-lab status

Prints whether the VM exists, whether it's running, its current IP, and (if known) your login details — without starting or stopping anything.

items.title: How much will this cost you
items.text:
At roughly $0.20/hour for the VM plus ~$3/month for the disk, a typical term's usage (a few hours a week) comes to well under $50. Your $300 credit will cover most of it. However, the trial period runs out in 90 days - a week or so shy of the term's end. So, expect to cover the remaining balance.

Do this when your trial runs out

  1. Open the Google Cloud Billing Console
  2. Click the billing account dropdown at the top of the page and select Manage billing accounts
  3. Click Create Account near the top left
  4. Enter a name for the account, select your country and currency, and click Continue
  5. Set up your payment method and click Submit and activate billing
  6. Find your new billing account: 
    gcloud billing accounts list
    Copy the ACCOUNT_ID (formatted as XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX) for your new billing account
  7. Link your project to the new billing account: 
    gcloud billing projects link YOUR_PROJECT_ID --billing-account=NEW_BILLING_ACCOUNT_ID

items.title: Install GNS3 client
items.text:
WindowsMacLinux
  • Download installer: GNS3-2.2.61-all-in-one.exe from GNS3 GUI Github repo

  • Run the installer. Choose components:

    • Runtime: GNS3 Desktop

    Attention

    Leave GNS3 VM unchecked

    • Tools: Wireshark, Dynamips, VPCS

    WinPcap compatibility mode

    During Wireshark installatin, accept to install Npcap in WinPcap compatibility mode (this is required by Dynamips emulation functions).

    • Install SuperPuTTY
      • Grab the installer (SuperPuttySetup-1.5.0.0.msi) from the project's Github page
      • Extract the zip file
      • Copy the contents of the folder into GNS3 installation folder, typically found at "C:\Program files\GNS3"
      • configure SuperPuTTy
      • Launch GNS3 client, go to Edit -> Preferences -> General -> Console applications
      • Click Edit
      • Select SuperPutty as your terminal application
  • Download installer: GNS3-2.2.61.dmg
  • Open the downloaded .dmg file and drag the GNS3 icon into your Applications folder
  • Launch and grant permissions

There are many ways to install GNS3 client on Linux, but probably the most straightforward way is to use pipx:

  • check if pipx is installed: pipx --version
  • if not installed, install it like this: 
    python3 -m pip install --user pipx
python3 -m pipx ensurepath
  • install GNS3 client: 
    pipx install "gns3-gui==2.2.61"
pipx inject gns3-gui PyQt6

Self contained

In case you're not familiar with pipx, pipx installs each Python application into its own separate, self-contained space rather than mixing it into one shared pool of packages, so installing or removing one app can't break another app's dependencies or your system's own Python setup — something plain pip install doesn't protect you from.

items.title: Install GNS3 server locally
items.text:
Important

Do this only if you have enough memory to spare. The GNS3 server requires you to dedicate a static amount of memory for its use. Each device (switch, router, vpcs) is an emulated instance with its own full copy of an operating system running in memory. A topology with a doze nodes needs a dozen OS' worth of RAM running simultaneously.

Budget for a minimum of 8GB RAM for GNS3 use.

Nested virtualization

Ensure your system supports nested virtualization, otherwise GNS3 will run painfully slow no matter how much RAM you set aside for its use.

Version compatibility

The client and server must be the same version. This course uses v2.2.61

WindowsMacLinux

Attention

Only Intel Mac is supported

  • Install VMware Fusion
  • Download GNS3 VM: GNS3.VM.VMware.Workstation.2.2.61.zip
  • Extract the zip file
  • Launch VMware Fusion, got to File -> Import then select the GNS3 .ova
  • Install Wireshark. Get the installer
  • Launch GNS3. Go to Edit -> Preferences -> GNS3 VM:
    • Ensure it's enabled
    • Look for RAM input field and type in desired allocation (8192 MB minimum)

Attention

This assumes you've already install the client

  • Install the server: pipx install gns3-server==2.2.61

  • Install ubridge. Required to create raw interfaces GNS3 needs: 

    git clone --depth 1 --branch v1.2.1 https://github.com/GNS3/ubridge.git
make -C ubridge
sudo install -m 755 ubridge/ubridge /usr/local/bin/ubridge
sudo setcap cap_net_admin,cap_net_raw=ep /usr/local/bin/ubridge
    The setcap step is required — without it uBridge can't create the raw interfaces GNS3 needs.

    If it fails

    You may need to install dependencies:

    Ubuntu/DebianFedora/RHEL

    sudo apt install build-essential libpcap-dev git

    sudo dnf groupinstall "Development Tools" && sudo dnf install libpcap-devel git

  • install dynamips:

    Ubuntu/DebianFedora/RHEL

    sudo apt install dynamips

    sudo dnf install dynamips

    Note

    Requires RPM Fusion's nonfree repo

  • Install vpcs: Build from source (v0.6.2). Details at https://github.com/GNS3/vpcs.git

  • Install Wireshark:

    Ubuntu/DebianFedora/RHEL 
    sudo apt get install wireshark
sudo dpkg-reconfigure wireshark-common  # answer "Yes" to non-superuser capture
sudo usermod -aG wireshark $USER

    ``` sudo dnf install wireshark sudo usermod -aG wireshark $USER

items.title: Install the VM
items.text:
• Download installer: GNS3.VM.Hyper-V.2.2.61.zip from GNS3 GUI Github repo
  • Extract the GNS3 VM zip file
  • Open the extract folder, and double-click on the install-vm.bat file. A console window will flash on the screen for a while and close automatically.
  • verify that the GNS3 VM installation completed. Open Hyper-V Manager and you should see it listed under "Virtual Machines".

items.title: Configure the VM
items.text:
• still inside Hyper-V Manager, go to GNS3 VM -> Settings and set Memory to a minimum of 8192 MB
  • Enable nested Virtualization: open a Powershell console as Administrator. Run the following commands one after the other: 
    Stop-VM -Name "GNS3 VM"
Set-VMProcessor -VMName "GNS3 VM" -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true
Set-VMMemory -VMName "GNS3 VM" -DynamicMemoryEnabled $false
Start-VM -Name "GNS3 VM"

Hyper-V conflict with the VM

Hyper-V puts GNS3 VM on a vSwitch so that the controller, which runs locally on the machine can communicate with the VM. The vSwitch owns the 172.16.0.0/12 address space. This is the same address space used by the VM's docker0 interface.

You must move the VM's docker's addressing out of this range to avoid potential conflict:

  • Access the GNS3 VM. Go to Hyper-V Manager and select GNS3 VM. Start it if not running.
    • Go to GNS3 VM -> Connect. This will launch a console window.
    • Press Enter and use your keyboard arrows to select Shell and press Enter
    • You should now have a shell prompt. When you're done, close the console window.

  • Edit /etc/docker/daemon.json:

    First, backup the existing configuration so you can recover it if anything goes wrong:

    sudo cp /etc/docker/daemon.json /etc/docker/daemon.json.bak

    Then, edit the file:

    {
    "data-root": "/opt/docker",
    "bip": "10.199.0.1/24",
    "default-address-pools": [
        { "base": "10.200.0.0/16", "size": 24 }
    ]
}

  • Then restart docker: 

    sudo python3 -m json.tool /etc/docker/daemon.json   # ensure the json is well formed
sudo systemctl restart docker

items.title: Verify setup
items.text:
• Launch GNS3
  • check "Enable the GNS3 VM"
    • Virtualization engine: Hyper-V
    • Action when closing GNS3: stop the GNS3 VM
  • Open a project and drag a few devices and cables onto the canvas

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
You must set up GNS3 before continuing.

Start here

Every activity follows the same structure:

  1. Predict first — written, before anything runs. Put some effort into this, but don't worry about getting it right the first time.
  2. Do this — lab instructions. Complete this, observe, then read the explanation.
  3. What just happened — the explanation.
  4. Record — what goes into the worksheet.
  5. If it went wrong — troubleshooting hints in case anything went wrong.

What matters

The worksheet you submit at the end of each lab session is proof of work (PoW), not proof of correctness (PoC). You won't be penalized for getting your predictions wrong or something breaking in your labs.

However, you should always seek clarification if you don't understand the task your are asked to perform.

items.title: Weekly activities
items.text:
Activity-led replacements for lecture time. Every activity follows the same shape:

  1. Predict first — written, before anything runs. This is the part that does the teaching.
  2. Do this — commands, no explanation.
  3. What just happened — the explanation, after the observation. This is answer-key material.
  4. Record — what lands on the worksheet.
  5. If it went wrong — the three or four failures that actually occur.

items.title: Ordering lives in one place
items.text: Each week's README.md holds the arc and the ordered index. Activity filenames carry no week number — the a1-/a2- prefixes are position within the week, and position changes. Moving an activity between weeks is a mv plus one line in two README.md files.

items.title: Files in a week directory
items.text:
File Audience Notes README.md instructor the arc, the ordered index, what the week assumes aN-*.md student one activity, self-contained, includes "What just happened" worksheet.md student predict → observe → explain, no answers instructor.md instructor timing, what goes wrong, what to say, the gaps topologies/ both exported .gns3project files, made once by the instructor

Distribute aN-*.md + worksheet.md. Keep instructor.md.

The activity files deliberately contain their own answers. Students who read ahead to "What just happened" before predicting are cheating themselves, not the grade — the grade lives in the project. If you want a clean split, the worksheet is the graded surface and the activities are reference.

items.title: The weeks
items.text: Week Directory Subject Cheapest node needed 1 week01-foundations/ what a network is; PDUs, layers, protocols VPCS (OL9 late in the week) 2 week02-devices/ NIC, hub, switch, router, NAT; topologies VPCS + OL9 3 week03-switching/ Ethernet, MAC learning, VLANs, STP OL9 (+ OVS for extensions) 4 week04-static-routing/ IPv4, the network layer, static routes OL9 5 week05-subnetting/ masks, VLSM, boundaries OL9

items.title: Goal
items.text:
• Become familiar with lab environment
  • Understand what makes a network
  • Name the layers of the OSI model
  • Understand what a protocol is

items.title: Deliverable
items.text: worksheet.md, sections 1–6. The PDU table from A2 is the one that matters; it gets referred back to in weeks 3, 4 and 5.

items.title: W1·A1 — Two nodes, one cable
items.text:
Time: 20 min

Needs: 2 VPCS and a cable

GNS3 project: w01-a1-two-nodes

Info

Times listed are approximate and provided as timing guidelines only. Take as much time as you need to complete the activity.

Question

What is a network made of?

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
Write these down before touching GNS3.

  1. Can two computers talk with just a cable running between them?
  2. What other property, if at all, do they require before they can communicate?

items.title: Do this — build it
items.text:
1. File → New blank project, name it w01-a1-two-nodes.
  2. Browse End Devices → drag VPCS onto the canvas twice.
  3. Click Add a link (the cable icon at the bottom of the device panel). Click PC1 → Ethernet0 → click PC2 → Ethernet0. Press Esc to put the cable tool away.
  4. Clidk the green ▶ in the top toolbar to start both.
  5. Right-click each → Console. You should get a PC1> (and PC2>) prompt immediately — no login required.

Congratulations! You've got yourself your first network!

Now, let's see if the two nodes can actually talk.

items.title: Do this — make them talk
items.text:
# on PC1
show ip
ping 192.168.10.100

show ip reports no address. The ping fails. Now:

# on PC1
ip 192.168.10.100/24
show ip

# on PC2
ip 192.168.10.200/24
show ip

# back on PC1
ping 192.168.10.200
save

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The cable was there the whole time and carried nothing. A link is not a network — it is one of the two things a network needs, and the other is addressing.
  • Nothing was configured on the link. Both hosts were configured, independently, and they agreed by accident of you typing compatible numbers. Nobody negotiated anything.
  • show ip also printed a MAC address. That one came with the interface.
    • We will talk about layers in a moment, but the presence of these two addresses is the first hint of that.
  • save writes the config so a stop/start does not lose it.

items.title: Do this — break it without touching the cable
items.text:
Both hosts still cabled, still working. On PC1 only:

ip 192.168.10.100/25
show ip

Still from PC1:

ping 192.168.10.200

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It fails. You didn't take the cable away, and both hosts carry addresses, yet PC2 didn't answer
  • PC1 reports not finding a gateway. Why?
  • /25 is the culprit, which will make sense once we've covered IPv4. For now, interpret it as the two hosts "thinking" they are in two distinct networks, despite still being connected by a cable.

items.title: Do this - capture the conversation
items.text:
• Right-click on the cable and press Start capture
  • Press Ok on the dialog that pops up
  • Run the ping again
  • Does Wireshark show any activity?

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The ping fails again
  • Wireshark doesn't show any activity. PC1 put nothing on the wire
  • Cables don't care about addresses. Hosts do.

Put it back:

# on PC1
ip 192.168.10.100/24
save

items.title: Record
items.text: Variable Observations PC1 IP / MAC PC2 IP / MAC Ping result before addressing Ping result after addressing Ping result with PC1 on /25 Your one-sentence explanation of the /25 failure

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No VPCS under Browse End Devices binary not built or not found GNS3 setup, then Edit → Preferences → VPCS Console window opens blank node not started green ▶ first; VPCS has no boot, so a blank window means it is not running Ping fails after addressing both typo, or addresses in different subnets show ip on both and compare the mask as well as the address Config lost after a restart no save save on each node

items.title: W1·A2 — Client-server vs peer-to-peer
items.text:
Time: 30 min

Needs: three OL9 PC nodes + one Ethernet switch

GNS3 project: w01-a2-roles

Info

Times listed are approximate and provided as timing guidelines only. Take as much time as you need to complete the activity.

Question

Where is the server?

items.title: Import the appliance
items.text:
• Download the OL9 PC appliance
  • In GNS3, go to File -> Import appliance then click through the import wizard.

  • When you reach Required files, click the Download button to download the disk image. This will take a minute.

    Info

    You only need to download the OL9 disk image once. All remaining appliances in this course reference the same disk image.

  • Complete the remaining steps

items.title: Build it
items.text:
• Browse Switches and drag an Ethernet switch on to the canvas
  • Browse End Devices and drag three OL9 PC 1.0 onto the canvas
  • Right-click each PC node, go to Change hostname and rename them to H1, H2, H3 respectively.
  • Run a cable between each host and the switch.
  • Click the green start button to run the topology
  • Click on the console button to bring up a console window for your hosts

Login credentials

Hover each PC to see the login credentials.

All OL9 nodes use the same login credentials.

Log on to H1:

sudo nmcli con mod 'System eth0' con-name eth0
sudo nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.11/24
sudo nmcli con up eth0

Log on to H2 and H3 and do the same. Their addresses are 192.168.10.12/24 and 192.168.10.13/24 respectively.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. In a client-server network of three machines, how many are running server software?
  2. If one machine fails, how many conversations stop?

items.title: Do this — client-server
items.text:
On H1 only:

echo 'the only copy of anything' > /tmp/index.html
cd /tmp && python3 -m http.server 8080 &

Background processes

The & at the end of the previous command is significant. It tells the shell to run the process in the background and give you back the prompt.

Press Enter to get the prompt back.

Run jobs to see what's running in the background. Each running job has a number.

Run fg to bring it in the foreground.

Run Ctrl+Z followed by bg to put it back in the background.

Run kill %<job_id> to stop it. E.g. kill %1

On H2 and H3:

curl http://192.168.10.11:8080/index.html

Run the next command on each of the three nodes:

ss -tln

See any differences?

Socket statistics

The ss command is a Linux command-line utility for monitoring network connections.

-tln means "show me the port numbers (-n) of any listening (-l) tcp (-t) processes on this system".

We will meet it again.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• ss -tln shows H1 listening on 0.0.0.0:8080. H2 and H3 listen for nothing. That asymmetry is the entire definition — one process waits, two initiate.
  • The server is a process, not a box. All three nodes are identical OL9 images with identical hardware. H1 is the server because of one command you ran on it, and it stops being one the moment you press Ctrl-C.

items.title: Do this — kill it
items.text:
On H1: kill %1.

Then on H2 and H3:

curl http://192.168.10.11:8080/index.html

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Both clients dead, simultaneously, from one failure. H2 and H3 are up, cabled, and can still ping each other — but neither is able to get what it wants, which is the web page that is no longer being served by anybody.
  • The dependency is on the role, not the link. Nothing about the network broke.
  • The key idea: Simplicity, but single point of failure

items.title: Do this — peer-to-peer
items.text:
On all three, each hosting its own content:

echo "content from $(hostname)" > /tmp/index.html
cd /tmp && python3 -m http.server 8080 &

# on H1
curl http://192.168.10.12:8080/index.html
curl http://192.168.10.13:8080/index.html

Then check the listeners again on each node:

Now kill the server on H2 and repeat every fetch.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every node listens and every node initiates. There is no structural difference between the machines, which is precisely what "peer" means.
  • Pulling H2 down made its content unavailable, but the rest of the network continued to function. Compare that to the client-server outage, where one failure took out every conversation on the network.
  • Nothing about the topology changed between the two halves of this activity. Same three nodes, same switch, same cables, same addresses. The model is a property of how the software is arranged, not of how the network is wired
  • On the flip side, this is more costly. You have three copies to keep in sync, three machines to secure, three addresses to keep track of.
  • The key idea: flexibility, but distribution burden.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Worksheet section 22:

Client-server Peer-to-peer Nodes with a listening socket Conversations lost when H1 fails Conversations lost when H2 fails

Plus one sentence: what command would you run on an unknown machine to decide whether it is acting as a server?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Connection failed but the server is running typo in either IP or port check any typos and rerun curl

items.title: W1·A3 — Where are the layers
items.text:
Time: 30 min

Needs: A2's topology

GNS3 project: w01-a2-roles (continue in it)

Info

Times listed are approximate and provided as timing guidelines only. Take as much time as you need to complete the activity.

Question

What does the OSI model tell us about how networks work?

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
How many different kinds of metadata does a request need to carry to retrieve a web page?

Can you name them?

items.title: Do this — capture one ping
items.text:
1. Start the web server on H1 (see previous activity if you don't remember how)

  2. Right-click the H2 link → Start capture. Wireshark opens on that link and starts empty.

  3. On H2:

    curl http://192.168.10.11:8080/index.html

  4. Read Wireshark. Select one packet and look at the details pane. Each row is a layer. How many rows are there?

  5. Click each layer (ignoring Frame, which is Wireshark's own metadata, not bytes on the wire) and watch the bottom pane highlight the bytes it owns.
  6. Watch carefully the status bar at the bottom of the screen. It shows the number of bytes the selected layer contains.
  7. Select one HTTP packet, click each layer in turn and write down the number of bytes in each layer.
  8. Expand each row and scan the contents.

items.title: What just happened?
items.text:
• By capturing on H2 cable, you were able to see the entire conversation between H1 and H2.

  • The messages were broken down into chunks called datagrams.

    The process of breaking down a message into datagrams is called fragmentation and is the job of the Transport layer.

  • Wireshark fills up with packets that make up that conversation. You can select each packet and examine it in detail.

  • Each packet is a nested structure of headers. Each header implements one of the layers in the OSI model

    We call this encapsulation

  • Each layer carries its own addresses, in its own format, and neither layer can read the other's. H1's MAC and H1's IP both identify H1 and have nothing to do with each other.

  • Look at the byte count in the packet. It's mostly headers.

items.title: Fill this in
items.text:
Select one HTTP packet and fill in this table with the details.

Ask if there is a term you don't understand.

Wireshark says Layer # Layer name PDU name Addresses at this layer Bytes Ethernet II 2 Data link frame src MAC, dst MAC 14 Internet Protocol Version 4 3 Transmission Control Protocol Hypertext Transfer Protocol Data — — — —

items.title: Record
items.text: Worksheet section 3: the completed PDU table

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Start capture greyed out or "wireshark not on path" Wireshark not on the client Install Wireshark Wireshark opens and stays empty capture started after the request start the capture first

items.title: W1·A4 — Speak a protocol by hand
items.text:
Time: 30 min

Needs: A2 topology

GNS3 project: w01-a2-roles (reuse it)

Info

Times listed are approximate and provided as timing guidelines only. Take as much time as you need to complete the activity.

Question

"protocol" is defined as "a set of rules for communications".

Who defines these rules?

How are these rules enforced?

What happens when you break the rules?

items.title: Predict first
items.text: If you have a typo in a URL, who notices - the server, your machine, both, or neither?

items.title: Do this — invent a protocol
items.text:
On H2:

nc -l -p 9000

On H1:

nc 192.168.10.12 9000

Type on either side and press enter. Then Ctrl-C both.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two processes exchanged bytes over a network with no protocol at all beyond "whatever you typed". It worked because neither end expected anything.
  • The number after the IP is called a port number. It's how the OS knows where to deliver the message.

Info

nc is a Linux utility for manipulating arbitrary connections. It is not a protocol itself.

items.title: Do this — speak HTTP correctly
items.text:
Start the web server on H1 if you stopped it previously:

cd /tmp && python3 -m http.server 8080

On H2, be the browser yourself:

nc 192.168.10.11 8080

Then type these three lines exactly — including the empty line at the end:

GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.10.11

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• A status line, some headers, a blank line, then a line of plain text. This is what a web browser does.
  • The blank line is a protocol element, not formatting. It means "headers finished, stop reading". Without it the server waits forever, because it has no other way to know you are done.
  • The nice thing about this is that it's all natural text understandable to humans. Protocols don't need to be complex or highly technical, although some are. Many protocols such as HTTP and ARP sound almost like human conversation.

items.title: Do this — break it on purpose
items.text:
Reconnect with nc each time. Try these one at a time and record the exact response:

Attempt What you send Exact server response 1 GET /index.html HTTP/1.1 + blank line, no Host: header 2 GET /nonexistent.html HTTP/1.1 + Host: + blank line 3 GIT /index.html HTTP/1.1 + Host: + blank line 4 GET /index.html + blank line (no version)

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Different failures, each with a specific reason.

  • The client was fine with whatever you typed. It forwarded GIT as willingly as GET. TCP delivered the bytes correctly and the bytes were nonsense — correct delivery of garbage is still correct delivery.

    This is an important insight. None of the layers below the Application layer were aware that anything went wrong. Only HTTP did. Each layer keeps only its own promises.

  • A protocol is therefore not "rules the network enforces". It is an agreement between the two endpoints, enforced by the endpoints, invisible to everything in between.

items.title: Record
items.text: Worksheet section 4: the exact server response to each of the four attempts, and one sentence naming who detected the error in attempt 3 and who did not.

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Server prints a request line then nothing happens you did not send the blank line press enter twice Connection refused server not running, or wrong port check the python3 -m http.server window is still open Reply is 501 Unsupported method rather than 400 Python's server classifies it that way record what you actually got — the point is that it refused

items.title: Week 2 — Devices and topologies
items.text:
Assumes: week 1. Students can address a node, read a capture, and name the layer a header belongs to. OL9 is installed.

Leaves students able to: state what makes a device a hub, a switch or a router, and prove it by measurement rather than by picture; explain NAT's asymmetry; describe a topology by its failure modes.

items.title: The arc
items.text:
Week 1 established that layers are real. This week asks: if the layers are real, what does a device do with each one? The answer is arranged as a ladder — a hub ignores every layer, a switch reads layer 2, a router reads layer 3, a NAT router rewrites it. Each rung is one activity and one measurement.

The centrepiece is A2, where the same node is turned from a switch into a router by configuration alone. Nothing sells "layer" like watching one box change which one it operates at.

# Activity Time Needs A1 Hub vs switch ★ 35 min 4 VPCS + hub + switch + Wireshark A2 One box, two devices ★ 50 min 1 OL9 (4 NICs) + 4 VPCS A3 The NIC owns the address 25 min 2 OL9 A4 NAT from both sides 45 min 3 OL9 A5 Topology as failure modes 40 min 4 VPCS + hub + switch A6 Sharing one wire 35 min 3 OL9

★ = keep these if the week compresses.

items.title: Sequencing note
items.text:
A1 before A2. A1 establishes what a switch does by watching it from outside; A2 then builds one and takes it apart. Reversed, A2 is just a configuration exercise.

A6 carries packet-vs-circuit switching, which the original week-1 syllabus covered as vocabulary. It is here because this is the first week with a link worth sharing.

items.title: Deliverable
items.text: worksheet.md, sections 1–6. Section 2's device-comparison table is the one students should keep; week 4 fills in the routing column properly.

items.title: The two gaps, stated plainly
items.text:
GNS3 has no physical layer. It does not model cable types, cable length, attenuation, or collisions. It will happily "connect" anything to anything.

Topic GNS3 What to do Straight-through vs crossover absent Packet Tracer models it and refuses the wrong cable; or crimp real cable in the room Auto-MDI-X absent discuss only — it is why the previous row stopped mattering after ~2000 Collisions, CSMA/CD absent week 3's unplugged activity, or Packet Tracer's animation Wi-Fi absent entirely Packet Tracer, or real hardware. This is the one unclosable gap

Tell students the simulator's limits while they are using it. A student who believes GNS3 models physics will be badly wrong later, and the honesty costs nothing.

items.title: W2·A1 — Hub vs switch ★
items.text:
Time: 35 min · Needs: 4 VPCS, an Ethernet hub, an Ethernet switch (both need dynamips, §0a), Wireshark on the client · GNS3 project: w02-a1-hub-vs-switch

The question: a hub and a switch have the same shape, the same ports and the same cables. What is actually different?

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Four VPCS on one Ethernet switch (Browse Switches), PC1…PC4 on ports Ethernet0…3.

# PC1 / PC2 / PC3 / PC4
ip 192.168.10.11/24        # .12 / .13 / .14
save

One subnet, no gateway, no router, and no configuration on the switch at all. Confirm PC1 can ping all three others.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
PC1 pings PC2. You are watching PC3's cable, and PC3 is not involved in any way.

  1. How many of the four packets appear on PC3's cable? _
  2. Same question, with a hub in place of the switch. _

Write both numbers down now.

items.title: Do this — the switch, watched from a bystander
items.text:
1. Right-click the PC3↔SW1 link → Start capture.
  2. On every PC: clear arp
  3. On PC1: ping 192.168.10.12
  4. Read Wireshark. Then run the ping again and read it again.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC3's cable carried the ARP request only — destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. Nobody knows where PC2 is yet, so the question goes to everybody.
  • It did not carry the ARP reply, and did not carry either ICMP packet. Those are addressed to a specific MAC, and by then the switch knew which port that MAC was behind.
  • The second ping put nothing at all on PC3's cable. The ARP caches were warm, so not even the broadcast was needed.
  • That contrast — broadcast arrives, unicast does not — is the entire behaviour of a switch, measured from a machine that is not in the conversation.

items.title: Do this — the hub, same everything else
items.text:
1. Delete SW1. Browse Switches → place an Ethernet hub where it was. Re-cable PC1…PC4.
  2. Repeat exactly: capture on PC3's link, clear arp everywhere, ping 192.168.10.12 from PC1, twice.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC3's cable carried everything: both ARP frames, and every echo request and reply between PC1 and PC2. The second ping was just as loud as the first.
  • No learning, no table, no filtering. A hub is an electrical repeater — a signal arriving on one port is regenerated out of every other port, and it has no idea what a MAC address is.
  • So every port is one collision domain: only one host can usefully talk at a time, and the wire's capacity is shared by everyone rather than given to each pair.
  • PC3 received traffic addressed to somebody else, in full. On a hub, every machine can read every conversation. This is not a security weakness in some deployments of hubs; it is what a hub is.

This is real. Those frames genuinely arrived on PC3's wire. Nothing was animated for you.

items.title: Do this — where the switch keeps what it knows
items.text: Put the switch back. Then right-click SW1 → Configure.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• There is nothing to see. Per-port VLAN settings and nothing else — no MAC table, no CLI, no console.
  • Every observation you just made had to be taken from outside the device, because GNS3's Ethernet switch offers no way in. That is a limitation of this switch, not of switches.
  • Week 3 replaces it with a Linux bridge, where the table you have been inferring can be printed, flushed and watched refilling.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Switch, 1st ping Switch, 2nd ping Hub, 1st ping Hub, 2nd ping ARP request on PC3's wire ARP reply on PC3's wire ICMP request on PC3's wire ICMP reply on PC3's wire

One sentence: what does the switch know after the first ping that it did not know before?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix "Could not find Dynamips" both hub and switch are dynamips devices §0a. This is the most common week-2 blocker No packets at all on PC3's link capture started after the ping it is live, not retrospective — start it first Switch behaves like the hub you re-cabled to a hub and forgot check the icon; hub and switch icons differ ARP never reappears caches stayed warm clear arp on every node, not just PC1 VPCS ping rejects your flags build differences plain ping 192.168.10.12 works on every build

items.title: W2·A2 — One box, two devices ★
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: one OL9 Lab Node with 4 adapters, 4 VPCS · GNS3 project: w02-a2-one-box

The question: what makes a device a switch rather than a router? Buy the wrong answer and every later week gets harder.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
1. Drag out one OL9 Lab Node, name it BOX. Right-click → Configure → Network → Adapters = 4.
  2. Four VPCS, PC1…PC4, cabled to BOX's Ethernet0…Ethernet3.
  3. Start everything. Console into BOX as root.
# on BOX — before anything else
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done
ip link show

On a QEMU node, GNS3's EthernetN is the guest's ethN, because the lab image boots with net.ifnames=0 biosdevname=0. On a marketplace appliance you would have to map them yourself.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
You have one physical box with four network ports.

  1. Can it be a switch? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. Can it be a router? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. Can it be both, one after the other, without rebooting or rewiring? ☐ yes ☐ no

items.title: Part 1 — Make it a switch
items.text:
# on BOX
ip link add name br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up

for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do
    ip addr flush dev $i
    ip link set $i master br0
    ip link set $i up
done

bridge link
ip -d link show br0

All four PCs in one subnet, no gateway:

# PC1 / PC2 / PC3 / PC4
ip 192.168.10.11/24        # .12 / .13 / .14

From PC1: ping .12, .13, .14. All three work.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• br0 has no IP address, and that is correct. This node is not a host on the segment; it is the segment.
  • The four interfaces were stripped of addresses on purpose. A port carrying an IP is a router leg, not a bridge port — that distinction is the whole activity.
  • The PCs share one subnet and need no gateway, because as far as they are concerned they are all on one wire. BOX is invisible to them. Nothing in any PC's configuration mentions it.
  • What did the work: the bridge, reading layer 2 only, forwarding on MAC addresses it learned by watching. It never looked at an IP header.

items.title: Part 2 — Make the same box a router
items.text:
Tear the switch down and build a router on the same hardware, same cables, same session:

# on BOX
ip link del br0                       # the switch is gone

ip addr add 192.168.1.1/24  dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.2.1/24  dev eth1
ip addr add 192.168.3.1/24  dev eth2
ip addr add 192.168.4.1/24  dev eth3
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do ip link set $i up; done

sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

ip addr show
ip route show

Now re-address the PCs — four subnets, and each one needs a gateway:

# PC1
ip 192.168.1.10/24 192.168.1.1
# PC2
ip 192.168.2.10/24 192.168.2.1
# PC3
ip 192.168.3.10/24 192.168.3.1
# PC4
ip 192.168.4.10/24 192.168.4.1

From PC1: ping 192.168.2.10, then 192.168.3.10, then 192.168.4.10.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The same box, the same cables, no reboot — and it is now a router. Nothing physical changed. What changed is which layer's addresses it reads and what it does with them.
  • ip route show filled itself in with four connected routes you never typed. Putting an address on an interface is an implicit claim that the subnet is out that port, and the kernel records it.
  • ip_forward=1 was the switch that made it a router at all. Without it, BOX has four addresses and forwards nothing — it is a host with four legs.
  • The PCs' configuration had to change too. They now need a gateway, because "not my subnet" is now a real category and somebody has to be asked. On the bridge, that category was empty.

items.title: Part 3 — Prove which layer each one used
items.text:
# on PC1, after pinging PC2 across the router
show arp

Compare with the Part 1 result, where PC1 had pinged PC2 through the bridge.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Through the bridge, PC1's ARP cache held PC2's MAC. PC1 addressed PC2 directly at layer 2; the bridge just moved the frame.
  • Through the router, PC1's ARP cache holds BOX's MAC, and PC2's does not appear at all. PC1 has never learned PC2's MAC and never will — it cannot, and does not need to.
  • So the frame PC1 sent was addressed to the router at layer 2 and to PC2 at layer 3, at the same time, in the same frame. The router rewrote the layer-2 addressing and left the layer-3 addressing alone.
  • That single observation is the most load-bearing fact in weeks 3, 4 and 5. Write it down properly.

items.title: Record
items.text:
As a bridge As a router IP addresses on BOX Subnets in use PCs need a gateway? Entries in ip route show MAC in PC1's ARP cache after pinging PC2 Layer it forwards on

One sentence: what, exactly, is the difference between a switch and a router?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Only eth0 exists adapters not set right-click → Configure → Network → Adapters = 4, then restart the node Addresses vanish after seconds NetworkManager nmcli device set ethN managed no on all four, first Bridge built, pings fail br_netfilter handing bridged frames to iptables sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0 Router built, pings fail forwarding off, or PCs have no gateway sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward; show ip on each PC and check the gateway column Router pings fail only between some pairs firewalld systemctl stop firewalld for this activity ip link del br0 refuses typo in the name ip link show type bridge to find it

items.title: Sidebar — the nmcli form
items.text:
Your course persists interfaces with nmcli. Same kernel objects, written to disk:

# the bridge
nmcli con add type bridge ifname br0 con-name br0 ipv4.method disabled ipv6.method disabled
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth0 master br0
nmcli con up br0

# the router leg
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name eth0 ipv4.method manual \
      ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.1/24
nmcli con up eth0

The ip forms above are for exploring, because they vanish on reboot and let you undo a mistake by restarting the node. Use nmcli when you want it to survive — which is what the project expects.

items.title: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address
items.text:
Time: 25 min · Needs: two OL9 Lab Nodes on a switch · GNS3 project: w02-a3-nic

The question: where does a MAC address live, and who decides what it is?
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Build it
items.text: H1 and H2, OL9, on an Ethernet switch. 192.168.10.11/24 and .12/24, nmcli device set eth0 managed no first on both. Confirm they ping.
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Where is your MAC address stored? ☐ the OS ☐ the network card ☐ the switch ☐ a server
  2. Can you change it? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. If you did, who would need to find out, and how would they?
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Do this — read it
items.text:
# on H1 and H2
ip link show eth0

Take the first three bytes of each MAC — the OUI, the Organisationally Unique Identifier — and look them up (ieee.org's OUI listing, or Wireshark's own resolution in the packet list).
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The address was there before you configured anything, and you never chose it. Compare with the IP address, which did not exist until you typed it in week 1.
  • The OUI identifies the manufacturer, and the remaining three bytes are that manufacturer's serial number for the adapter. The address is globally unique by administrative agreement, not by any technical mechanism — vendors buy OUIs and promise not to reuse the tail.
  • Your OUI will resolve to a virtualisation vendor, not a card maker, because these NICs are emulated. That is honest and worth noticing: the "hardware" address of a virtual machine is assigned by software, which is a hint about how firm any of this really is.
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Do this — change it
items.text:
Start a capture on H1's link. On H2, note the current state:

# on H2
ping -c1 192.168.10.11
ip neigh show

H2 now holds H1's MAC. On H1:

ip link set eth0 down
ip link set eth0 address 02:11:22:33:44:55
ip link set eth0 up
ip link show eth0

Back on H2, immediately:

ip neigh show
ping -c1 192.168.10.11
ip neigh show
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The address changed, in software, in one command. "Burned-in" has not been literally true for a long time — the card holds a default and the OS may override it.
  • H2's first ip neigh show still listed the old MAC, marked REACHABLE or STALE. H2 had no way to be told; nobody announces a MAC change.
  • The ping still worked, and the capture shows why: H2 sent to the stale address, got nothing, the entry aged into FAILED, and H2 re-ARPed. The cache is self-correcting, but only by timing out — there is a window during which H2 is confidently wrong.
  • 02: is not in any OUI database. The second-least-significant bit of the first byte is the locally administered flag, and setting it is how you say "I made this up, do not look for a vendor". Check your own: 02 = 0000 0010.
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Do this — see it from the switch's side
items.text: If A1's topology is still around, put H1 and H2 on the Ethernet switch with two VPCS bystanders, capture on a bystander's link, and change H1's MAC again while pinging.
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The switch had learned the old MAC on H1's port and has no idea it is gone. Frames for the old address keep going to that port until the entry ages out — 300 seconds by default.
  • The new address is learned the instant H1 transmits, because switches learn from source addresses on arriving frames. The switch was never told anything; it overheard.
  • Week 3 prints that table and watches this happen line by line.
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: Record
items.text: Value H1 original MAC / resolved vendor H2 original MAC / resolved vendor H1 new MAC H2's ip neigh immediately after the change H2's ip neigh after the next ping Is 02:11:22:33:44:55 locally administered? How can you tell?
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix RTNETLINK: Device or resource busy interface still up ip link set eth0 down first Cannot assign requested address odd first byte = multicast bit set first byte must be even; 02 is the conventional choice Ping fails and stays failed switch's table still holds the old address wait for ageing, or ping from H1 once to teach it immediately MAC reverts after a reboot you used ip, which does not persist nmcli con modify eth0 802-3-ethernet.cloned-mac-address 02:11:22:33:44:55 ip neigh never shows the stale entry you looked too late run it immediately; the window is short
path: W2·A3 — The NIC owns the address

items.title: W2·A4 — NAT from both sides
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: three OL9 Lab Nodes (the router needs 2 adapters), Wireshark · GNS3 project: w02-a4-nat

The question: the router at home has one public address and a dozen devices behind it. Which address does the internet see, and why can nothing on the internet start a conversation with your laptop?

items.title: Build it
items.text:
inside 192.168.10.0/24                 outside 203.0.113.0/24

   INSIDE ────────── eth0  NATRTR  eth1 ────────── OUTSIDE
   .11                .1            203.0.113.1     203.0.113.5

NATRTR needs Adapters = 2. On all three nodes, nmcli device set ethN managed no first.

# NATRTR
ip addr add 192.168.10.1/24  dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 203.0.113.1/24   dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# INSIDE
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.10.1

# OUTSIDE
ip addr add 203.0.113.5/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up

Deliberately do not give OUTSIDE a route back to 192.168.10.0/24. That omission is the experiment.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. INSIDE pings OUTSIDE. Does it work, given OUTSIDE has no route back? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. Now turn NAT on. Same question. ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. OUTSIDE tries to ping INSIDE. Does that work? ☐ yes ☐ no

items.title: Do this — without NAT
items.text:
Capture on both links at once — INSIDE↔NATRTR and NATRTR↔OUTSIDE. Then:

# on INSIDE
ping -c2 203.0.113.5

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• No replies. Both captures explain it together: the echo request appears on both links, so the router forwarded it correctly and OUTSIDE received it. OUTSIDE generated a reply to 192.168.10.11, consulted its routing table, found nothing, and dropped it.
  • The failure is one-directional and invisible from the sender. INSIDE sees silence and cannot distinguish "not delivered" from "no route home". Two captures can; one cannot.
  • Remember this shape. Week 4's headline activity is the same failure on a bigger topology.

items.title: Do this — turn NAT on
items.text:
# on NATRTR
nft add table ip nat
nft 'add chain ip nat postrouting { type nat hook postrouting priority 100 ; }'
nft add rule ip nat postrouting oifname "eth1" masquerade

nft list ruleset

Both captures still running. On INSIDE:

ping -c2 203.0.113.5

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It works now, and OUTSIDE still has no route to 192.168.10.0/24. Nothing was added to OUTSIDE.
  • Compare the two captures for the same ping:
inside link outside link source 192.168.10.11 203.0.113.1 destination 203.0.113.5 203.0.113.5
  • The router rewrote the source address in the IP header on the way out and restored it on the way back. OUTSIDE never learned that INSIDE exists; it held a conversation with the router.
  • This is a layer-3 device editing a layer-3 header — genuinely different from anything in A1 or A2, both of which forwarded packets unaltered. The end-to-end principle, that addresses mean the same thing everywhere, has just been broken on purpose.

items.title: Do this — read the translation table
items.text:
# on NATRTR, immediately after a ping
grep -c . /proc/net/nf_conntrack
cat /proc/net/nf_conntrack

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• One line per conversation, recording both the original and the translated addressing. The router must remember, because a reply arriving for 203.0.113.1 is meaningless unless it can be matched back to 192.168.10.11.
  • So NAT is stateful, and a hub, a switch and a plain router are not. This box now has a memory that fills up, times out, and can be exhausted.
  • Entries have a timeout. Wait, re-run, and watch them disappear.

items.title: Do this — try to get in
items.text:
# on OUTSIDE
ping -c2 192.168.10.11

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It fails, and it cannot be made to work by adding a route — try it: ip route add 192.168.10.0/24 via 203.0.113.1 on OUTSIDE and ping again. Still nothing useful, and the conntrack table is why. There is no entry, so the router has no idea which inside host a packet for 203.0.113.1 belongs to.
  • NAT is asymmetric by construction. Outbound creates state; inbound requires state that only outbound can create.
  • That asymmetry is why NAT is so often mistaken for a firewall. It is not one — it blocks unsolicited inbound traffic as a side effect of not knowing where to send it, which is a very different thing from a policy decision, and it is exactly the misunderstanding this activity exists to prevent.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Without NAT With NAT Src address on the inside link Src address on the outside link Ping INSIDE → OUTSIDE Ping OUTSIDE → INSIDE Rows in /proc/net/nf_conntrack

One sentence: why can OUTSIDE not reach INSIDE even after you add a route?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix nft syntax error on the chain line shell ate the ; keep the single quotes exactly as written Nothing changes after the rule forwarding off sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward must be 1 /proc/net/nf_conntrack missing module not loaded yet it loads with the first NAT rule; send a ping first Works even before NAT you gave OUTSIDE a return route remove it; the missing route is the point Both captures look identical you captured the same link twice check the link names in the Wireshark title bars

items.title: Sidebar — the iptables form
items.text:
Older material and much of the internet writes this rule as:

iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth1 -j MASQUERADE

On OL9 that command is a compatibility front-end that programs the same nftables engine. Both work; nft is what the system actually runs.

items.title: W2·A5 — Topology as failure modes
items.text:
Time: 40 min · Needs: 4 VPCS, an Ethernet hub, two Ethernet switches, Wireshark · GNS3 project: w02-a5-topology

The question: topologies are taught as shapes to memorise. Shapes are not the point — what breaks, and what everyone can overhear, are the point.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
For each of the three builds below, predict before building:

Frames a bystander sees Hosts lost if the centre fails Hosts lost if one edge cable fails Bus (hub) Star (switch) Star with a redundant link

items.title: Build 1 — Bus, approximated by a hub
items.text:
Four VPCS on an Ethernet hub, 192.168.10.11….14/24.

# on each PC
ip 192.168.10.11/24

Capture on PC3's link. From PC1: ping 192.168.10.12. Then delete the PC4↔hub cable and re-test PC1↔PC2. Then stop the hub itself.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every frame reached every host. One shared medium, one collision domain, and no privacy between stations.
  • Losing one edge cable cost exactly one host. Losing the hub cost all four.
  • A real bus was worse than this: one cable with taps, where a single break severed the segment into two halves that could not hear each other. The hub is a bus with the failure mode improved and the overhearing intact.

items.title: Build 2 — Star, with a switch
items.text: Replace the hub with an Ethernet switch. Same addressing. Repeat all three tests.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• A bystander sees broadcasts only — A1's result, arrived at from a different direction.
  • Edge-cable failure: still one host, same as the bus.
  • Centre failure: still everything. The star did not fix that, and this is the honest finding. A star is not more resilient than a bus; it is more private and it isolates collisions. Those are real gains and they are not this one.
  • The redundancy question is therefore still open, which is what Build 3 is for.

items.title: Build 3 — Add a redundant link
items.text:
1. Add a second Ethernet switch SW2. Move PC3 and PC4 to it.
  2. Link SW1↔SW2. Confirm all four PCs ping each other.
  3. Now add a second link between SW1 and SW2, for redundancy.
  4. Ping PC1 → PC3 again. Watch the GNS3 link indicators and any capture you have running.

Stop this one quickly. Delete the second inter-switch link as soon as you have seen the effect. It will not damage anything, but it will make the topology unusable and can load your machine.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The network collapsed. One broadcast entered the loop, was flooded by both switches to each other, was flooded again, and multiplied without limit. A capture fills faster than it can be read.
  • Nothing decremented anything. There is no TTL in an Ethernet frame — that field exists at layer 3, and week 1's teardown showed you exactly where. A looping frame at layer 2 has nothing to stop it.
  • So redundancy at layer 2 is not free and not additive. Adding a cable made the network worse than having no redundancy at all.
  • The fix has a name and a whole activity in week 3: spanning tree, a protocol whose entire job is to find loops and switch them off, keeping them available for the day a link dies.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Complete the prediction table with observations, then:

Bus (hub) Star (switch) Star + redundant link Cables for 4 hosts Collision domains Bystander sees Centre fails One edge cable fails Behaviour as built

Two sentences: which topology would you deploy, and what would you have to add first?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Build 3 does not collapse second link not actually up check both links are solid green; GNS3 draws pending links differently GNS3 becomes unresponsive during Build 3 the loop is doing its job delete a link; if the GUI will not respond, stop the nodes from the toolbar Cannot delete a link cable tool still armed press Esc, then right-click the link → Delete Pings fail in Build 3 even after removing the loop switch tables are scrambled stop and start both switches No difference between hub and switch results one of them is not the device you think check the icons

items.title: W2·A6 — Sharing one wire
items.text:
Time: 35 min · Needs: three OL9 Lab Nodes + an Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: w02-a6-sharing

The question: two conversations, one wire. Packet switching and circuit switching are two answers to that, and they are usually taught as history. Here they are two tc commands, and you can measure the difference.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
H1 .11, H2 .12, SRV .13, all /24, all on one Ethernet switch, nmcli device set eth0 managed no first on each.

On SRV, something worth downloading:

dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/big.bin bs=1M count=50
cd /tmp && python3 -m http.server 8080

SRV's single cable is the shared wire. Everything below happens on it.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
The wire runs at 10 Mbit/s. H1 starts a download. Halfway through, H2 starts one too.

  1. What happens to H1's download? ☐ stops ☐ slows ☐ unaffected
  2. What does H2 get? ☐ nothing until H1 finishes ☐ half ☐ full speed
  3. If H2 never starts, should H1 get the whole 10 Mbit/s? ☐ obviously ☐ not necessarily

items.title: Do this — cap the shared wire
items.text:
On SRV, in a second console:

tc qdisc add dev eth0 root tbf rate 10mbit burst 32kbit latency 400ms
tc qdisc show dev eth0

Now, one flow at a time. On H1:

curl -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.13:8080/big.bin

Record the average speed curl prints. Then run it on H1 and H2 simultaneously — count down out loud, or paste both commands and press enter together — and record both.

H1 speed H2 speed Sum H1 alone — H2 alone — Both at once

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Both downloads ran at once, and each got roughly half. Neither waited for the other, neither was refused, and the sum stayed at the link's capacity.
  • Nothing negotiated that split. The two flows' packets simply interleaved on the wire, each one independently addressed and independently forwarded. Capture the link and you will see frames from both conversations alternating with no pattern and no reservation.
  • That is packet switching. The wire is shared per-packet, allocation is emergent, and nobody asked permission. Its virtue is that H1 alone got the whole link — no capacity was set aside for a conversation that was not happening.
  • Its cost is that neither flow got a promise. Add ten more hosts and everyone's speed falls; nothing breaks, everything degrades. That trade is the whole design.

items.title: Do this — reserve capacity instead
items.text:
Replace the shared cap with a reservation per host — half the link each, and a hard ceiling so neither can borrow from the other:

# on SRV
tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 30
tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:  classid 1:1  htb rate 10mbit ceil 10mbit
tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:10 htb rate 5mbit  ceil 5mbit
tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:20 htb rate 5mbit  ceil 5mbit
tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:30 htb rate 1mbit  ceil 1mbit

tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1: prio 1 u32 \
   match ip dst 192.168.10.11/32 flowid 1:10
tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1: prio 1 u32 \
   match ip dst 192.168.10.12/32 flowid 1:20

tc -s class show dev eth0

Repeat all three measurements.

H1 speed H2 speed Sum H1 alone — H2 alone — Both at once

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• H1 alone now gets 5 Mbit/s, not 10. Half the wire sat idle, reserved for a conversation that did not exist. Nothing was broken; the capacity was simply not available to anyone else.
  • With both running, each still got 5 — exactly what each got alone. The arrival of a second flow changed nothing for the first.
  • That is circuit switching's bargain: capacity is allocated in advance, so performance is predictable and unaffected by other traffic — and unused capacity is wasted rather than shared.
  • The telephone network worked this way for a century, and its failure mode is the one you have met: not a slow call, but no dial tone. When the circuits are gone they are gone, however idle they are.

items.title: The comparison
items.text:
Packet switched (tbf) Circuit switched (htb with ceilings) One flow, half the link idle uses it all wastes it Second flow arrives first flow slows first flow unaffected Guarantee offered none exact Failure mode under load everything degrades new conversations refused Who decides the split nobody whoever wrote the config

Neither is correct. The internet chose the left-hand column because most traffic is bursty and idle reservations are ruinously expensive at scale — and it has been reinventing the right-hand column ever since, under names like QoS, DiffServ and traffic shaping, whenever something needed a promise.

items.title: Record
items.text: Both measurement tables, the comparison filled in, and one sentence: your video call and your backup upload share one link. Which column do you want, and for which of the two?

items.title: Clean up
items.text: tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Speeds nowhere near 10 Mbit/s virtual links are fast; tbf burst too small raise burst to 64kbit; the ratio between rows matters, not the absolute number Both flows get the full rate you shaped the wrong direction tc shapes egress; the download leaves SRV, so it must be on SRV's eth0 Reserved test behaves like the shared one filters not matching tc -s class show dev eth0 — the class counters must be non-zero Simultaneity is hard to arrange human reaction time run the longer transfer first (count=200) so overlap is easy

items.title: Shape of the week
items.text:
Session Do Note 1 A1, A3 A1 is the week's anchor; A3 is short and fills the rest 2 A2 needs the full session; it is the hardest and most valuable 3 A4, then A5 or A6 A5 sets up week 3; A6 closes the packet-vs-circuit topic

Compressed to one session: A1 then A2, nothing else.

items.title: RAM budget
items.text:
This is the first week that can exhaust a student laptop. The OL9 template asks for 1 GB per node.

Activity OL9 nodes Approx. RAM A1 0 negligible A2 1 1 GB A3 2 2 GB A4 3 3 GB A5 0 negligible A6 3 3 GB

Students on 8 GB machines running the GNS3 VM (which itself wants 8 GB pinned — Appendix A4) will not fit A4 or A6. Have them stop the previous activity's nodes, and consider running A4 and A6 as demonstrations rather than individual builds if the room's hardware is thin. Note that A1 and A5, the two most important activities, cost nothing.

items.title: What actually goes wrong
items.text:
• A1: "Could not find Dynamips." The hub and switch are dynamips devices, and this stops the activity dead. It should have been fixed in week 1 §0a; check before the session.
  • A2: interfaces losing their addresses. Every OL9 activity from here to the end of term needs nmcli device set ethN managed no first. Students will forget. Put it on the board.
  • A2 part 3 is the payload of the whole week and it is one command (show arp on PC1). Do not let students skip it because it looks small. If they leave with one fact, this is the fact.
  • A4: firewalld. Pings across the router may be dropped. systemctl stop firewalld on the router. This will recur all term; consider disabling it in the image and telling students you did.
  • A5 Build 3 will lock up a slow machine. Warn first, and tell them how to stop the nodes from the toolbar before they build it. Nothing is damaged, but a student who cannot get control back panics.
  • A6's absolute speeds will be nonsense on fast hosts. Redirect attention to the ratio between rows. If tbf shapes unconvincingly, raise burst.

items.title: Things to say out loud
items.text:
• After A1's hub run: "Every machine on that hub read a conversation it was not part of. That was normal office networking until about 1998."
  • After A2: "Nothing on that box changed except which header it read. Hold on to that when someone tells you a router is a kind of computer — every one of these is a kind of computer."
  • After A4: "NAT is not protecting you. It is failing to know where to send things, and you are benefiting from its confusion."
  • After A5 Build 3: "You have just built the problem that the whole of next week's spanning tree exists to solve. Do not let anyone tell you STP is theoretical."

items.title: The gaps, and how to be honest about them
items.text:
GNS3 models no physical layer at all. Say so explicitly rather than letting students infer that cables are fungible in reality.

Topic Handling Straight-through vs crossover Packet Tracer refuses the wrong cable and is genuinely better here. A 10-minute PT demo covers it Auto-MDI-X discussion only; it is why the previous row stopped mattering Collisions / CSMA/CD week 3's unplugged activity. GNS3's hub does not collide Wi-Fi cannot be done in GNS3 at any effort. Packet Tracer, or real hardware. Decide this term whether wireless is an outcome — if it is, you need PT alongside

items.title: Assessment
items.text: Still ungraded. The running project starts next week; use the last ten minutes of session 3 to hand out ../../project/README.md and ../../project/milestone1-switching/, so students arrive in week 3 having read the scenario.

items.title: Prep checklist
items.text:
• [ ] dynamips confirmed working on every machine (A1 blocker)
  • [ ] firewalld decision made — disabled in the image, or students told to stop it
  • [ ] RAM guidance for 8 GB machines, per the table above
  • [ ] Packet Tracer available if you are covering cabling or Wi-Fi
  • [ ] Project brief distributed at the end of session 3

items.title: Week 2 worksheet — Devices and topologies
items.text:
Name: ____ Date: ______

Marks are for the prediction being present and for explaining the gap — not for being right.

items.title: 1 — Hub vs switch
items.text:
Predict. PC1 pings PC2. Packets appearing on PC3's cable — switch: _ hub: _

Observe.

Switch 1st Switch 2nd Hub 1st Hub 2nd ARP request ARP reply ICMP request ICMP reply

Explain. What does the switch know after the first ping that it did not know before, and how did it find out?

items.title: 2 — One box, two devices
items.text:
Predict. Can one box be a switch and then a router without rewiring? ☐ yes ☐ no

Observe.

As a bridge As a router IP addresses on BOX Subnets in use PCs need a gateway? Entries in ip route show MAC in PC1's ARP cache after pinging PC2 Forwards on layer

Explain. Through the router, PC1's ARP cache holds the router's MAC and never PC2's. Why can PC1 still reach PC2?

Apply. In one sentence, the difference between a switch and a router:

items.title: 3 — The NIC owns the address
items.text:
Predict. Can you change a MAC address? ☐ yes ☐ no · Who needs to find out? ______

Observe.

Value H1 MAC / vendor H1 new MAC H2's ip neigh immediately after H2's ip neigh after next ping

Is 02:11:22:33:44:55 locally administered? How can you tell from the number alone?

items.title: 4 — NAT from both sides
items.text:
Predict. OUTSIDE has no route back to 192.168.10.0/24. With NAT on, does INSIDE→OUTSIDE work? ☐ yes ☐ no

Observe.

Without NAT With NAT Src address, inside link Src address, outside link INSIDE → OUTSIDE OUTSIDE → INSIDE Rows in /proc/net/nf_conntrack

Explain. You added a route on OUTSIDE and it still could not reach INSIDE. Why not?

Apply. Is NAT a firewall? Answer in two sentences, one for each side of it.

items.title: 5 — Topology as failure modes
items.text:
Observe.

Bus (hub) Star (switch) Star + redundant link Cables for 4 hosts Collision domains Bystander sees Centre fails One edge cable fails Behaviour as built

Explain. Adding a redundant cable made the network worse. Ethernet frames have no TTL — connect those two facts.

items.title: 6 — Sharing one wire
items.text:
Predict. H1 is downloading. H2 starts too. H1's transfer ☐ stops ☐ slows ☐ unaffected

Observe.

Shared (tbf) H1 Shared H2 Reserved (htb) H1 Reserved H2 alone both at once

Explain. Under reservation, H1 alone got half the link. Where did the other half go?

Apply. Your video call and your backup upload share one link. Which scheme for which, and why?

items.title: 7 — Carried forward
items.text:
Three activities this week ended with "week 3 does this properly" or similar. Name them and what was left open.

Activity What was left unfinished

items.title: Week 2 topologies
items.text:
GNS3 projects this week uses, one per activity:

Activity Project Export worth keeping? A1 w02-a1-hub-vs-switch yes — no OL9 nodes, so the export is tiny and works anywhere A2 w02-a2-one-box yes — the 4-adapter OL9 node is the fiddly part A3 w02-a3-nic no A4 w02-a4-nat yes — 3 nodes, 2 subnets, slow to cable A5 w02-a5-topology no — rebuilding it is the activity A6 w02-a6-sharing yes

File → Export portable project, base images unticked.

items.title: A5 is deliberately not exported
items.text: Building the bus, the star and the loop by hand is the activity. Handing out a finished version removes the only part that teaches anything.

items.title: Note on adapter counts
items.text: A2 and A4 need OL9 nodes with more than the default one adapter. That setting travels with the exported project, which is most of why exporting them is worth it — it is also the single most common thing students get wrong when building from scratch.

items.title: Week 3 — Ethernet and switching
items.text:
Assumes: weeks 1–2. Students can read a capture, know a switch forwards on MAC addresses, and have already watched a redundant link destroy a network (W2·A5 Build 3).

Leaves students able to: print, flush and age a switch's forwarding table; distinguish broadcast flooding from unknown-unicast flooding; measure a broadcast domain; cut one in half with VLANs; and explain what spanning tree is for from having needed it.

items.title: The arc
items.text:
Week 2 measured the switch from outside, because GNS3's Ethernet switch shows you nothing at all. This week replaces it with a Linux bridge on an OL9 Switch, where every piece of state is a command. The week is therefore structured as: here is the table you have been inferring since week 2 → here is what it does when it misses → here is its boundary → here is how to move the boundary → here is the protocol that keeps it from melting.

# Activity Time Needs A1 The MAC address table ★ 45 min 1 OL9 Switch + 4 VPCS A2 Flooding what it does not know 35 min A1 + 1 OL9 PC A3 The broadcast domain, measured 25 min 4 OL9 PCs + 1 switch A4 VLANs cut the segment ★ 45 min A1's topology A5 Storm, then spanning tree ★ 50 min 2 OL9 Switches + 4 VPCS A6 Filling the table (extension) 30 min Open vSwitch + Docker A7 CSMA, unplugged (no computers) 40 min a room A8 Configuration that survives ★ 80 min 2 OL9 Switches + 2 OL9 PCs + 1 VPCS

★ = keep if compressed. A6 and A7 are extensions and neither is assumed later.

items.title: Why a Linux bridge and not the built-in switch
items.text:
The GNS3 Ethernet switch has no console, no CLI, and nothing in Configure beyond per-port VLANs. It behaves correctly and shows you nothing, which is fine for scenery and useless as a subject. A Linux bridge is the same software that switches packets on every KVM host in the world, runs on the same OS as the rest of the course, and prints every piece of its state.

Keep using the built-in switch wherever a switch is merely present — it costs almost no RAM.

items.title: The one thing GNS3 cannot do
items.text: CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA cannot be demonstrated here. GNS3 models no shared medium, so no collision ever occurs, and its hub does not collide either. A7 is an unplugged room activity, and it is better than a simulation would be. Packet Tracer can animate a collision, if you want the picture as well.

items.title: Deliverable
items.text:
worksheet.md. Plus: the running project starts this week — see ../../project/milestone1-switching/. Milestone 1 is graded; this week's activities are not.

The relationship is deliberate: A1–A5 hand students every technique milestone 1 needs, on a topology of four hosts and one switch. Milestone 1 gives them requirements, three switches, no commands, and a network that has to survive a cable being pulled.

items.title: W3·A1 — The MAC address table ★
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Switch (6 adapters) + 4 VPCS · GNS3 project: w03-a1-mac-table

The question: since week 2 you have been saying "the switch learned where PC2 is". Learned it where? Show the table.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
One OL9 Switch named SW1, with PC1…PC4 (VPCS) on Ethernet0…3.

Set Adapters = 6 (right-click → Configure → Network). You only need four now, but A4 continues in this same project and adds a fifth port for the link between two switches. Spare adapters cost nothing, and adding them later means shutting the node down again.

# on SW1
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done

ip link add name br0 type bridge
ip link set br0 up

for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do
    ip addr flush dev $i
    ip link set $i master br0
    ip link set $i up
done

bridge link
ip -d link show br0

# PC1 / PC2 / PC3 / PC4
ip 192.168.10.11/24        # .12 / .13 / .14
save

Confirm PC1 pings all three. br0 has no IP address and must not have one — this node is the segment, not a host on it.

items.title: What ip -d link show br0 told you
items.text:
Three fields to find now, because the rest of the week uses all three:
