Field Meaning Default ageing_time how long a learned entry survives, in centiseconds 30000 = 300 s stp_state spanning tree on/off 0 = off vlan_filtering VLAN support on/off 0 = off

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Before any traffic, how many entries are in the table? _
  2. PC1 pings PC2. How many entries afterwards, and whose? _
  3. Which packet taught the switch where PC2 is — PC1's request or PC2's reply? _

items.title: Do this — collect the MACs first
items.text:
show ip on each VPCS prints its MAC. You cannot read the table without these.

Node MAC address PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4

items.title: Do this — read the table
items.text:
# on SW1 — the interesting rows only.
# 'permanent' and 'local' entries are the bridge's own port addresses, not learned ones.
bridge fdb show br br0 | grep -v permanent | grep -v local

# forget everything learned so far
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do bridge fdb flush dev $i master; done
bridge fdb show br br0 | grep -v permanent | grep -v local

The second listing is empty. Now, on PC1:

clear arp
ping 192.168.10.12

And immediately on SW1, re-run the bridge fdb show.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two entries, and only two: PC1's MAC on eth0, PC2's on eth1. Check them against your table above. PC3 and PC4 are absent — the switch has never heard from them and has no reason to care.
  • The rule, in one sentence: a bridge learns from the source address of frames that arrive, and forwards on the destination. Nothing announces itself; the switch overhears.
  • So PC2's entry came from PC2's reply, not from PC1's request. The request taught it only about PC1. Traffic in one direction teaches only one direction, which is a fact week 4 will make expensive.
  • This is the table you have been inferring since W2·A1, and it was inferable because it is completely determined by what the switch has heard.

items.title: Do this — watch it forget
items.text:
Ageing is in centiseconds, unusually for iproute2. 30 seconds is 3000:

# on SW1
ip link set dev br0 type bridge ageing_time 3000
cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/ageing_time        # cross-check: 3000

Then from PC1: ping 192.168.10.12, and on SW1 run bridge fdb show br br0 once immediately, once after 15 seconds, once after 35.

Put it back afterwards: ip link set dev br0 type bridge ageing_time 30000.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The dynamic entries vanished on their own. Nothing deleted them and nothing went wrong.
  • A MAC table is a cache, not a configuration. It is never right, only recently correct, and a switch that has been idle knows nothing. Compare the ARP cache from week 1 — same idea at a different layer, and both must expire for the network to tolerate change (W2·A3 showed you what happens when something moves).
  • The default 300 s is a compromise: too short and the switch floods constantly; too long and it keeps sending frames to a port where nothing lives any more.

items.title: Do this — move a host
items.text: With ageing back at 300 s, ping from PC4 so the switch learns it. Then stop PC4, re-cable it from Ethernet3 to a free port, start it, and — without sending any traffic from it — check the table. Then ping from PC4 and check again.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The entry still named the old port, and would have until it aged out. A switch cannot detect a move; it can only be told, and the only way to tell it is to transmit.
  • One frame from PC4 corrected it instantly. Learning is not a periodic process — it happens on every arriving frame, always.

items.title: Record
items.text: Entries before any traffic Entries after PC1 → PC2 Which frame taught the switch about PC2 Entries after 35 s at ageing_time 3000 Port recorded for PC4 after moving it, before it transmits Port after PC4 transmits

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Pings fail once the bridge is built br_netfilter handing bridged frames to iptables sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0 Interfaces regain addresses on their own NetworkManager nmcli device set ethN managed no on all four, then rebuild bridge fdb show lists only permanent rows no traffic yet, or you filtered too hard ping first; drop the grep -v to see everything Table never ages you set 3000 seconds, not centiseconds cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/ageing_time and compare Only eth0 exists adapter count Configure → Network → Adapters = 6, restart the node

items.title: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know
items.text:
Time: 35 min · Needs: A1's topology, with PC1 replaced by an OL9 PC · GNS3 project: w03-a1-mac-table (continue in it)

The question: in week 2 a bystander's cable carried a broadcast. This is a switch flooding an ordinary unicast frame — one addressed to a specific machine that is not the bystander. Easy to confuse with broadcast flooding, and worth separating properly.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Adjust the topology
items.text:
PC1 must become an OL9 PC for this activity, because VPCS cannot pin a static ARP entry. Delete the VPCS PC1, drop in an OL9 PC in its place on Ethernet0, and:

# on the new PC1
nmcli device set eth0 managed no
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0
ip link set eth0 up
ping -c1 192.168.10.12

Note PC1's new MAC — the table you filled in during A1 is now out of date for this row.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
PC1 sends a frame addressed to PC2's MAC. The switch has no entry for that MAC.

  1. Does the switch drop it? ☐ drop ☐ flood ☐ hold it and ask
  2. Does PC3's cable carry it? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. Is this frame a broadcast? ☐ yes ☐ no
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Do this — remove both reasons to broadcast
items.text:
Two things normally prevent this experiment: PC1 would ARP (a broadcast, which muddies the result), and the switch would already know PC2. Remove both.

# on PC1 — pin PC2's MAC, so no ARP is needed
ip neigh replace 192.168.10.12 lladdr <PC2-MAC> dev eth0 nud permanent
ip neigh show

# on SW1 — forget PC2, and only PC2
bridge fdb del <PC2-MAC> dev eth1 master
bridge fdb show br br0 | grep -v permanent | grep -v local

Start a capture on the PC3↔SW1 link. Then on PC1:

ping -c1 192.168.10.12

Read the capture. Then run the ping a second time and read it again.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC3's cable carried the echo request — and it is not a broadcast. Look at the destination MAC in the capture: it is PC2's real address, not ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. PC3 received a frame addressed to somebody else.
  • The switch did that on purpose. Faced with a destination it could not place, it did the only thing that preserves connectivity: send it everywhere except where it came from, and let the wrong recipients discard it.
  • PC3's NIC dropped it silently, because the destination MAC was not its own. The frame arrived, was examined, and was discarded — no error, no log, nothing. That filtering is done by the receiving card, not by the network.
  • The second ping put nothing on PC3's cable. PC2's reply taught the switch where PC2 is, so the flooding stopped after exactly one frame.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: The distinction, stated
items.text:
Broadcast flooding (W2·A1) Unknown-unicast flooding (here) Destination MAC ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff a real host's address Why it floods the address means "everyone" the switch cannot place the address Stops when never — always floods the switch learns that MAC Who processes it every host one host; the rest discard

Flooding is not a property of broadcast frames. It is what a switch does with any destination it cannot place, and week 2's example happened to be a broadcast.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Do this — the security consequence
items.text: Leave the static ARP entry in place. On SW1, flush PC2 again, and this time capture on PC3's link and PC4's link simultaneously before pinging.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every port got the frame. For as long as a switch does not know where a host is, traffic for that host is delivered to everyone — a hub, temporarily, for one destination.
  • Now consider forcing that state to persist. If the table could be kept permanently full of useless entries, the switch would flood everything, permanently, and any port could read any conversation. That attack is real, it is called MAC flooding or CAM table overflow, and A6 performs it.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Clean up
items.text:
# on PC1
ip neigh del 192.168.10.12 dev eth0
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: Record
items.text:
Destination MAC of the flooded frame Was it a broadcast? Did PC3's cable carry it? 1st ping / 2nd ping What stopped the flooding Who discarded the frame at PC3

One sentence distinguishing broadcast flooding from unknown-unicast flooding.
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix ARP frames still appear static entry not applied ip neigh show — the line must read PERMANENT bridge fdb del says "No such file or directory" wrong port, or already flushed bridge fdb show first and copy the exact dev Nothing on PC3's link at all the switch had already re-learned PC2 flush again, then ping immediately Flooding never stops PC2 is not replying ping PC2 from the switch's own console? No — check PC2 is started and addressed VPCS PC1 will not take the ip neigh command it is not Linux PC1 must be an OL9 PC for this activity
path: W3·A2 — Flooding what it does not know

items.title: W3·A3 — The broadcast domain, measured
items.text:
Time: 25 min · Needs: four OL9 PCs + an Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: w03-a3-broadcast

The question: "broadcast domain" is defined in every textbook as "the set of devices that receive a broadcast". Fine — count them.

All four hosts must be OL9 PCs. VPCS has no sysctl and will not answer a broadcast ping, so a topology with VPCS in it silently under-counts.

items.title: Build it
items.text: PC1…PC4, all OL9 PCs, on one switch (the built-in Ethernet switch is fine here — it is scenery). 192.168.10.11….14/24, nmcli device set eth0 managed no on each.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. PC1 sends one packet to 192.168.10.255. How many replies come back? _
  2. How many packets crossed the wire in total? _
  3. If two of the four hosts were switched off, would the switch still send it to their ports?

items.title: Do this
items.text:
By default Linux ignores broadcast pings, which is itself worth a moment. Turn that off on the responders only:

# on PC2, PC3 and PC4 — not PC1
sysctl -w net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts=0

Start a capture on PC4's link. Then on PC1:

ping -b -c2 192.168.10.255

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Three hosts answered one packet. That set — the hosts that received it, whether or not they answered — is the broadcast domain, and it is exactly the set of ports the switch floods to.
  • ping reported the extra replies as DUP!. From the sender's point of view that is an anomaly; it is the only shape ping has for "more than one machine is answering", because the tool was designed for one-to-one.
  • The switch delivered it to every port regardless of whether anything was listening. A powered-off host still gets the frame sent at it; nothing about flooding depends on the far end existing.
  • The icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts default is the good part: the switch delivered, each host decided. Layer 2 has no policy and no opinion; the hosts have both. That division is exactly what "layer" means, and it is the cleanest example of it this term.

items.title: Do this — count what a broadcast costs
items.text:
Keep the capture running. On PC1:

ip neigh flush all
ping -c1 192.168.10.12

Look at PC4's capture.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC4's cable carried the ARP request, an ordinary broadcast that had nothing to do with PC4. PC4's kernel had to receive it, parse it, decide it was not the target, and discard it.
  • Every host in the domain pays that cost, for every broadcast, forever. With four hosts it is invisible. With four hundred on one segment it is a real load — and every one of them is doing it for every ARP, every DHCP discover, and every piece of discovery chatter on the network.
  • That is the argument for splitting a broadcast domain, and A4 is how it is done.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Hosts in the topology Replies to one broadcast ping Hosts in the broadcast domain Did PC4's cable carry PC1's ARP for PC2? Default value of icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts

One sentence: who delivered the broadcast, and who decided whether to answer?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix ping -b refuses you must be root log in as root Zero replies icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts still 1 run the sysctl on the responders, not the sender Fewer replies than hosts a VPCS node is in the topology all four must be OL9 Operation not permitted on sysctl not root as above Only one reply, no DUP! you pinged a host address, not the broadcast address .255 for a /24

items.title: W3·A4 — VLANs cut the segment ★
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: A1's topology (OL9 Switch + 4 VPCS), Wireshark · GNS3 project: w03-a1-mac-table (continue in it)

The question: A3 showed that every broadcast costs every host in the domain. Split the domain without buying a second switch and without changing a single address.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
Four hosts, one subnet, one switch, all pinging happily. You are about to put ports 0–1 in VLAN 10 and ports 2–3 in VLAN 20, changing no IP address on any host.

  1. Can PC1 (VLAN 10) still ping PC2 (VLAN 10)? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. Can PC1 still ping PC3 (VLAN 20)? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. If not — what is wrong with the addressing? _

items.title: Do this — the cheap version first, for contrast
items.text:
Before building it properly, see the same effect on the built-in switch. If you still have a GNS3 Ethernet switch topology from week 2: right-click it → Configure, set ports 0–1 to VLAN 10 and ports 2–3 to VLAN 20, all type access. Ping .12 and then .13 from PC1.

.12 works. .13 fails. Correct behaviour, two mouse clicks, and no way whatsoever to see why. That is why the rest of this activity is on the bridge.

items.title: Do this — VLANs on the bridge
items.text:
# on SW1
ip link set dev br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1

bridge vlan add dev eth0 vid 10 pvid untagged
bridge vlan add dev eth1 vid 10 pvid untagged
bridge vlan add dev eth2 vid 20 pvid untagged
bridge vlan add dev eth3 vid 20 pvid untagged

# remove the default VLAN 1 membership, or nothing is separated
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do bridge vlan del dev $i vid 1; done

bridge vlan show

Start a capture on PC3's link. From PC1:

clear arp
ping 192.168.10.12
ping 192.168.10.13

Then on SW1:

bridge fdb show br br0 | grep -v permanent

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• .12 worked. .13 failed. Same subnet, same mask, same switch, correct addressing on both, and no route needed. Nothing at layer 3 can explain this.
  • PC1's ARP broadcast stopped appearing on PC3's capture. The broadcast domain has been cut in two, which is the whole objective — A3's cost is now paid by two hosts instead of four.
  • Every fdb entry now carries a vlan field. There is no longer one forwarding table; there is one table per VLAN, and a MAC learned in VLAN 10 is invisible to VLAN 20. Two switches, sharing a chassis.
  • The switch defines the segment, not the addressing. That sentence is what the entire week exists to earn, and this is where it is paid.
  • Deleting vid 1 was not optional. Ports stay in the default VLAN otherwise, everything remains mutually reachable, and the activity appears not to work.

items.title: Do this — a trunk, and the tag itself
items.text:
Add a second OL9 Switch SW2 (same build as A1), move PC3 and PC4 onto it, and link SW1:eth4↔SW2:eth4. On both switches:

# member of both VLANs, and tagged — note the absence of 'pvid untagged'
bridge vlan add dev eth4 vid 10
bridge vlan add dev eth4 vid 20
bridge vlan show

Start a capture on the SW1↔SW2 link and ping across it within VLAN 10.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The frames on the trunk carry an 802.1Q tag — Wireshark shows a 802.1Q Virtual LAN layer between Ethernet and IP, with ID: 10 in it. Expand it and note that it is 4 bytes, inserted into the middle of a header you thought you already knew from week 1.
  • The same frames on the access ports at either end have no tag. The tag exists only between switches, because it exists to answer one question — which VLAN did this arrive in? — that only a switch asks. Hosts neither send nor see it.
  • pvid untagged on an access port means exactly that: frames arriving here belong to this VLAN, and frames leaving here go out with the tag stripped.
  • The maximum frame grew by 4 bytes. Standard Ethernet allows 1518; a tagged frame is 1522. That is a real and recurring source of trouble on equipment that was not told to expect it.

items.title: Do this — the question the design leaves open
items.text: From PC1 in VLAN 10, try to reach PC3 in VLAN 20 one more time. Then try to think of any configuration on SW1 that would let it through.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• There is none. A bridge cannot move a frame between VLANs, by construction — that would defeat the separation you built it for.
  • Traffic between VLANs must go up to layer 3 and come back down, which means a router, which is week 4. Every real network runs this arrangement, and the phrase for it is "router on a stick".
  • Notice what you have therefore built: a network that is deliberately broken between two groups of hosts, with the repair postponed to another device. That is a design decision, not a fault, and it is the normal state of every campus network you have used.

items.title: Record
items.text: PC1 → PC2 (both VLAN 10) PC1 → PC3 (VLAN 10 → 20) Any IP address changed? ARP broadcast on PC3's cable, before / after New field in bridge fdb show Extra bytes in a tagged frame What is needed to connect VLAN 10 to VLAN 20

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Everything still reachable vid 1 not removed the for loop deleting vid 1 is mandatory All pings fail, including within a VLAN ports missing pvid untagged bridge vlan show — access ports must show PVID Egress Untagged No 802.1Q layer on the trunk capture you captured an access link capture the SW1↔SW2 link specifically Trunk works one way only one switch's trunk port is missing a VLAN both ends need both vid lines bridge vlan says "Operation not supported" vlan_filtering still 0 set it on br0 first

items.title: W3·A5 — Storm, then spanning tree ★
items.text:
Time: 75 min · Needs: two OL9 Switches + 4 VPCS · GNS3 project: w03-a5-stp

The question: in W2·A5 you added a redundant cable and the network died. Redundancy is supposed to be good. Fix it.

This activity deliberately builds a broadcast storm. Nothing is damaged, but the topology becomes unusable while it runs and it will load your machine. Know how to stop the nodes from the toolbar before you start.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Two OL9 Switches, SW1 and SW2, built exactly as in A1 but with eth0–eth3 bridged on each. PC1 .11 and PC2 .12 on SW1; PC3 .13 and PC4 .14 on SW2.

Cable both inter-switch links now — SW1:eth3↔SW2:eth3 and SW1:eth2↔SW2:eth2 — but hold the second one administratively down so that only one is live:

# on SW1
ip link set eth2 down
bridge link

Confirm all four PCs ping each other. That is your working baseline. You will cable nothing else for the rest of this activity; every "cable" you pull or restore from here is an ip link set command, which is faster and cannot leave a stale link in the project.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. SW1:eth3 fails. What reaches PC3 from PC1?
  2. You bring eth2 up so that both links are live at once. What happens to PC1 → PC3?
  3. Where, exactly, does a looping frame stop?
  4. If you turn on a protocol that switches one of the two links off, how is that redundancy?

items.title: Part 1 — Why anyone runs a second cable
items.text:
Right now the two switches are joined by exactly one working link. Everything on the far side of it depends on that one cable, that one pair of connectors, and nobody catching it with a chair leg.

Break it, with a continuous ping running from PC1 to PC3:

# on SW1
ip link set eth3 down

The ping stops. Not slows — stops. PC3 and PC4 are still powered, still configured, still perfectly healthy, and completely unreachable. Nothing on any host indicates what is wrong or where.

Now bring the spare into service by hand:

# on SW1
ip link set eth2 up

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The spare path worked. Traffic resumed over a different cable, and nothing on any PC was reconfigured to make that happen — the switches simply had another way across.
  • A human did it. Someone had to notice the outage, work out which link had failed, know that a spare existed, and type a command. Count the time that took you, and remember that you already knew the answer and were sitting in front of the right machine.
  • That is the case for redundancy, and it is why the second cable is bought: the alternative to a spare path is a site outage that lasts until a person physically finds the fault.
  • It is also the case for automating this. Everything after here exists to remove the human from the paragraph above.

Leave eth2 up and bring eth3 back:

# on SW1
ip link set eth3 up

items.title: Part 2 — So just leave both cables up
items.text:
Which is the obvious idea. Both links are now live and you have just done it.

Check the counters first, so you have a "before":

# on SW1
ip -s link show eth3

Start a capture on the SW1↔SW2 link — right-click the link → Start capture — and from PC1:

ping 192.168.10.13

Watch for two seconds, then stop the capture. It grows at a rate you have not seen before and will fill a disk if you leave it. Then on SW1:

ip -s link show eth3
ip -s link show eth2

Then take the second link back down immediately: ip link set eth2 down on SW1.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Read the capture. It is thousands of copies of one frame — the same ARP request, the same source MAC, the same target, arriving microseconds apart. PC1 sent that request once.
  • That is the observation that proves this is a loop and not merely a busy network. Nobody is generating this traffic. One frame is being copied.
  • The packet counters went from hundreds to enormous, climbing while you watched, on a network with four idle hosts on it.
  • SW1 flooded PC1's broadcast to SW2 over both links; SW2 flooded each copy back over the other; and so on, doubling, with nothing anywhere to stop it.

items.title: Why it never stops
items.text:
Two mailing lists, each subscribed to the other. Someone posts one message. List A forwards it to list B, which forwards it back to list A, which forwards it on again. Neither list is broken and neither is doing anything other than its one job — faithfully passing on what it receives. Nothing in the message records how many times it has been forwarded, so nothing can ever decide it has been around enough times and drop it.

  • There is no hop count in an Ethernet frame. Week 1's teardown showed you exactly where TTL lives — in the IP header, one layer up. A frame circulating at layer 2 is never examined by anything that could count its hops, because at layer 2 nothing is counting.
  • Worse than the traffic: the MAC tables are being corrupted. Each switch sees PC1's address arriving on both ports, alternately, and rewrites the entry each time. Even frames that are not looping now go to the wrong port. This is why a storm takes out unicast traffic too, and why the network does not merely slow down — it stops.

So you are holding a contradiction. The second cable is the thing you must have for the network to survive a failure, and it is the thing that destroys the network the moment you use it.

items.title: How spanning tree resolves that
items.text: Read this before Part 3. It is the whole point of the activity.

items.title: 1. Keep the cable, and refuse to use it
items.text:
You already know the fix, because you did it by hand in Part 1: hold the spare down. The frames only loop because there are two live paths; with one path there is no circle.

The difference is that you are going to have the switch refuse to forward on that port, rather than shut the port off. The cable stays connected, powered, and listening. It carries no user traffic and it is ready instantly. A port in that state is called blocking.

items.title: 2. The hard part is agreeing which port
items.text:
Now the real problem appears, and it is not the one you would guess. The switches have to agree on which port blocks. If each decides on its own:

  • both might block, and the network splits into two halves that cannot reach each other;
  • or neither blocks, and the storm continues.

And there is no controller. No switch is in charge of the others, none of them was told what the topology is, and each can only see its own ports. So the question spanning tree actually answers is:

How do independent devices, with no coordinator, all reach the same decision?

items.title: 3. Agree on a landmark first
items.text:
You cannot answer "which of my ports should block?" by looking only at yourself — it depends on what everyone else does.

But it becomes easy the moment every switch agrees on one reference point somewhere on the network. Then each switch asks itself the same purely local question: which of my ports is on my best way to that point? Keep that one. Everything else can block. Nobody has to negotiate with anybody, and yet the answers fit together.

So before anything else, the switches choose one of themselves to be that reference point — the root. Each announces itself with a number, the lowest number wins, and because every switch hears the same numbers, every switch works out the same winner without being told.

That number is the bridge ID, and it is two things joined together:

priority a number you set — the part you control MAC address the switch's own address — the part you cannot

Priority is compared first. The MAC is only consulted when priorities are equal, which is why it is a tiebreak and not the rule. Two switches, both left at the default:

SW1 SW2 priority 32768 32768 MAC 0c:1a:…:5e 0c:1a:…:3f bridge ID 32768.0c1a…5e 32768.0c1a…3f ← root, its MAC is lower

Now set SW1's priority to 4096:

SW1 SW2 priority 4096 32768 MAC 0c:1a:…:5e 0c:1a:…:3f bridge ID 4096.0c1a…5e ← root 32768.0c1a…3f

SW1 wins now, and SW2's lower MAC never gets looked at, because the comparison was already decided at the first field. Lower wins, at every step. The default is 32768, the range is 0–65535, and real switches accept it only in steps of 4096.

You will read your own values with cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/bridge_id.

items.title: 4. "Best way" has to be measured
items.text:
If a switch has two ways to reach the root, which is better? Add up the links along each route. Each link contributes a number based on its speed, and a faster link contributes less, because you would rather your traffic took the fast route:

Link speed Contributes 1 Gb/s 4 100 Mb/s 19 10 Mb/s 100

Add them along a path and you have that path's cost. Lower total is better. Say that to yourself once, because it runs against the instinct that a bigger number means a better link. bridge link prints the real cost of each of your ports — read it there rather than assuming.

Cost is a distance to the root. It cannot be computed until a root exists, which is why the root is elected first and why every decision below is described as being relative to it.

items.title: 5. Now the three port roles are just three questions
items.text:
"Which one of my ports do I use to reach the root?" — the root port. The port with the lowest cost to the root. Exactly one per switch, and the root itself has none, because it is already there.

"This cable has a switch on each end — which of the two is responsible for carrying it?" — the designated port. One per cable: whichever end has the lower cost to the root. This role exists because if both ends forwarded the same cable's traffic, that is the loop. Every port on the root is designated, since nothing beats a cost of zero.

"What is left over?" — blocking. Not a root port, not a designated port, so it forwards nothing. That is where the circle gets broken.

Worked through on a triangle, which is also the shape you will build for milestone 1. SW1 is root at priority 4096, all links gigabit, so each contributes 4:

Switch Bridge ID Cost to root SW1 4096.aa…01 0 — it is the root SW2 32768.aa…02 4 direct, or 8 via SW3 → 4 SW3 32768.aa…03 4 direct, or 8 via SW2 → 4 Cable SW1 end SW2 end SW3 end Outcome SW1–SW2 cost 0 cost 4 — SW1's port designated; SW2's is its root port SW1–SW3 cost 0 — cost 4 SW1's port designated; SW3's is its root port SW2–SW3 — cost 4 cost 4 tie — see below

Six ports, and every one has a role: SW1 two designated, SW2 one root and one designated, SW3 one root and one blocking. Exactly one port blocks, which is exactly one more than the number of loops you had.

items.title: 6. What happens on a tie
items.text:
The SW2–SW3 cable has cost 4 at both ends. Neither is closer to the root, so cost cannot decide it, and something has to.

The rule is: lowest cost, then lowest bridge ID, then lowest port number. Here bridge ID settles it — …02 beats …03, so SW2's port is designated and SW3's blocks.

That tiebreak looks arbitrary because it is arbitrary, deliberately. A tiebreak does not have to be fair or meaningful. It has to be identical everywhere, so that every switch applying it alone arrives at the answer every other switch arrived at. Bridge IDs and port numbers are used for no better reason than that they are unambiguous and everybody already knows them.

This matters for what you are about to build. Your two switches have two links of the same speed between the same pair of bridges — so the costs tie and the bridge IDs tie, and the decision falls all the way through to port number. You can predict which port will block before you turn STP on.

items.title: Part 3 — Turn it on
items.text:
With eth2 still down, enable STP on both bridges:

# on SW1 and on SW2
ip link set dev br0 type bridge stp_state 1

bridge link
cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/bridge_id
cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/root_id

Which switch is root, and did the MAC tiebreak decide it? Now bring the second link up and wait about 30 seconds:

# on SW1
ip link set eth2 up

# then, on both
bridge link

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• One of the four inter-switch ports settled into blocking while the rest reached forwarding. The cable is physically connected, electrically fine, and carrying no user traffic at all. No storm.
  • Check it against your prediction: the blocking port is on the non-root switch, and which of its two ports it is was decided by port number, because everything above that tied.
  • bridge_id and root_id: where they are equal, that bridge is the root. Both switches agree on one root with nothing coordinating them, exactly as in §3 — they compared IDs, and the lowest won.
  • The delay was real. Classic 802.1D holds a port in listening then learning for 15 seconds each before forwarding. That 30-second silence is why a PC plugged into an unconfigured switch port can fail to get an address, and it is the reason RSTP exists.

items.title: Part 4 — Make it earn its keep
items.text:
First, move the root deliberately rather than accepting whichever MAC happened to be lower:

# on SW1 — take over as root
ip link set dev br0 type bridge priority 4096
cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/root_id        # on both switches

Now repeat Part 1 exactly — with a continuous ping running from PC1 to PC3, fail the forwarding inter-switch link:

# on SW1
ip link set eth3 down

Watch the ping. Then bridge link on both switches.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• This is Part 1 with the human removed. The blocked port took over on its own. Nobody noticed the outage, diagnosed it, or typed anything — which is the answer to the fourth prediction. STP does not take your second cable away; it keeps it switched off and ready, and switches it on for you.
  • The ping stopped for a while and then resumed. Count the lost packets: classic STP takes tens of seconds to reconverge, and that is a genuine outage — shorter than the one in Part 1 by however long it would have taken a person to get there.
  • Lowering priority moved the root by decision. Left alone, the root is whichever bridge has the lowest MAC address — which is to say, an arbitrary device chosen by accident of manufacture, quite possibly the oldest and slowest thing you own, sitting in a cupboard. Every real deployment sets this explicitly, and now you know what goes wrong if nobody does.

Bring the link back up: ip link set eth3 up.

Note: Linux implements classic 802.1D, not Cisco's PVST+. Timings and behaviour match the standard rather than Packet Tracer's output. If you compare the two platforms, expect that difference and do not treat either as wrong.

This setting does not survive a reboot. ip link set ... priority is for exploring. Milestone 1 requires a deliberately chosen root that is still chosen after a restart, which is nmcli's job — see A8.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Seconds of outage in Part 1, and what ended it Copies of one ARP request in the storm capture eth3 packet count, before / during the storm Which layer's header has a hop count, and which does not Bridge ID of each switch, and which is root Which port blocked, and which tiebreak decided it Seconds of ping loss in Part 4, and what ended it

Two sentences: what does STP cost, and what does it buy?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix GNS3 unresponsive during Part 2 the storm is doing its job stop the nodes from the toolbar, then ip link set eth2 down Capture file is enormous you left it running two seconds is plenty; stop it before reading No storm at all second link not up at both ends, or STP left on from a previous run bridge link; stp_state must be 0 for Part 2 Both ports forwarding, no blocking STP enabled on only one bridge it must be on both Ping never recovers in Part 4 still converging classic STP takes ~30 s; wait before concluding Root keeps changing you set priority on both set it on one only A different port blocked than you predicted port numbering, or the costs did not tie bridge link prints each port's cost — check them before blaming the prediction Pings fail after the storm tables scrambled bridge fdb flush dev ethN master on each port, or restart both bridges

items.title: W3·A6 — Filling the table (extension)
items.text:
Time: 30 min · Needs: the Open vSwitch appliance + Docker on the GNS3 server (../../gns3-lab0-switching.md §D0) + 3 OL9 PCs or VPCS · GNS3 project: w03-a6-overflow

The question: A2 ended with a claim — that a switch whose table is permanently full behaves like a hub, and that this is an attack. Test it.

Why a third switch appears here. Every tool in this course has a ceiling, and this activity is the first place we hit one. The GNS3 Ethernet switch shows you nothing at all; the Linux bridge shows you everything it has, but it does not have this. To overflow a forwarding table in a classroom you must first make it small, and OVS exposes that as a setting (other-config:mac-table-size) while the Linux bridge on OL9's kernel does not — its per-port learning limit, fdb_max_learned, arrived in kernel 6.2 and OL9 ships older.

So Open vSwitch is not a better switch that you should have been using all along, and nothing later in the course switches over to it. It is an instrument, brought out for one measurement — the same way you reach for Wireshark rather than replacing ping with it. You will meet it once more, in the security material, for port mirroring, which the Linux bridge also cannot do.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Import the OVS appliance (§D0), place it as SW1, and cable PC1 .11, PC2 .12, PC3 .13 to its first three ports.

# on SW1
ovs-vsctl show

If it is empty:

ovs-vsctl add-br br0
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2; do ovs-vsctl add-port br0 $i; ip link set $i up; done
ovs-vsctl show

Confirm the hosts ping each other, then:

ovs-appctl fdb/show br0

items.title: What just happened
items.text: • The same table as A1, from a different management layer — port, VLAN, MAC, and an explicit age in seconds, which neither the built-in switch nor the Linux bridge gives you. You can watch entries count up in real time.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. A switch's forwarding table is full and a frame arrives for an address not in it. What happens?
  2. Roughly how many entries does a real access switch hold? _
  3. Why would an attacker want the table full?

items.title: Do this — shrink the table, then fill it
items.text:
# on SW1
ovs-vsctl set bridge br0 other-config:mac-table-size=4
ovs-appctl fdb/flush br0
ovs-appctl fdb/show br0

Start a capture on PC3's link. Establish normal behaviour first: from PC1, ping -c1 PC2, twice. PC3's cable should be quiet on the second attempt, exactly as in W2·A1.

Now generate traffic from many different source addresses. On PC1 (must be OL9):

for i in $(seq 1 20); do
    mac=$(printf '02:00:00:00:00:%02x' $i)
    ip link add link eth0 name fake$i address $mac type macvlan
    ip link set fake$i up
    ip addr add 192.168.10.$((100+i))/24 dev fake$i
    ping -c1 -W1 -I fake$i 192.168.10.12 >/dev/null 2>&1
done

ovs-appctl fdb/show br0        # run this on SW1

Then, from PC1's real interface, ping PC2 again — and read PC3's capture.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Twenty different source MACs arrived on one port, and the switch learned every one of them, because that is all learning is. It has no way to know they are fictitious.
  • The table hit its limit and started evicting real entries to make room. PC2's entry was among the casualties.
  • So PC1's next ordinary ping to PC2 was flooded — and PC3's cable carried it, exactly as in A2, but now permanently rather than for one frame, because the fake addresses keep the table full.
  • A switch under this attack is a hub. Every port can read every conversation, and nothing on any host indicates that anything is wrong. Connectivity is perfect. That is what makes it useful to an attacker and hard for a user to notice.

items.title: Clean up
items.text:
# on PC1
for i in $(seq 1 20); do ip link del fake$i; done

# on SW1
ovs-vsctl remove bridge br0 other-config mac-table-size
ovs-appctl fdb/flush br0

items.title: What defends against this
items.text:
Not part of the build — read and answer.

  • Real switches implement port security: a limit on how many MAC addresses one port may learn, and an action when it is exceeded (drop, alarm, shut the port).
  • Note where the limit sits: per port, not per switch. A legitimate port has one or two hosts behind it; twenty is already implausible. The defence works because the attack has to be loud on one port.
  • Note also what is not a defence: encryption protects the contents but not the fact of the conversation, and VLANs limit the blast radius without stopping it inside a VLAN.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Table size you set Entries after the flood PC3's cable, before the flood, 2nd ping PC3's cable, after the flood What the switch did wrong

One sentence: the switch behaved exactly as designed. So what is the actual flaw?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Docker errors on placing the appliance no Docker on the GNS3 server §D0 — the GNS3 VM has it; a bare Linux server needs it installed mac-table-size has no effect typo in other-config ovs-vsctl list bridge br0 and check the field macvlan creation fails not root, or name collision run as root; clean up leftovers with ip link del fake$i Table never overflows pings failed, so no frames were sent drop the >/dev/null and check they are transmitting Flooding stops on its own fake entries aged out re-run the loop, or lower mac-aging-time

items.title: W3·A7 — CSMA, unplugged (no computers)
items.text:
Time: 40 min · Needs: a room, one six-sided die per group, sticky notes · GNS3 project: none

The question: everything else this week was measured. This one cannot be — GNS3 models no shared medium, so no collision ever happens in it, and its hub does not collide either. So we run the protocol with people.

This is not a consolation prize. CSMA is a set of rules about timing and hearing, and a room full of people is a better instrument for that than any simulator.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
Six to eight students per group, seated in a circle. The medium is speech in the room: only one person can be understood at a time, and everyone can hear everyone.

Each student gets three sticky notes — three frames to transmit. Each note has a destination written on it (another student's name). The round ends when every note has been delivered.

One student is the recorder and does not transmit. They track: attempts, collisions, successful deliveries, and the round's total elapsed time.

items.title: Round 1 — No protocol (ALOHA)
items.text:
Rule: when you have a frame, say "[name], frame one" out loud. Whenever you like.

A transmission succeeds only if nobody else was speaking at any point during it. If two people overlap at all, both frames are lost and must be re-sent.

Recorder: count collisions.

items.title: Discuss
items.text:
• What is the collision count? What fraction of attempts succeeded?
  • What happened as the room got busier — did it get gradually worse, or did it fall off a cliff?
  • Nobody was doing anything wrong. The failures come from the rules, not the participants.

items.title: Round 2 — CSMA/CD (Ethernet on a shared medium)
items.text:
Rules:

  1. Carrier Sense — before speaking, listen. If someone is talking, wait until they stop.
  2. Multiple Access — anyone may speak once it is quiet.
  3. Collision Detection — you can hear yourself and the room while speaking. If you hear another voice start during yours, stop immediately, mid-word. Do not finish.
  4. Backoff — after a collision, roll the die. Wait that many seconds before trying again. After a second collision on the same frame, roll and double the wait. Then double again. (This is binary exponential backoff, and the doubling is the whole trick.)

Same three frames each. Recorder: collisions, deliveries, total time.

items.title: Discuss
items.text:
• Collisions dropped sharply. Why did carrier sense not eliminate them entirely?
  • Answer: two people can both hear silence at the same moment and both start. Sensing removes collisions during a transmission, not collisions at the start of one. That residual window is irreducible, and it is exactly why detection and backoff are still needed.
  • Why stop mid-word? Finishing a frame you know is ruined wastes the medium for everyone. On real Ethernet, a station detecting a collision stops and sends a jam signal — deliberately making the damage unambiguous so every other station also gives up quickly.
  • Why double the wait? Repeated collisions mean the room is busy; backing off further is how the stations collectively find a rate the medium can carry, with no coordinator and no one able to count the others.
  • Where the "CD" went. Modern Ethernet is switched and full-duplex: every station has its own cable, and there is no shared medium to collide on. CSMA/CD is disabled on every link you have used this term. You have been learning the rules for a world that mostly ended around 2000 — which is worth knowing precisely, because the exam and the textbook both still assume it.

items.title: Round 3 — CSMA/CA and the hidden node (Wi-Fi)
items.text:
Rearrange: one student is the access point in the centre. Two students sit at opposite ends of the room, facing away from each other, and are told to behave as though they genuinely cannot hear one another. Everyone can hear the AP.

Round 3a. Play by CSMA/CD's rules. The two distant students both have frames for the AP.

  • Both sense silence — correctly, from where they sit — and both transmit.
  • The AP hears a collision. Neither sender does. Both believe they succeeded.
  • This is the hidden node problem, and it is why Wi-Fi cannot use CSMA/CD. A radio cannot listen while transmitting on the same channel, and "the medium is quiet here" does not mean "the medium is quiet at the receiver" — which is the only place that matters.

Round 3b. Now add the rules Wi-Fi actually uses:

  1. Before transmitting, wait for silence plus a random number of slots (roll the die). Always, even when nothing is in the way.
  2. Send RTS — "AP, may I send?"
  3. The AP replies CTS — "go ahead" — and everyone in range hears the CTS, including the hidden node, who now stays quiet.
  4. Transmit.
  5. The AP sends ACK. No ACK means it did not arrive — that is the only way the sender ever finds out.

items.title: Discuss
items.text:
• Count the messages needed to deliver one frame: RTS, CTS, data, ACK. Four for one. That overhead is why advertised Wi-Fi speeds and real Wi-Fi speeds differ so much, and it is not waste — it is the price of not being able to hear a collision.
  • Why does CSMA/CA stand for Collision Avoidance? Because avoidance is all that is available: detection is impossible, so the protocol spends effort making collisions unlikely instead of cheap.
  • Round 2 stations only waited when the medium was busy. Round 3 stations wait every time. Why is that necessary here and not there?

items.title: Record
items.text:
Round 1 (ALOHA) Round 2 (CSMA/CD) Round 3b (CSMA/CA) Total attempts Collisions Frames delivered Time to deliver all Messages per delivered frame

Then, in your own words:

  1. Carrier sense reduced collisions but did not eliminate them. Why not?
  2. Why can Wi-Fi not detect collisions?
  3. Which of these three protocols runs on the switched links you built this week? (Careful.)

items.title: Instructor note
items.text: Question 3's answer is none of them — switched full-duplex Ethernet has no contention at all. Students who answer "CSMA/CD" have learned the textbook rather than the week. Let them say it, then ask which cable is shared.

items.title: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★
items.text:
Time: 80 min · Needs: two OL9 Switches (SW1, SW2), two OL9 PCs (PC1, PC-MGMT), 1 VPCS · GNS3 project: w03-a8-persistent

The question: everything you have built this week disappears when the node restarts, and none of it can be administered from anywhere except the console. Both of those are unacceptable in a building you do not want to visit. Fix both.

This activity is milestone 1 in miniature — VLANs, a trunk, redundancy, a management network and persistence, on two switches instead of three. Nothing here is a new idea. What is new is writing it so it stays written.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Node Type Attaches to VLAN Address SW1 OL9 Switch — — 192.168.10.201 in VLAN 99 SW2 OL9 Switch — — 192.168.10.202 in VLAN 99 PC1 OL9 SW1:eth0 10 192.168.10.11/24 PC2 VPCS SW2:eth0 10 192.168.10.12/24 PC-MGMT OL9 SW2:eth1 99 192.168.10.200/24

Two inter-switch links: SW1:eth2↔SW2:eth2 and SW1:eth3↔SW2:eth3. Yes, that is a loop — A5 taught you what to do about it, and this time it will be configured to stay done.

PC1 and PC-MGMT are OL9 rather than VPCS because both need to run ssh, which VPCS cannot.

Everything is in 192.168.10.0/24, management included. That is deliberate and it is the same arrangement milestone 1 uses: it makes the point that the switch defines the segment, not the addressing — VLAN 99 is a separate broadcast domain even though its addresses look like everyone else's.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. You configure everything with ip and bridge as in A4 and A5, then restart the node. What is left?
  2. PC-MGMT is plugged into SW2. Can it administer SW1, which it has no cable to?
  3. Can PC1, in VLAN 10, log into a switch?
  4. SW1 is the root of the spanning tree. Does that make it the switch you manage?
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Part 1 — The same bridge, written down
items.text:
Running state, and stored configuration. Both kinds of command change the machine, so the difference is not that one is real and the other is pretend.

ip and bridge change the machine as it is running now. The change is in the kernel's memory, it takes effect the instant you press return, and it is gone when the node restarts. Nothing anywhere records that you wanted it.

nmcli con add writes a stored configuration — a statement of what this machine's networking should be. NetworkManager then keeps the running state matching it: at boot, when a cable is plugged in, and whenever else it decides to re-apply.

That second half matters beyond surviving a restart. If a card has stored configuration saying "ask the network for an address", and you set an address by hand, yours exists only in running state — and the stored one wins the moment NetworkManager acts on it. Nothing warns you. Any activity where something on the wire hands out addresses is an activity where the difference stops being academic.

On SW1, build the bridge — but this time as configuration on disk rather than as commands to a running kernel:

# on SW1
nmcli con add type bridge ifname br0 con-name br0 \
      bridge.vlan-filtering yes \
      bridge.vlan-default-pvid 0 \
      bridge.stp yes \
      bridge.priority 4096 \
      ipv4.method disabled ipv6.method disabled

Six settings, and each one is something you did by hand earlier in the week:

Setting The A4/A5 command it replaces bridge.vlan-filtering yes ip link set dev br0 type bridge vlan_filtering 1 bridge.vlan-default-pvid 0 the mandatory for loop deleting vid 1 from every port bridge.stp yes ip link set dev br0 type bridge stp_state 1 bridge.priority 4096 ip link set dev br0 type bridge priority 4096 ipv4.method disabled not putting an address on the bridge — A2's whole point

bridge.vlan-default-pvid 0 deserves a second look. In A4 you had to delete vid 1 from every port or nothing was separated, and the activity appeared not to work. That default is what put it there. Setting it to 0 means new ports get no automatic VLAN at all, so the only VLANs a port has are the ones you gave it — which is the behaviour you wanted in the first place.

Now the ports. An access port in VLAN 10, and the management port:

# on SW1
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth0 master br0 con-name p-eth0 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10 pvid untagged"

And the two trunks, tagged members of both VLANs:

# on SW1
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth2 master br0 con-name p-eth2 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10,99"
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth3 master br0 con-name p-eth3 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10,99"

nmcli con up br0
bridge vlan show
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• bridge-port.vlans is the whole of A4 in one property. "10 pvid untagged" is an access port — frames arriving here belong to VLAN 10, and frames leaving here have the tag stripped. "10,99" with no pvid untagged is a trunk — a tagged member of both VLANs.
  • Compare bridge vlan show with what you got in A4. It is the same kernel state. NetworkManager is not a different mechanism; it is the same mechanism with a file behind it.
  • VLAN 99 is on the trunks. It has to be: PC-MGMT is attached to SW2 and has to reach SW1, and the only path between them is the trunk. A management VLAN that stops at each switch manages nothing.

Repeat all of it on SW2, with two changes — eth1 is an access port in VLAN 99 for PC-MGMT, and SW2 is not the root, so leave its priority alone:

# on SW2
nmcli con add type bridge ifname br0 con-name br0 \
      bridge.vlan-filtering yes bridge.vlan-default-pvid 0 bridge.stp yes \
      ipv4.method disabled ipv6.method disabled

nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth0 master br0 con-name p-eth0 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10 pvid untagged"
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth1 master br0 con-name p-eth1 \
      bridge-port.vlans "99 pvid untagged"
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth2 master br0 con-name p-eth2 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10,99"
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth3 master br0 con-name p-eth3 \
      bridge-port.vlans "10,99"

nmcli con up br0
bridge link

PC1 and PC2 get their addresses as usual. Confirm PC1 can ping PC2 — VLAN 10 across the trunk — and check bridge link on both switches: one port blocking, no storm, exactly as A5 predicted.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Part 2 — Giving a switch an address
items.text:
Your bridges have deliberately had no IP address all week. A2 explained why: a switch is not a host on the segment, it is the segment, and a port carrying an IP is a router leg rather than a bridge port.

So where does a management address go? Not on a port — that would put it in whichever VLAN the port belongs to and make it a host there. It goes on an interface attached to the bridge from the inside, inside one VLAN. The bridge is a switch with many VLANs; you are plugging a small management host into one of them, and that host happens to be the switch's own IP stack.

Two steps. First tell the bridge that it is itself a member of VLAN 99 — not a port, the bridge:

# on SW1 and SW2
nmcli con modify br0 bridge.vlans "99"
nmcli con up br0
bridge vlan show          # note the new line for br0 itself, not for any ethN

Then create the interface that lives in that VLAN and carries the address:

# on SW1
nmcli con add type vlan ifname br0.99 con-name mgmt dev br0 id 99 \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.201/24 \
      ipv6.method disabled
nmcli con up mgmt

# on SW2 — same, with .202

On PC-MGMT, which is an ordinary host on an access port and therefore needs no tagging at all:

# on PC-MGMT
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name mgmt0 \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.200/24 ipv6.method disabled
nmcli con up mgmt0

ping -c2 192.168.10.202      # the switch it is plugged into
ping -c2 192.168.10.201      # the switch it is not
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: The path those pings take
items.text:
┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ SW1 IP stack  192.168.10.201/24   │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │                                 no tag — an ordinary interface
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ br0.99        8021q VLAN device   │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │                                 tag 99 popped up / pushed down
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ br0           the CPU port        │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
      ────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────    self: vid 99 tagged
                                          │
      ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
      │ SW1   bridge forwarding · per-VLAN FDB · VLAN filter           │
      └─────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────┬──────┘
            │eth0  10 untagged                        │eth2     │eth3
            │                                         │         │
       PC1 ─┘                                         │         │           two inter-switch links,
                                                      │         │           both tagged members of 10 and 99
                                                      │         ╳ one blocked by STP
                                                      │         │           tag 99 rides the forwarding one
                         PC-MGMT ─┐                   │         │
                                  │                   │         │
       PC2 ─┐                     │                   │         │
            │                     │                   │         │
            │eth0  10 untagged    │eth1  99 untagged  │eth2     │eth3
      ┌─────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────────┬─────────┬──────┐
      │ SW2   bridge forwarding · per-VLAN FDB · VLAN filter           │
      └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
      ────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────    self: vid 99 tagged
                                          │
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ br0           the CPU port        │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ br0.99        8021q VLAN device   │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
                        ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ SW2 IP stack  192.168.10.202/24   │
                        └───────────────────────────────────┘

(Rendered version for slides or print: topologies/a8-management-path.svg.)

Each switch is drawn with its ports facing the other and its own IP stack facing away — because that is what a management interface is: an attachment to the bridge from the inside, not one of the ports. PC-MGMT is in VLAN 99 on SW2:eth1, and your two pings take quite different journeys.

.202, the switch it is plugged into. Untagged into eth1, so it takes that port's PVID and becomes a VLAN 99 frame. FDB lookup happens inside VLAN 99, the destination MAC is the bridge's own, so the result is not "out a port" but "deliver locally" — egress toward br0, which VLAN filtering checks like any other port. br0 is a member of 99 and the entry is tagged, so the frame arrives at br0.99 still carrying its header, and br0.99 pops it. The frame never leaves SW2.

.201, the switch it has no cable to. Identical until the FDB, which this time points out the forwarding trunk — tagged, because eth2 is a tagged member. SW1 classifies it on ingress by that tag, looks up VLAN 99, finds its own MAC, and hands it up its own br0 → br0.99. This is the concrete reason VLAN 99 has to be on the trunks: without it the frame is dropped by ingress filtering at SW1:eth2 and SW1 is unreachable, cable or no cable.

Both replies retrace the same steps in the other direction, br0.99 pushing the tag back on.

And PC1, in VLAN 10, gets as far as the FDB and no further: neither bridge has a vid 10 self entry, so there is no path from VLAN 10 to either IP stack. That is prediction 3, and the isolation is one line of VLAN membership enforced at one place.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• bridge vlan show now has a line for br0 itself. Every other line is a port — a way into the switch from outside. This one is the switch's own way in, from inside. That is the difference between a bridge port and a management interface, and it is the thing milestone 1 makes you work out.
  • PC-MGMT reached SW1, which it has no cable to, through SW2 and across a trunk. That is what makes this a management network rather than a management port.
  • SW1 and SW2 are still not hosts in VLAN 10, 20 or 30. They have exactly one address each, reachable from exactly one VLAN.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Part 3 — Actually managing something
items.text:
A ping proves a switch is alive. It does not administer anything. From PC-MGMT:

ssh admin@192.168.10.201
bridge vlan show
exit

Now do it to the whole fleet from one chair, without logging into anything:

# on PC-MGMT
for s in 201 202; do
    echo "=== switch at .$s ==="
    ssh admin@192.168.10.$s 'bridge link'
done

And from PC1, in VLAN 10, try exactly the same thing:

# on PC1
ssh admin@192.168.10.201
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• That is the answer to "why does a switch need an address." Not to be pinged — to be read, audited and changed from somewhere other than a chair in front of it. Two switches is already too many consoles to walk to; a building has forty.
  • The loop over .201 and .202 is a real operations task — collecting the state of every device to compare it against what you think you deployed. It is also how you find the one switch somebody changed by hand at 2am.
  • PC1 hung and failed, and the reason matters. Nothing blocked it. There is no firewall rule and no password involved — VLAN 10 and VLAN 99 are separate broadcast domains with no router between them, so the packet had nowhere to go. It is the same reason PC1 cannot reach a host in VLAN 20: not forbidden, unreachable.
  • Notice what that means for milestone 2. Once a router arrives and VLANs can reach each other, PC1 will be able to reach the switches, and keeping it out stops being a happy accident of topology and becomes a decision somebody has to make and configure.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Part 4 — Changing the network from somewhere else
items.text:
SW1 is currently root, and PC-MGMT is plugged into SW2. Confirm both facts from PC-MGMT without touching a console:

# on PC-MGMT
for s in 201 202; do ssh admin@192.168.10.$s 'cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/root_id'; done

Both should print SW1's bridge ID. Now move the root to SW2 — from PC-MGMT, over the network:

# on PC-MGMT
ssh admin@192.168.10.202 'sudo ip link set dev br0 type bridge priority 2048'

Wait about 30 seconds, then re-run the loop above, and check bridge link on both.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The root moved, and your management did not care. You reached both switches before, and you reach both switches now. The root is a spanning-tree decision about which way frames travel; the management address is a host interface in a VLAN. They have nothing to do with each other, and nothing about being root makes a switch more or less administrable.
  • Read that against the two states you have now seen: at the start the root was SW1, a switch PC-MGMT has no cable to. Now it is SW2, the switch PC-MGMT is plugged into. Neither arrangement is more correct, and neither changed how you administer anything.
  • The blocked port moved too. Re-run the reasoning from A5 §5 and check that the port now blocking is the one the rules say should block.
  • If your session stalled for a few seconds before returning — that is STP reconverging, and you watched a live outage from inside a management session. It is exactly what a topology change feels like from the chair.

You can cut yourself off this way. You have just changed, over the network, the thing that decides how the network forwards. A worse change — putting SW2:eth1 in the wrong VLAN, say — would strand PC-MGMT with no path to anything, and the only recovery is the GNS3 console. That is not a lab artefact. Being locked out of a device you are configuring is a standard hazard with a standard answer: keep console access, and do not change the thing you are reaching the device through.

Put the root back where you meant it, and this time persistently, so it is still true after a restart:

# on SW2, via ssh from PC-MGMT
sudo nmcli con modify br0 bridge.priority 32768
sudo nmcli con up br0

SW1 already carries bridge.priority 4096 from Part 1, so it takes the root back.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: Part 5 — The only test that counts
items.text:
Stop both switches from the GNS3 toolbar. Start them again. Wait for them to boot, touch nothing, and from PC-MGMT:

# on PC-MGMT
for s in 201 202; do
    echo "=== switch at .$s ==="
    ssh admin@192.168.10.$s 'bridge vlan show; bridge link; cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/root_id'
done

Then ping PC2 from PC1.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Everything came back: the bridge, VLAN filtering, every port's VLAN membership, both trunks, STP, the chosen root, and the management address. You typed nothing after the reboot.
  • Do the same experiment mentally for A4 and A5, which built the identical network with ip and bridge. After that reboot there is no br0 at all. Those commands were never wrong — they are for exploring, and they let you undo a mistake by restarting the node. They simply do not persist, and were never meant to.
  • Milestone 1 will be restarted during marking. This part is the one that decides whether it still works when it is.
path: W3·A8 — Configuration that survives, and a switch you can log into ★

The heaviest week so far, and the first graded one. Milestone 1 is handed out at the end of session 1 so students have the whole week to see the activities as preparation.

Session Do Note 1 A1, A2 hand out milestone 1 in the last 10 minutes 2 A4, A3 A4 first — it is the week's second anchor and A3 is short 3 A5, then A7 if time A5 needs a full hour; A7 works well as a closer with no machines

Compressed: A1, A4, A5. A2 and A3 are each 25–35 minutes and can be homework.

items.title: RAM budget
items.text:
Both role templates used this week are 512 MB — OL9 Switch and OL9 PC — so the whole week is cheaper than it looks. The built-in Ethernet switch in A3 costs nothing.

Activity Nodes RAM Notes A1 1 Switch 512 MB + 4 VPCS (negligible) A2 1 Switch + 1 PC 1 GB PC1 must be an OL9 PC A3 4 PCs 2 GB all four must be OL9 PCs — VPCS silently under-counts A4 1–2 Switches 0.5–1 GB 2 for the trunk section A5 2 Switches 1 GB + 4 VPCS A6 1 Docker + hosts — Docker on the server required A8 2 Switches + 2 PCs 2 GB the week's longest activity

A3 and A8 tie at 2 GB, which is the week's peak and comfortable on any machine that can run the GNS3 VM at all. If you are working from older notes that put A3 at 4 GB, that was the general-purpose node at 1 GB each; the PC template halves it.

items.title: What actually goes wrong
items.text:
• br_netfilter. Bridged frames get handed to iptables and pings fail with a correct-looking bridge. sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=0. This will bite in A1, A4 and A5. Consider setting it in the image.
  • A1's ageing time is in centiseconds and iproute2 is otherwise consistent about seconds. Students set 3000 expecting 3000 seconds. Have them cross-check with cat /sys/class/net/br0/bridge/ageing_time.
  • A4's vid 1 deletion is the single most-skipped line in the week. Without it, VLANs appear not to work and students conclude they mistyped something. Put it on the board.
  • A2 requires PC1 to be OL9. Students who try ip neigh in VPCS get a syntax error and assume the activity is broken.
  • A5's storm can lock a slow laptop. Show them the toolbar stop button before they build it. Also insist they remove the second link promptly — students leave it running while discussing.
  • A5 part 3 convergence takes ~30 s and students conclude it failed at 10 s. Say the number in advance.

items.title: Things to say out loud
items.text:
• After A1's ageing demo: "That table is never right. It is only recently correct. Every switch you will ever touch is working from a slightly stale memory."
  • After A4: "You broke that network on purpose and it is now more correct than it was. Every campus network you have used is deliberately broken this way."
  • After A5 part 1: "Nothing was wrong with either switch. Both behaved exactly as designed. The fault was in the topology, and the topology was the thing you were told to add for reliability."
  • After A7 question 3: ask which cable is shared. Wait.

items.title: The platform gap, handled
items.text:
CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA cannot be demonstrated in GNS3 at all. There is no shared medium and no collision model; the hub does not collide either. A7 exists because of that, and it teaches the topic better than an animation would — students who have had to stop mid-word remember why jam signals exist.

If you want the picture as well, Packet Tracer animates a collision in Simulation mode. Ten minutes, projected, is enough.

items.title: Assessment
items.text:
Milestone 1 opens this week. See ../../project/milestone1-switching/. The activities are ungraded and are deliberately a superset of the techniques the milestone needs — A1 gives them the table, A4 the VLANs, A5 the redundancy, A2 the evidence technique for proving traffic is absent.

Watch for the common misread: students think the milestone is A1–A5 repeated with more nodes. It is not — it gives requirements and no commands, and the marks are in the design decisions and the evidence. Say that when handing it out.

  • [ ] Milestone 1 brief printed for session 1

items.title: STP priority
items.text:
The requirement for steps of 4096 comes down to how a switch creates its Bridge Identifier (ID) when using the standard Extended System ID field.

To understand this, we have to look at the exact binary breakdown of the Bridge Priority field.The 16-Bit Priority Field SplitOriginally, the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) allocated a full 16-bit binary field purely for the Bridge Priority. This allowed any number from 0 to 65,535.

However, when VLANs (Virtual Local Area Networks) were introduced, switches needed to run a separate instance of STP for each VLAN (Per-VLAN Spanning Tree or PVST). To avoid needing a unique MAC address for every single VLAN instance, the IEEE updated the standard. They split that original 16-bit field into two distinct parts:

  • Bridge Priority (4 bits): The leftmost (most significant) bits.
  • Extended System ID (12 bits): The rightmost bits, used exclusively to hold the VLAN ID.

|===============================================================| | Original 16-bit Field | |===============================================================| | 4-bit Bridge Priority | 12-bit Extended System ID | (Multiples of 4096) (Holds the VLAN ID, 1 to 4094) | |===============================================================|

items.title: Why the Math Forces 4096
items.text:
In binary, the 12 bits reserved for the VLAN ID can represent any number from 0 to 4,095 (2¹² = 4096 total values).Because the 4 priority bits sit to the left of these 12 bits, changing the very lowest priority bit means you are changing the 13th bit of the overall 16-bit number.

In binary place values, the 13th bit represents the number 4096 (2¹²).Therefore, you can only manipulate the four leftmost bits. Your configuration options are limited to the following binary combinations:

  • 0000 (plus VLAN ID) = 0 0001 (plus VLAN ID) = 4096 0010 (plus VLAN ID) = 8192
  • 0011 (plus VLAN ID) = 12288 ...up to 1000 = 32768 (the default) ...up to 1111 = 61440

items.title: How the Switch Calculates the Final Value
items.text:
When you assign a base priority to a switch, the hardware takes your base number and mathematically adds the VLAN ID to it to create a completely unique Bridge ID for that specific VLAN.

For example, if you configure your base priority to be 4096:

  • For VLAN 1: The absolute priority becomes (4096 + 1 = 4097).
  • For Slots in VLAN 10: The absolute priority becomes (4096 + 10 = 4106).

Because the switch uses those 12 bits for the VLAN ID, it is physically impossible for a standard hardware switch to accept a base priority like 2048, as that would require changing the 12th bit—which is strictly reserved for the VLAN architecture.

(Note: Software-based bridges, like the native Linux kernel network bridge, do not natively use the 12-bit Extended System ID modification for VLANs in the same way, which is why software bridges uniquely allow any arbitrary number from 0 to 65535, including 2048).

items.title: Week 4 — IPv4, the network layer and static routing
items.text:
Assumes: weeks 1–3. Students can turn an OL9 node into a router (W2·A2), know that a router rewrites layer-2 addressing while leaving layer-3 alone, and have a VLAN'd network from week 3 that is deliberately unable to route between its segments.

Leaves students able to: read and predict a routing table; explain longest-prefix match by interrogating the kernel; diagnose a one-directional routing failure from two captures; account for every address change along a multi-hop path; connect two VLANs with a router; name the device that generated an ICMP message and say what decision it was reporting; and explain why a documented IPv4 feature can work perfectly in a lab and nowhere else.
path: Week 4 — IPv4, the network layer and static routing

items.title: The arc
items.text:
Week 2 built a router whose subnets were all directly connected — it needed no routes, because every destination was out one of its own ports. This week is about the other case: destinations you are not attached to, which is every destination that matters.

The week's spine is a failure. A2 builds a network that is correctly configured at every visible point and works in one direction only, and the diagnosis requires captures at two places at once. Everything before it is preparation and everything after it is consequence.

The base topology is the course's standard one:

  LAN1 192.168.100.0/24      transit 10.0.0.0/30      LAN2 192.168.200.0/24

  PC1 ─── SW1 ─── R1 ═══════════════════════════ R2 ─── SW2 ─── PC2
  .10             .1  10.0.0.1         10.0.0.2  .1             .10
# Activity Time Needs A1 The routing table 40 min 1 router, 1 PC, 1 switch A2 The one-way route ★ 50 min 2 routers, 2 PCs, 2 switches A3 What changes at each hop ★ 45 min A2's topology A4 TTL, and what traceroute really is 35 min A2's topology A5 Routing between VLANs 45 min 1 router, 1 switch, 4 VPCS A6 The error channel ★ 45 min A2's topology A7 Echo, and what ping does not prove 45 min A6 finished A8 The options nobody uses ☆ 45 min A4 finished + a NAT node A9 Forge the packet ☆ 50 min A6 + A7 finished; 3 PCs, 1 switch

★ = keep if compressed. ☆ = extension; homework or drop.

Plus one non-activity document: reading-why-protocol-extensions-die.md, assigned after A8. No commands, nothing to submit.
path: Week 4 — IPv4, the network layer and static routing

items.title: Sequencing note
items.text:
A2 before A3. A2 produces a failure that A3 then explains completely. Reversed, A3 is a tour of header fields with no reason to care.

A5 closes week 3's open question — W3·A4 ended by proving a switch cannot move traffic between VLANs and postponing the fix. Students have been carrying that for a week. Pay it off.

A6 before A7, and both after A4. A4 teaches one ICMP message type and turns it into a tool without ever saying what ICMP is. A6 supplies the model — where ICMP sits inside IP, who generates a message, and the quoted-packet mechanism the whole protocol rests on. A7 then depends on that mechanism directly: path MTU discovery is unexplainable until students have seen an error quote their own packet back at them.

A8 after A4, and it needs the reading. A8's payoff is a comparison between A4's traceroute and the designed feature that was supposed to do the same job and lost. The activity states the conclusion; the reading is where it becomes a general rule about how the internet evolves. Assigning one without the other wastes both.

A9 caps A6 and A7, and it forges rather than reads. A6 and A7 build ICMP on paper — where it sits, what it quotes, how PMTU discovery uses that quote. A9 hands students scapy and has them construct the messages by hand, culminating in a forged fragmentation-needed error that changes a third host's path MTU without being either endpoint. It is the security payoff of A6's quoted-datagram lesson, and it needs both A6 and A7 done first or it lands as syntax with no meaning.
path: Week 4 — IPv4, the network layer and static routing

items.title: The second half of the week is about the network describing itself
items.text: A1–A5 are about forwarding: where a packet goes and why. A6–A9 are about the network's own commentary on that — the error channel, the query channel, a designed self-description mechanism that died, and finally forging the commentary itself to see that none of it is authenticated. Students who have only done A1–A5 can build a network. Students who have done A6–A9 can find out what is wrong with one, and why they cannot fully trust what it tells them.
