items.title: W4·A1 — The routing table
items.text:
Time: 40 min · Needs: one OL9 Router, one OL9 PC, one Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: w04-a1-routing-table

The question: a host has one cable and can reach the entire internet through it. What does it consult to decide where to send each packet, and how does it choose when more than one entry fits?

items.title: Build it
items.text:
LAN1 192.168.100.0/24      10.0.0.0/30

  PC1 ─── SW1 ─── R1 ───────────
  .10             .1  10.0.0.1

R1 is an OL9 Router, PC1 an OL9 PC, and SW1 a plain Ethernet switch — the LAN needs one, even with a single host on it. Nothing is cabled to R1:eth1; the subnet on it exists purely to be somewhere PC1 is not attached.

An OL9 Router has four network adapters, and NetworkManager will take over any you leave alone — which undoes your addressing a moment after you type it. So tell it to leave all four alone, even though this activity only uses two.

# on R1
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done
ip addr add 192.168.100.1/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/30      dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# on PC1
nmcli device set eth0 managed no
ip addr add 192.168.100.10/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
PC1 has one address and no routes you have typed.

  1. How many entries are in its routing table? _
  2. Can it reach 192.168.100.50? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. Can it reach 10.0.0.1, which is on the router it is plugged into? ☐ yes ☐ no

items.title: Do this — the table you did not write
items.text:
# on PC1
ip route show
ping -c1 192.168.100.1
ping -c1 10.0.0.1

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• There is one entry, and you never typed it: 192.168.100.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link. Assigning an address to an interface is an implicit claim that its whole subnet is reachable out that port, and the kernel records that claim as a route. proto kernel means exactly "I did this, you did not".
  • 192.168.100.1 worked — it matches the connected route, so PC1 sends it directly, ARPing for the destination itself.
  • 10.0.0.1 failed, with Network is unreachable, and note where the error came from: PC1's own kernel, instantly, before anything was transmitted. Confirm with a capture — the wire is silent. A host with no matching route does not try and fail; it does not try.
  • 10.0.0.1 is on the router PC1 sends everything through, two cables away. Physical connectivity is irrelevant. The table is the whole of the decision.

items.title: Do this — a default route
items.text:
# on PC1
ip route add default via 192.168.100.1
ip route show
ping -c1 10.0.0.1

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• One line, and every destination in the world is now attempted. default is 0.0.0.0/0 — a prefix of length zero, which matches everything, and is therefore the entry of last resort.
  • This is what "default gateway" means, and it is the entry your laptop gets from DHCP.
  • It says nothing about whether the destination exists. It says where to send things you have no better idea about. Every failure from here on is somewhere else's problem, which is why diagnosing them needs A2's technique.

items.title: Do this — interrogate the decision
items.text:
Add more specific routes and ask the kernel which one it would use. First, though, give R1 two extra addresses on the interface PC1 is plugged into:

# on R1
ip addr add 192.168.100.2/24 dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.100.3/24 dev eth0
ip addr show eth0

An aside — one interface, several addresses. An interface is not limited to one address. eth0 now answers to .1, .2 and .3 at once: same cable, same MAC, same subnet, and R1 replies to ARP for all three. Older documentation calls these aliases and names them eth0:0, eth0:1; the ip command simply lists them for what they are, a set of addresses on one interface. Real uses:

  • one server hosting several services that each need their own address rather than sharing one
  • renumbering — a router holds the old and the new gateway address simultaneously, so hosts move across a few at a time instead of all at the instant of the change
  • a management address kept apart from the service address, so the box stays reachable when the service address moves elsewhere

W4·A5 gives one router several addresses a different way: separate VLAN subinterfaces, one address each. Several addresses on one interface, or several interfaces on one port — both are common, and they are not the same mechanism.

Here they do something more specific: with three addresses on R1, three routes can each point at a different one. What that buys you is the point of what follows.

# on PC1
ip route get 192.168.100.50
ip route get 10.0.0.1
ip route get 8.8.8.8

ip route add 10.0.0.0/24 via 192.168.100.2
ip route get 10.0.0.1

ip route add 10.0.0.0/30 via 192.168.100.3
ip route get 10.0.0.1

ip route get 10.0.0.9
ip route show match 10.0.0.1
ip route show

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• ip route get is the routing table's own answer, not your reading of it — use it instead of arguing about which line applies. Read carefully what it reports: the decision, as a next hop, an outgoing interface and a source address. It does not report which entry produced that decision.
  • That distinction is why R1 needed three addresses. Had all three routes pointed via 192.168.100.1, all three answers would have come back exactly the same and you could not tell which route produced them — the packets reach the same box either way. Giving each route its own next hop is what makes the choice visible, and it costs nothing, since .1, .2 and .3 are all R1.
  • Three destinations, three answers, one table: 10.0.0.1 → via .3, the /30. 10.0.0.9 → via .2, the /24, since it is outside the /30. 8.8.8.8 → via .1, the default. Longest prefix wins, always, regardless of the order lines appear in or the order you added them.
  • The rule has a good reason: a longer prefix is a more specific claim, and the most specific applicable claim is the one most likely to be correct. It is how a global routing table can hold a broad statement and a narrow exception at once, with no conflict.
  • ip route show match 10.0.0.1 asks the other half of the question: not which route wins but which routes could have won. It lists all three. Note that it does not put them in order of preference — the order is the table's own. route get names the winner; show match names the list the winner was chosen from.

items.title: Do this — take the default away
items.text:
# on PC1
ip route del default
ip route del 10.0.0.0/24
ip route del 10.0.0.0/30
ip route show

ping -c1 192.168.100.1
ping -c1 10.0.0.1

Sort the two results into "still works" and "does not".

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Direct delivery survives; everything else does not. The connected route is the only thing a host truly needs and the only thing it gets for free.
  • Those are the two cases a host distinguishes, every time it sends anything: is the destination inside a prefix I am attached to? If yes, ARP for it and send. If no, ARP for a gateway and send it there instead, with the destination IP untouched.
  • Week 1's /25 break (W1·A1) was this decision going wrong. PC1 classified PC2 as "not local" and had no gateway to fall back on. You now have the vocabulary for what you saw in week 1.

items.title: Record
items.text: Entries before you added any Where the Network is unreachable error came from Prefix length of default Next hop chosen for 10.0.0.1 / 10.0.0.9 / 8.8.8.8 The rule that chose them The one thing ip route get does not tell you Destinations still reachable with no default route

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Routes disappear after a moment NetworkManager nmcli device set eth0 managed no before addressing ip route add → Nexthop has invalid gateway gateway not in a connected subnet the next hop must be directly reachable ip route get shows a different source address multiple addresses on the interface expected; note which it chose and why All three ip route get answers are identical your routes share a next hop route get reports the decision, not the entry — check the routes point at .1, .2, .3 ip addr add → RTNETLINK answers: File exists address already on the interface ip addr show eth0; nothing to fix, carry on ip route show match prints them in an odd order table order, not specificity order it lists candidates; only route get ranks Ping to 10.0.0.1 still fails with the default route ip_forward off on R1, or firewalld sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward; systemctl stop firewalld Everything reachable with no routes at all you are pinging the local interface ping the router's address, not your own

items.title: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire
items.text:
Time: 30 min · Needs: one Ethernet switch, one OL9 Router, 2 VPCS · GNS3 project: w04-a10-multinet

The question: A5 gave two subnets two broadcast domains (VLANs) and a router to join them. Here is a stranger arrangement: two subnets on one wire, one broadcast domain, no VLANs at all. Does a router still have anything to do? And is anything actually being routed?
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. PC1 (192.168.10.11) and PC2 (192.168.20.12) are plugged into the same switch, on the same wire. Will PC1 reach PC2 on its own, with no router? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. If a router is needed even though they share a wire, what does that tell you about how a host decides "local" versus "remote"? _
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: Build it
items.text:
One switch, two VPCS, one OL9 router — all on the same switch, one broadcast domain:

PC1 .11 ─┐
PC2 .12 ─┼─[ SW1 ]─ R1 eth0
          │
   one wire, one broadcast domain

Give the two PCs addresses in two different subnets, each pointing at the router:

# PC1 — subnet 192.168.10.0/24
ip 192.168.10.11/24 192.168.10.1

# PC2 — subnet 192.168.20.0/24
ip 192.168.20.12/24 192.168.20.1

Now the unusual part. R1 has one network card, but it needs a foot in both subnets — so give eth0 two addresses, one per subnet, and turn on forwarding:

# on R1
nmcli device set eth0 managed no
ip link set eth0 up

ip addr add 192.168.10.1/24 dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.20.1/24 dev eth0     # a second address on the same card

sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
ip addr show dev eth0

The second ip addr add is a secondary address — one interface wearing two subnet identities. That is the whole trick.
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: Do this — it works, and it is routed
items.text:
From PC1:

ping 192.168.20.12
traceroute 192.168.20.12
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It works — and traceroute shows one hop, 192.168.10.1, the router. Even though PC1 and PC2 are on the same physical wire and could hear each other directly, the traffic detoured through R1. Nothing went straight across.
  • Why the detour? PC1 reads its own netmask, sees 192.168.20.12 is not in 192.168.10.0/24, and therefore treats it as remote — so it does not ARP for PC2 at all. It hands the packet to its gateway (192.168.10.1) instead. PC2 does the mirror image on the way back. The hosts' idea of "local vs remote" is decided entirely by the subnet mask, not by what is physically reachable.
  • This is genuine routing, and ip_forward is what makes it happen. The packet arrives at R1 inside a frame addressed to the router's MAC, but its IP destination is PC2, not the router. With forwarding off, Linux would drop it — "not my address." With forwarding on, R1 looks the destination up, finds 192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected on the same card, re-frames the packet to PC2's MAC, decrements the TTL, and sends it back out the interface it came in on. Turn forwarding off (sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0) and the ping stops — proof the router is doing real work, not just sharing a wire.
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: Do this — the catch: there is no isolation
items.text:
Start a capture on PC1's link (right-click the link → Start capture). Then, from PC2, make it send a broadcast — the simplest is to clear its ARP and ping its gateway so it has to ARP:

# on PC2
clear ip                # VPCS: forget learned addresses
ping 192.168.20.1
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC1's cable sees PC2's ARP broadcast, even though the two are in different subnets. There is only one broadcast domain here — the mask separates them at layer 3, but nothing separates them at layer 2. Compare this with A5: there, a capture on one VLAN's cable stayed silent during the other VLAN's traffic. Here it does not.
  • This arrangement has a name — multinetting (two subnets sharing one segment via secondary addresses). It is real, but it is a stopgap, not a design: you meet it when someone ran out of addresses and bolted a second subnet onto an existing wire, or mid-migration. The clean way to put two subnets on shared switch hardware is VLANs (A5), precisely because VLANs give the layer-2 separation multinetting lacks.
  • The missing isolation is not just untidy — it is a security property you have given up. Any host on the wire can hear every other host's broadcasts regardless of subnet, which is exactly the shared medium the network-security activities exploit (see NS·A3 — ARP spoofing and MITM: a single broadcast domain is what lets an attacker sit in the middle). Two subnets that look separate but share a broadcast domain are separate only on paper.
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: Record
items.text:
PC1 → PC2: worked? how many hops? Why the traffic went through R1 despite sharing a wire What ip_forward=0 on R1 does to the ping The two addresses on R1's single eth0 What PC1's cable saw during PC2's ARP How many broadcast domains — here, versus A5's VLANs

One sentence: what separates the two subnets here, and what does not?
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix PC1 cannot reach PC2 at all forwarding off, or a missing address on R1 ip_forward=1, and both ip addr add lines on eth0 traceroute shows no router hop PCs given the same subnet by mistake they must be in different subnets (.10.0/24 and .20.0/24) PCs reach R1 but not each other ip_forward still off sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 Capture on PC1 stays silent capture on the wrong link, or PC2 did not broadcast capture PC1's own link; on PC2 clear ip then ping its gateway Second ip addr add "already assigned" you reused a subnet the two addresses must be in different subnets
path: W4·A10 — Two subnets on one wire

items.title: W4·A2 — The one-way route ★
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: two OL9 Routers, two OL9 PCs, two Ethernet switches, Wireshark · GNS3 project: w04-base — keep this project; A3 and A4 continue in it

The question: every interface is up, every address is correct, every subnet is right, and the ping fails. Find out why without guessing.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
LAN1 192.168.100.0/24      transit 10.0.0.0/30      LAN2 192.168.200.0/24

  PC1 ─── SW1 ─── R1 ═══════════════════════════ R2 ─── SW2 ─── PC2
  .10             .1  10.0.0.1         10.0.0.2  .1             .10

R1 and R2 are OL9 Routers, PC1 and PC2 OL9 PCs, SW1 and SW2 plain Ethernet switches. Each LAN gets a switch even though only one host sits on it — that is what a LAN is, and A6 and A8 will both plug something else into SW1.

Tell NetworkManager to leave every interface alone before you address anything, or it will undo your work a moment after you type it. A router has four adapters, so that means all four, even though this topology only uses two:

# on R1 and on R2
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done

# on PC1 and on PC2
nmcli device set eth0 managed no

# R1
ip addr add 192.168.100.1/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/30      dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# R2
ip addr add 192.168.200.1/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 10.0.0.2/30      dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1

# PC1
ip addr add 192.168.100.10/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.100.1

# PC2
ip addr add 192.168.200.10/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.200.1

Check the transit link works before going further: from R1, ping -c1 10.0.0.2.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
R1 knows about 192.168.100.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/30. R2 knows about 192.168.200.0/24 and 10.0.0.0/30. Neither has been told about the other's LAN.

  1. PC1 pings PC2. Where does the packet get to before it stops? _
  2. What error will PC1 report? _

items.title: Part 1 — Add one route, not two
items.text:
Deliberately configure only the forward direction:

# on R1 only
ip route add 192.168.200.0/24 via 10.0.0.2
ip route show

Add nothing to R2. Then from PC1:

ping -c2 192.168.200.10

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• No replies, and ping gives you nothing to work with — no error, just silence and 100% loss. The most useless failure mode there is.
  • Every check you can make from PC1 passes. Its address is right, its gateway responds, its route is correct, the cable is up. The fault is not visible from either endpoint, and this is the situation that makes people start changing things at random.

items.title: Part 2 — Diagnose it properly
items.text:
Do not guess. Capture at two places at once: the PC1↔R1 link and the R2↔PC2 link. Then ping again.

Fill this in from the captures:

Link Echo request seen? Echo reply seen? PC1 ↔ R1 R2 ↔ PC2

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The request appears on both links. It crossed both routers and was delivered to PC2. The forward path is perfect.
  • PC2's capture shows it generating a reply — and the reply never reaches PC1.
  • On R2, ask the kernel directly:
# on R2
ip route get 192.168.100.10

Network is unreachable. R2 received a perfectly good packet, answered it, and had nowhere to send the answer.

  • A route describes one direction only. R1 was told how to reach LAN2. Nothing told R2 how to reach LAN1, and nothing ever would — routers do not learn return paths from traffic the way a switch learns MAC addresses. This is the single most important difference between what week 3's switch did and what a router does.
  • Notice how thoroughly the endpoints were unable to see this. PC1 saw silence. PC2 saw a normal request and answered it, entirely satisfied. Only two simultaneous observations located the fault, and the location was a third device that reported nothing.

items.title: Part 3 — Fix it
items.text:
# on R2
ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 10.0.0.1
ip route show

From PC1: ping -c2 192.168.200.10.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It works, immediately, with no other change. Two routes for one conversation — one per direction, on different devices.
  • Count what a two-router path required: two static routes, and neither router can be checked in isolation. Now imagine ten routers, where every pair needs this and every new subnet touches every device. That arithmetic is the entire argument for dynamic routing protocols, and it is why the course arrives at OSPF later.

items.title: Part 4 — The same fault, disguised
items.text:
Remove R2's route and instead add a wrong one:

# on R2
ip route del 192.168.100.0/24
ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 10.0.0.2      # its own address
ip route get 192.168.100.10

Ping again from PC1, and check the transit-link capture.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The route was accepted, and nothing warned you. ip route get answers confidently — but read its answer closely, because there is no via in it:
192.168.100.10 dev eth1 src 10.0.0.2
  • A next hop that is one of the router's own addresses is not a next hop. The kernel discards it and treats the whole /24 as directly attached to eth1 — the transit link. So R2 does not forward these packets anywhere. It tries to deliver them on the transit link itself.
  • The capture shows exactly that: R2 ARPing for 192.168.100.10 on the transit wire, and getting no answer, because PC1 is on the far side of R1 and was never on this cable.
  • R2 also sends R1 an ICMP redirect — "to reach 192.168.100.10, send to 192.168.100.10" — because it is sending the packet back out the interface it came in on. When the ARP finally fails, it sends host unreachable. A6 explains that channel properly. For now note only that both messages came from R2 and describe R2's decision, not the destination.
  • Compare with Part 1: a missing route fails loudly at the kernel and silently at the endpoint. A wrong route is accepted everywhere, answers ip route get confidently, and then fails somewhere else entirely, in a way that points at the wrong device. "There is a route" is not the same as "the route is right", and the only proof is end-to-end traffic.
  • Put the correct route back before continuing to A3.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Echo request on PC1↔R1 / R2↔PC2 Echo reply on PC1↔R1 / R2↔PC2 ip route get 192.168.100.10 on R2, before the fix Which device held the fault Which devices reported an error Static routes needed for one two-router conversation

Two sentences: why could neither endpoint diagnose this, and what did you need instead?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Transit ping fails before you start /30 mask wrong, or wrong interfaces cabled ip addr show on both; 10.0.0.0/30 holds only .1 and .2 Both directions work in Part 1 you added routes to both routers ip route show on R2 — it must not know LAN1 No packets in either capture forwarding off on R1 sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward Request reaches R2 but not PC2 firewalld on PC2 systemctl stop firewalld Part 4's ip route get shows a via the address is not R2's own it must be R2's own transit address, or the fault is a different one No ARP requests in the Part 4 capture wrong link captured capture the transit link — that is where R2 is now ARPing

items.title: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: A2's topology, working in both directions · GNS3 project: w04-base (continue)

The question: one packet crosses three links to get from PC1 to PC2. Which parts of it are the same on all three, and which are different on every one?

Have your week 1 PDU table in front of you. This activity is that table, in motion.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Collect the addresses first
items.text:
You cannot read the captures without these. Twelve values; get them all before you start.

# on each of PC1, R1, R2, PC2
ip addr show
ip link show
Node Interface IP MAC PC1 eth0 192.168.100.10 R1 eth0 192.168.100.1 R1 eth1 10.0.0.1 R2 eth1 10.0.0.2 R2 eth0 192.168.200.1 PC2 eth0 192.168.200.10
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
PC1 pings PC2. For the echo request, on each of the three links:

Src MAC Dst MAC Src IP Dst IP PC1 ↔ R1 R1 ↔ R2 R2 ↔ PC2

Fill it in from your address table before capturing. Guessing wrong here is the point.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Do this
items.text:
Start captures on all three links simultaneously. Then:

# on PC1
ping -c1 192.168.200.10

Find the echo request in each capture and fill the table in again, from observation.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The two IP addresses are identical on all three links. Source 192.168.100.10, destination 192.168.200.10, from end to end. Neither router touched them.
  • Both MAC addresses are different on every link, and none of the six values appears twice. PC1's MAC exists only on the first link; PC2's only on the last.
  • So PC1 and PC2 never learn each other's MAC addresses, ever. They cannot: MACs have no meaning beyond one segment, and there are three segments here.
  • Layer 3 addressing is end-to-end. Layer 2 addressing is hop-by-hop, rewritten completely at every router. That is not an implementation detail; it is why the two layers exist separately, and your week 1 table is the picture of one moment in that process.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Do this — confirm it from the hosts
items.text:
# on PC1
ip neigh show

# on PC2
ip neigh show
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC1 holds R1's MAC. PC2 holds R2's MAC. Neither holds the other's, and neither ever will, however long you ping.
  • This is W2·A2 part 3 again, now with the full path visible. The frame PC1 sent was addressed to R1 at layer 2 and to PC2 at layer 3 — two destinations, in one frame, meaning different things.
  • The everyday consequence: "can you ping it?" and "is it on your network?" are completely different questions, and the ARP cache answers the second.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Do this — what else changed
items.text: Compare the IP header of the same echo request across the three captures, field by field. Two things differ.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• TTL decreased by one at each router. Started at 64 (Linux), 63 after R1, 62 after R2. Decrementing it is a router's obligation, and A4 is about what it is for.
  • The header checksum changed on every link. It has to: it covers the TTL field, so a router that changes the TTL must recompute it. Every router on the internet does this arithmetic for every packet.
  • Nothing else moved. Not the addresses, not the identification, not the payload. A router touches the smallest possible number of fields — everything else it forwards untouched, because everything else belongs to the endpoints.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Do this — the reply, for symmetry
items.text: Same three captures, now reading the echo reply.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every MAC pair reversed, per link, independently. Every IP pair reversed, once, end to end.
  • The reply's TTL started fresh at 64 from PC2 and arrived at PC1 as 62. The two directions count down separately, because they are separate journeys that happen to use the same wires.
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: Record
items.text:
The completed three-link table, prediction and observation side by side, plus:

Times the source IP changed Times the source MAC changed MAC in PC1's ARP cache for PC2 TTL on link 1 / link 2 / link 3 Header fields a router modified

One sentence each: what is layer-3 addressing for, and what is layer-2 addressing for?
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Only two captures show the packet routing broken again re-check A2 part 3's route on R2 MACs look identical across links you are reading the same capture twice check each Wireshark window's title bar TTL is 128, not 64 a non-Linux stack somewhere note the value; the decrement is what matters PC2's MAC appears in PC1's ARP cache the two are on the same segment — cabling error re-check the topology; there must be a router between them Cannot find the request in a capture too much other traffic filter on icmp
path: W4·A3 — What changes at each hop ★

items.title: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is
items.text:
Time: 35 min · Needs: A2's topology, working · GNS3 project: w04-base (continue)

The question: A3 showed the TTL counting down. What happens when it reaches zero, and why does that turn out to be the most useful diagnostic tool in networking?
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. PC1 sends a packet with TTL = 1 towards PC2. Where does it stop? _
  2. Does PC1 find out? ☐ yes ☐ no · If so, from whom? _
  3. TTL = 2? _
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Do this — walk the path by hand
items.text:
Start a capture on the PC1↔R1 link. Then:

# on PC1
ping -c1 -t 1 192.168.200.10
ping -c1 -t 2 192.168.200.10
ping -c1 -t 3 192.168.200.10
TTL Who answered What kind of message 1 2 3
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• TTL 1: R1 answered — Time to live exceeded. R1 decremented 1 to 0, discarded the packet, and sent you a message saying so.
  • TTL 2: R2 answered, the same way.
  • TTL 3: PC2 answered normally, with an echo reply.
  • You just learned the identity of every device on the path, in order, without any of them being configured to tell you anything. Each one identified itself by the source address of its complaint.
  • The reply came from the router's own address — the interface the packet arrived on. That is why a traceroute shows you the near side of each router, and why the same router can appear under different addresses in traceroutes from different directions.
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Do this — what it is actually for
items.text:
TTL exists to stop loops, not to enable traceroute. Rebuild A2 part 4's routing loop:

# on R2
ip route del 192.168.100.0/24
ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 10.0.0.2

Capture the transit link, then from PC1: ping -c1 192.168.200.10.
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The packet bounced within R2 until the TTL hit zero, then died. The loop was self-limiting.
  • Compare with W3·A5's broadcast storm, where a loop at layer 2 multiplied without bound and took the network down. Same topology mistake, radically different outcome, because layer 3 has a hop counter and layer 2 has none.
  • That contrast is the best single argument for why the IP header carries a field that seems, at first sight, like pointless overhead on every packet ever sent.

Restore the correct route: ip route del 192.168.100.0/24; ip route add 192.168.100.0/24 via 10.0.0.1.
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Do this — the automated version
items.text:
# on PC1
tracepath 192.168.200.10

(traceroute if it is installed; tracepath is part of iputils and always present.)
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It is the loop you just ran by hand: TTL 1, TTL 2, TTL 3, collecting who complains at each step. Nothing more sophisticated is happening.
  • Knowing that tells you exactly when to distrust it:
  • A router configured not to send ICMP errors shows as *. That is not a broken hop — it is a silent one, and the path may be perfect.
  • Each probe is a separate packet that may take a different route. A traceroute is a sample of several journeys, not a photograph of one.
  • It shows the forward path only. After A2, you know that the return path can be completely different and completely broken, and traceroute will not tell you.
  • tracepath also reports the MTU along the way, which is week 1's -M do experiment automated in the same style.
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Do this — one asymmetry worth seeing
items.text:
# on PC1
tracepath 192.168.200.10

# on PC2
tracepath 192.168.100.10
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The two lists are not mirror images: each shows the interface addresses facing towards the sender. R1 appears as 192.168.100.1 from one side and 10.0.0.1 from the other, and both are the same router.
  • A single machine having several addresses, and answering by whichever one faces you, is normal and is why "the router's IP address" is not a well-formed phrase.
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: Record
items.text: TTL Responder Message 1 2 3 What TTL is actually for What happened to the looping packet Why a layer-2 loop is worse Two reasons a traceroute hop might show * R1's address as seen from PC1 / from PC2
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix ping -t seems to do nothing on some systems -t means "timeout" on Linux iputils it is TTL; check ping --help No Time to live exceeded ICMP errors blocked by firewalld on the router systemctl stop firewalld on R1 and R2 tracepath shows only * as above same fix TTL 2 answered by R1 again R2 not forwarding sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward on R2
path: W4·A4 — TTL, and what traceroute really is

items.title: W4·A5 — Routing between VLANs
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one Ethernet switch, one OL9 Router, 4 VPCS · GNS3 project: w04-a5-intervlan

The question: week 3 ended with a network deliberately split into two VLANs that could not reach each other, and a promise that a router would fix it. Collect.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
Rebuild week 3's network, but not week 3's switch. In W3·A4 you built the switch by hand, because how a switch keeps VLANs apart was the thing being taught. Here it is not — the router is. So use a plain Ethernet switch and set its ports from a dialog box.

Drop in an Ethernet switch named SW1, right-click it → Configure, and set the ports:

Port Type VLAN Ethernet0, Ethernet1 access 10 Ethernet2, Ethernet3 access 20

Cable PC1 .11 and PC2 .12 to the VLAN 10 ports; PC3 .13 and PC4 .14 to the VLAN 20 ports. Leave every address in 192.168.10.0/24 for now, exactly as week 3 left them.

Confirm the week 3 result still holds: PC1 → PC2 works, PC1 → PC3 fails.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. You are about to attach a router. Will PC1 → PC3 work once it is cabled in? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. What else has to change? _

items.title: Part 1 — The addressing has to change first
What just happened
items.text:
• Two VLANs must be two subnets. A router forwards between networks, and if both sides are 192.168.10.0/24 there is nothing to forward between — every host would classify every other host as local and never consult a gateway at all.
  • Week 3 kept one subnet across both VLANs deliberately, to prove that the switch defines the segment and the addressing does not. That was a demonstration, not a design. Real VLANs come with their own subnet, and the reason is exactly this.
  • Note the direction of the dependency: the layer-2 decision (which VLAN) forces the layer-3 decision (which subnet), and not the other way round.

items.title: Part 2 — Router on a stick
items.text:
Add an OL9 Router named R1 and cable its eth0 to SW1:Ethernet4. That one port has to carry both VLANs, so set it differently from the others — Configure → Ports:

Port Type VLAN Ethernet4 dot1q 1

dot1q means "put a tag on everything leaving this port, so the other end can tell the VLANs apart". The VLAN number on a dot1q port is the one exception: traffic in that VLAN leaves untagged. Set it to 1, which nothing else uses, and VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 both leave tagged — which is what R1 needs.

Then, on R1, one physical interface carrying two VLANs:

# on R1
nmcli device set eth0 managed no
ip link set eth0 up

ip link add link eth0 name eth0.10 type vlan id 10
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.20 type vlan id 20

ip addr add 192.168.10.1/24 dev eth0.10 ; ip link set eth0.10 up
ip addr add 192.168.20.1/24 dev eth0.20 ; ip link set eth0.20 up

sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
ip addr show
ip route show

From PC1: ping 192.168.20.13.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It works, over a single cable that carries both VLANs.
  • eth0.10 and eth0.20 are sub-interfaces — one physical port, two logical ones, distinguished entirely by the 802.1Q tag you met in W3·A4. The router puts a tag on when sending and reads it when receiving; that 4-byte field is the whole mechanism.
  • ip route show gained two connected routes and you typed neither. As far as the routing table is concerned these are two ordinary attached networks, and nothing about the forwarding decision knows or cares that they share a wire.
  • The arrangement is called router on a stick, and the stick is the trunk.

items.title: Part 3 — Watch the tag flip
items.text: Capture the SW1↔R1 link — the one carrying both VLANs. From PC1, ping PC3 once, and examine the echo request and the echo reply.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The request arrives at R1 tagged VLAN 10 and leaves tagged VLAN 20. Same packet, same IP addresses, different tag — and a different destination MAC, because it is now on a different segment (A3's rule, applied on one cable).
  • Both frames are on the same wire, microseconds apart, in different broadcast domains. That is worth sitting with: the separation VLANs provide is entirely a matter of labels that the devices agree to respect.
  • Which is also the honest limitation. VLAN separation is enforced by configuration, not by physics. A misconfigured trunk port re-joins two segments you believed were separate, and nothing physical will tell you.

items.title: Part 4 — Separation you can still prove
items.text: Capture on PC2's access link (VLAN 10) while PC3 and PC4 (VLAN 20) ping each other, and while PC3 ARPs.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC2's cable stays silent throughout. The broadcast domains are still two, and the router did not merge them — it connected them at layer 3 while leaving layer 2 untouched.
  • So you now have both properties at once: broadcast isolation from the VLANs, reachability from the router, and a single point where traffic between the two groups can be inspected, filtered or refused.
  • That last point is the real reason organisations do this. Once all inter-VLAN traffic goes through one device, that device can have a policy — which is where firewalling lives in every campus network you have used.

items.title: Record
items.text:
PC1 → PC3 before the router Address changes required Sub-interfaces created on R1 Connected routes on R1, and who added them VLAN tag on the trunk, request / reply Traffic on PC2's cable during VLAN 20 activity

Two sentences: why must two VLANs be two subnets, and what does the router not merge?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Router reachable in one VLAN only Ethernet4 is still an access port Configure → Ports — it must be type dot1q Nothing works after adding sub-interfaces eth0 itself is down ip link set eth0 up before the sub-interfaces ip link add ... type vlan fails 8021q module not loaded modprobe 8021q Hosts reach the router but not each other forwarding off sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward Everything worked before you added the router all four ports are in the same VLAN check the port table: 0–1 in VLAN 10, 2–3 in VLAN 20 Trunk capture shows one VLAN untagged the trunk's VLAN is set to 10 or 20 set Ethernet4 to VLAN 1 — its own VLAN is the one that leaves untagged Cannot find the port settings you placed an Ethernet hub, not a switch a hub has no VLANs; delete it and place a switch

items.title: W4·A6 — The error channel
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: A2's topology, working · GNS3 project: w04-base (continue)

The question: Every failure so far has looked identical from the keyboard — "it doesn't work". The network has in fact been telling you exactly what went wrong and which device decided so. This is how to read it.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. ping 203.0.113.1 from PC1, which has no route to it. How many packets leave PC1? _
  2. A UDP datagram to a port nothing is listening on. What comes back, and from whom? _
  3. A host that is switched off. Who reports "host unreachable" — the missing host, or something else? _

items.title: Do this — five failures, five origins
items.text:
Start a capture on the PC1↔R1 link and leave it running for all five.

# 1 — no route on your own machine
# on PC1
ip route show
ping -c1 203.0.113.1

# 2 — no route on a router
# on PC1
ping -c1 198.51.100.7

# 3 — route exists, host absent
# on PC1
ping -c1 -W5 192.168.200.99

# 4 — host present, nothing listening
# on PC1
echo hello | ncat -u -w1 192.168.200.10 9999

# 5 — a device that refuses on purpose
# on R2
nft add table inet filter
nft add chain inet filter forward '{ type filter hook forward priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet filter forward ip daddr 192.168.200.10 icmp type echo-request \
    reject with icmp type admin-prohibited
# on PC1
ping -c1 192.168.200.10
# Packets seen leaving PC1 Reply came from Type Code Meaning 1 2 3 4 5

Now change case 5 from reject with icmp type admin-prohibited to drop and repeat:

# on R2
nft flush ruleset
nft add table inet filter
nft add chain inet filter forward '{ type filter hook forward priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet filter forward ip daddr 192.168.200.10 icmp type echo-request drop
# on PC1
ping -c1 192.168.200.10

What came back this time? _

Clean up before continuing: nft flush ruleset on R2.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Case 1 put nothing on the wire at all. Check the capture — it is empty. PC1's kernel looked in its routing table, found nothing, and refused before transmitting. "Network is unreachable" here is a local error message, not an ICMP packet, and no device on the network ever learned you tried. Distinguishing a local refusal from a network report is the first split in any diagnosis, and A1 is where you learned why the lookup happens first.
  • Case 2 came from R1 — Type 3, Code 0, net unreachable. R1 was the first device that had to make a forwarding decision it could not make, so R1 is the one that complained.
  • Case 3 came from R2, not from the absent host — obviously, since nothing is there to answer. R2 has 192.168.200.0/24 directly connected, so it ARPed for .99, got no reply, and only then reported Type 3 Code 1. That is why it took seconds rather than milliseconds. The device that reports an error is the device that discovered it.
  • Case 4 came from PC2 itself — Type 3 Code 3, port unreachable. Note what just happened: a network-layer protocol reported a transport-layer fact. ICMP has no ports of its own, yet this message identified one. Part 2 explains how.
  • Case 5, reject vs drop. Both stopped the traffic. Only one told you. Silence is a configuration decision someone made, not an absence of information — and from PC1 it is indistinguishable from a cable being unplugged.

items.title: Do this — what is inside an ICMP error
items.text:
Pick any of the Type 3 messages in Wireshark and expand it fully.

Bytes of your original packet quoted back Can you see the destination port you sent to? ☐ yes ☐ no

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every ICMP error carries the original IP header plus the first 8 bytes of the datagram that caused it. Not a description of your packet — your packet.
  • For TCP and UDP, those 8 bytes are exactly the source and destination ports. So the host receiving the error can attribute it to one specific socket instead of "something, somewhere, failed".
  • That is how case 4 could name a port: it quoted your datagram back at you.
  • This is the mechanism the entire protocol rests on. A7's path MTU discovery is impossible without it, and A9's forged errors are dangerous because of it.

items.title: Do this — where ICMP actually sits
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c1 192.168.200.10 &
tcpdump -i eth0 -v -n icmp -c1

Read the IP header in that output, not the ICMP part.

IP protocol number carrying ICMP Protocol number for TCP / for UDP

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• ICMP travels inside IP, in the same slot TCP (6) and UDP (17) occupy. Protocol 1. There is no extra layer and no shim.
  • Yet RFC 792 calls ICMP "an integral part of IP", required in every implementation. It is encapsulated like a guest and behaves like the host — a protocol whose job is to let the network layer talk about itself.
  • Here is the evidence. A TCP or UDP checksum includes a pseudo-header built from the IP addresses, because those are separate protocols that need to verify they were delivered to the right place. The ICMPv4 checksum covers only the ICMP message. It does not check, because it is not a guest.
  • The ICMP header is 8 bytes: type, code, checksum, then four bytes whose meaning depends entirely on the type. In an error they are unused; you will meet two more uses in A7.

items.title: Do this — an ICMP message when nothing is wrong
items.text:
Cable a second link, R2:eth2 to SW1, and address it.

Notice what that does to the topology: R1 and R2 are now both on LAN1. Everywhere else in this week a router-to-router link is a point-to-point cable with nothing else on it. Here two routers deliberately share one broadcast domain, because that is the only arrangement in which the message you are about to see can arise at all.

# on R2
ip addr add 192.168.100.2/24 dev eth2
ip link set eth2 up

# on R1 — point the route to LAN2 at R2's LAN1 address
ip route replace 192.168.200.0/24 via 192.168.100.2
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=1

# on PC1
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=1
ping -c2 192.168.200.10
ip route get 192.168.200.10
Did the ping succeed? ☐ yes ☐ no ICMP type seen on the capture Next hop PC1 uses after the ping

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The ping worked. R1 forwarded it correctly, exactly as asked. And R1 also sent PC1 an ICMP message.
  • Type 5, Redirect. It is not an error and nothing failed. It is advice: "for that destination, R2 is a better first hop than me — you are both on my segment, so stop sending it through me." Here the four type-dependent bytes carry the address of the better gateway.
  • PC1 believed it. ip route get now names 192.168.100.2, from a route PC1 was never configured with and no administrator typed.
  • So ICMP is not the failure channel. It is IP's control channel, and errors are merely its most visible use. The other everyday query is timestamp request/reply (types 13 and 14), which asks a host for its clock — no fault involved.
  • In IPv6 the healthy case dominates completely: neighbour discovery, the replacement for ARP, is ICMPv6. A perfectly working IPv6 network emits ICMP continuously and would not function without it. You will see that directly in the IPv6 project.

Restore before A7:

# on R1
ip route replace 192.168.200.0/24 via 10.0.0.2
# on R2
ip addr del 192.168.100.2/24 dev eth2 ; ip link set eth2 down

items.title: Record
items.text: Failure Anything on the wire? Reported by Type/Code No route locally No route at a router Host absent Port closed Rejected Dropped Why case 3 took seconds What an ICMP error quotes, and why IP protocol number for ICMP Why ICMP's checksum has no pseudo-header An ICMP message that means nothing is wrong

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No ICMP errors anywhere firewalld running systemctl stop firewalld on every node Case 4 returns nothing firewalld on PC2 swallowing the reply systemctl stop firewalld on PC2 Case 5 gives port unreachable, not admin prohibited bare reject uses the default use reject with icmp type admin-prohibited Case 3 returns nothing, just a timeout R2 rate-limiting or filtering sysctl net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit; stop firewalld Errors stop appearing during a burst kernel ICMP rate limit (1000 ms default) expected — send one packet at a time No redirect seen send_redirects=0 on R1, or the route still points via 10.0.0.2 re-run both commands, in order Redirect seen but ip route get unchanged accept_redirects=0 on PC1 set it to 1

items.title: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: A6 finished and restored · GNS3 project: w04-base (continue)

The question: A6 was about ICMP reporting failures. Ping is the opposite — a query, and the least representative thing in the protocol. It is also the tool you will trust most and should trust least.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Two pings to the same host, running at once. How does each one recognise its own replies?
  1. What is inside a ping's payload, and who chose it? _
  2. A router cannot forward a packet that is too large, and you have forbidden fragmentation. What comes back? _
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Do this — the echo message
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c3 192.168.200.10

Capture it and expand one request and one reply.

Request Reply Type Code Identifier Sequence

Now run two at once, in two terminals on PC1:

ping 192.168.200.10
ping 192.168.200.10

Identifier of the first: _ · of the second: _
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Echo request is type 8, echo reply is type 0. Both use code 0 — the code field carries no information here at all.
  • The four type-dependent bytes from A6 are used here as Identifier and Sequence.
  • ICMP has no ports. With two pings running, replies arrive at one host and must be sorted out somehow — so ICMP invented a demultiplexing field of its own. That is exactly what a port is, reinvented, in a protocol that lacks them. When you meet ports properly at the transport layer, this is the problem they solve.
  • Sequence numbers are what make loss and reordering visible. Ping's summary line is arithmetic over those numbers, nothing more.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Do this — the payload is yours
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c1 -s 32 -p 48656c6c6f20323632300a 192.168.200.10

In another terminal on PC1, before running it:

tcpdump -i eth0 -X -c2 icmp

What do you see in the payload of the reply? _
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The payload is arbitrary, chosen by the sender, and returned verbatim. RFC 792 requires only that it come back unchanged; it says nothing about what it may contain.
  • The default payload is not empty — it holds a timestamp, and that is how ping computes round-trip time. The sender does that arithmetic. The network contributes nothing to the measurement and no device on the path is aware it is being timed.
  • Arbitrary content, echoed reliably, in a protocol firewalls habitually permit, is a data channel. Tools exist that tunnel entire login sessions through ping payloads. "We allow ICMP" is a statement about a protocol number — it says nothing whatever about what crosses the boundary.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Do this — the message that is really a mechanism
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c1 -M do -s 1472 192.168.200.10      # fits exactly
ping -c1 -M do -s 1473 192.168.200.10      # one byte too many

Now shrink the transit link and sweep again:

# on R1
ip link set dev eth1 mtu 1400

# on PC1
ping -c1 -M do -s 1472 192.168.200.10
ping -c1 -M do -s 1372 192.168.200.10
ip route get 192.168.200.10
Type/Code returned by the oversized packet Which device sent it MTU value carried in the message MTU PC1 now caches for that destination
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Type 3, Code 4 — fragmentation needed and DF set. It is filed under "destination unreachable", but nothing is unreachable and nothing has failed. This is the mechanism of path MTU discovery.
  • Here the four type-dependent bytes carry the next-hop MTU. The router does not merely refuse — it tells you the number to use. That field was reserved in the original specification and put to work later.
  • PC1 cached it per destination, which you can see in ip route get. Everything it sends that way from now on will fit.
  • This only works because of A6. The error quotes your original packet, so PC1 knew which destination to shrink for. Without those quoted bytes the message would be useless.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Do this — break it, and see why blocking ICMP is expensive
items.text:
# on R1
nft add table inet f
nft add chain inet f out '{ type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet f out icmp type destination-unreachable drop

# on PC2
python3 -m http.server 8080 &

# on PC1
curl -o /dev/null -m 20 http://192.168.200.10:8080/
ping -c1 192.168.200.10
Did the small ping still work? ☐ yes ☐ no Did the HTTP transfer complete? ☐ yes ☐ no What error did you get?

Clean up: nft flush ruleset on R1, ip link set dev eth1 mtu 1500.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Small packets pass. Large ones vanish. The sender is never told why, so it retransmits the same oversized packet forever.
  • This is a path MTU black hole, and it is one of the hardest faults in networking to diagnose: connections establish (the handshake is small), then hang the moment real data flows. Ping works. Traceroute works. Everything "looks fine".
  • "Block ICMP, it's a security risk" is common advice and this is what it produces. The protocol you filtered was the one that would have told you.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Do this — what ping actually proves
items.text:
# a host that answers ping and serves nothing
# on R1
systemctl stop sshd
# on PC1
ping -c1 192.168.100.1
ssh 192.168.100.1

# a host that ignores ping and works perfectly
# on PC2
nft add table inet f
nft add chain inet f in '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet f in icmp type echo-request drop
# on PC1
ping -c2 -W2 192.168.200.10
curl -m5 -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://192.168.200.10:8080/

Clean up: nft flush ruleset on PC2, systemctl start sshd on R1.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Reachable is not usable. R1 answered every ping while providing nothing you wanted.
  • Silent is not down. PC2 ignored every ping while serving pages perfectly.
  • So both conclusions people routinely draw from ping — "it pings, so it's fine" and "it doesn't ping, so it's down" — are unreliable, and they fail in opposite directions.
  • Put beside A4's caveats about traceroute, you now have a calibrated view of the two tools you will otherwise over-trust for the rest of your career. Neither is wrong. Both answer a narrower question than the one you meant to ask.
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: Record
items.text: Echo request / reply type numbers What Identifier is for, and what it resembles Who computes round-trip time Why an echo payload is a security concern Type/Code that carries the next-hop MTU Why path MTU discovery needs A6's quoted bytes Symptom of a path MTU black hole One thing ping proves, and two it does not
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No ICMP at all firewalld systemctl stop firewalld everywhere -p rejected pattern longer than 16 bytes ping -p takes at most 16 bytes, repeated to fill -M do behaves oddly shell or ping variant on Linux iputils, -M do sets DF; check ping --help No frag needed message MTU change did not apply, or the error is filtered ip link show eth1; stop firewalld Cached MTU not visible kernel caches per destination and expires it re-run the oversized ping, then ip route get immediately curl succeeds despite the drop rule rule on the wrong chain or node — it must be output on R1 nft list ruleset on R1 Port 8080 refused python3 -m http.server not running, or stopped with the terminal restart it with &
path: W4·A7 — Echo, and what ping does not prove

items.title: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: A4 finished; a NAT node for part 4 · GNS3 project: w04-base (continue) · Extension activity

The question: The IPv4 header can grow. It was designed to carry extra instructions — record your path, timestamp each hop, take a route I choose. Those features still work here and are effectively dead everywhere else. Finding out why explains more about how networks evolve than the features themselves ever could.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. How large can an IPv4 header be? _ How large is the one you have been looking at all week?
  1. If a packet records the address of every router it passes, how many can it hold? _
  2. Will ping -R work to an address on the real internet? ☐ yes ☐ no · Why? _
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Do this — make the header grow
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c1 -R 192.168.200.10

Capture it. Find the IHL field in the IP header of both the request and the reply.

Ordinary ping With -R IHL value Header length in bytes Addresses listed in the option —
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• IHL is 4 bits, counting 32-bit words. Minimum 5 — that is the 20-byte header you have used all week. Maximum 15. So the header can reach 60 bytes and no further: 40 bytes for options, for all time.
  • Record Route spends 3 bytes on its own bookkeeping and 4 on each address. (40 − 3) ÷ 4 = 9 addresses, maximum, ever, on any path.
  • Every router on the path appended its own address as your packet went by. The network described its own path, as a designed feature — no tricks, no assumptions, no TTL games.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Do this — the ceiling gets worse
items.text:
# on PC1
ping -c1 -T tsonly    192.168.200.10
ping -c1 -T tsandaddr 192.168.200.10

Entries recorded by tsandaddr: _
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Address and timestamp is 8 bytes per hop, so the same 40-byte budget holds four.
  • Nine hops was generous in 1981. Four was never generous. A path across the modern internet is routinely fifteen or twenty hops, so these options could not describe the network they were built to describe — even if everything else about them had gone perfectly.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Do this — the option that got them banned
items.text:
# on R1 and R2
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=1

# on PC1
traceroute -g 192.168.100.1 192.168.200.10

Then turn it off and repeat:

# on R1 and R2
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0
# on PC1
traceroute -g 192.168.100.1 192.168.200.10
Worked with accept_source_route=1? ☐ yes ☐ no Worked with accept_source_route=0? ☐ yes ☐ no Default value on a fresh system
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The sender chose the path. Not the routers — the sender, from outside the network, deciding which links its packet would traverse.
  • Nearly every protection a network has rests on an assumption about where traffic came from: this arrived on the outside link so treat it as untrusted; that arrived on the inside link so trust it more. If the sender controls the path, it controls which link its packet appears to arrive on, and every one of those assumptions can be deliberately arranged to be wrong.
  • Which is why the default is 0 on every modern system, and why networks discard these packets on sight rather than trusting anyone's configuration.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Do this — the lab is not the internet
items.text:
First, store PC1's address. It has been 192.168.100.10 since A2, set with ip addr add, which means it exists only in PC1's running kernel. A NAT node hands out addresses, and a card with nothing stored can be handed one — which would take w04-base's addressing apart during an extension activity, in a project five other activities depend on.

# on PC1
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name lan1 \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.100.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.100.1
nmcli con up lan1

That distinction — a change to the running machine, versus a stored configuration NetworkManager keeps the running machine matching — is W3·A8, part 1.

Now attach a NAT node to SW1, LAN1's switch, so PC1 has a route out, then:

# on PC1
ping -c1 -R 192.168.200.10        # inside the lab, from part 1
ping -c1 -R 1.1.1.1               # the real internet
Inside the lab To the internet Reply received? Addresses recorded
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Same command, same protocol, two different worlds. Your lab implements the standard faithfully. The internet does not, and has not for a long time.
  • Nothing is broken and no rule was violated. Every operator between you and that address made a local, individually sensible decision to discard or ignore packets carrying options — and the sum of those decisions removed a documented capability from reality without anyone withdrawing it from the specification.
  • This is the activity. Everything before it was setup for this comparison.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: Do this — two traceroutes, one winner
items.text:
You have now built the same thing twice:

A4's traceroute A8's Record Route Mechanism rig TTL to expire early, collect the complaints ask the network to write its path down Designed for this job? no — a side effect of a loop-prevention counter yes, explicitly Hop limit none 9 Needs routers to do anything new? no yes Works on the internet today yes, universally no
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The elegant, purpose-built, standards-blessed mechanism lost completely to a hack that abuses a loop counter.
  • It won for one reason: it asks the network for nothing new. It requires no cooperation, no capability, no permission. It needs routers to do the single thing they already do when a packet runs out of hops — complain — and it therefore works through equipment that has never heard of traceroute and would refuse it if asked.
  • That is the general rule, and it is worth more than any of the options in this activity: mechanisms that require the network to cooperate die; mechanisms that exploit what the network already does survive.

Read reading-why-protocol-extensions-die.md before the next session. It takes this from one header field to the way the whole internet now evolves — and it explains why the newest transport protocols encrypt almost everything about themselves.
path: W4·A8 — The options nobody uses, and why that is the lesson

items.title: W4·A9 — Forge the packet
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: A6 and A7 finished · GNS3 project: w04-a9-forge (a fresh three-node project — see Topology) · Extension activity

The question: In A6 and A7 you read ICMP. Now build it. When you can assemble a packet field by field, two things become obvious that no capture can show you: exactly which fields the protocol fixes and which it leaves to you, and that nothing checks whether you are telling the truth.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Can you send an echo reply that nobody requested? _
  2. If you set the ICMP type to a number IANA never assigned, what happens? _
  3. Can you make one host believe a third host's network path is tiny — without being either of them? _

items.title: Topology
items.text:
10.10.0.0/24

   ATTACK       TARGET       VICTIM (for the last part)
    .10          .20           .30
      └────────────┼────────────┘
                  SW1

Three OL9 PCs on one Ethernet switch — one broadcast domain, which is what lets a forged reply reach a host that never asked for it.

Run scapy as root (sudo scapy). Capture on TARGET's link throughout.

items.title: Do this — build echo from nothing
items.text:
# on ATTACK, in scapy
p = IP(dst="10.10.0.20")/ICMP()/b"built by hand"
sr1(p, timeout=2)
Default ICMP type scapy chose Did a reply come back? ☐ yes ☐ no Type of the reply

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Three lines built a complete, valid echo request — IP() for the network layer, ICMP() for the message, a payload of your choosing — and a real host answered it. You have now constructed the protocol you spent two activities observing.
  • ICMP() defaulted to type 8. Change it explicitly and watch the taxonomy hold:
sr1(IP(dst="10.10.0.20")/ICMP(type=8), timeout=2)     # echo — answered
sr1(IP(dst="10.10.0.20")/ICMP(type=99), timeout=2)    # unassigned — silence
  • Type 8 is answered. Type 99 is discarded without a word. The type field is a fixed vocabulary; invent a word and no one understands it. The payload, by contrast, was whatever you typed. Fixed taxonomy, free payload — exactly the split A7 named.

items.title: Do this — the reply nobody asked for
items.text:
# on ATTACK
send(IP(dst="10.10.0.20")/ICMP(type=0, id=0x1234, seq=1)/b"unsolicited")

Watch TARGET in the capture.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• You sent an echo reply (type 0) that answered no request. TARGET received it and did nothing — it had no outstanding ping with that identifier, so the reply matched nothing and was dropped.
  • Harmless here, but note the shape of it: ICMP messages carry no proof of who sent them or that they were solicited. The receiver's only defence is "did I ask for this?" — and for error messages, as the next part shows, even that check is weak.

items.title: Do this — forge an error, and change a stranger's connection
items.text:
This is the capstone. Recall A7: a fragmentation needed error (type 3, code 4) carries a next-hop MTU, and the receiver caches it per destination. That message is unauthenticated. So you can send it yourself.

# on ATTACK — tell TARGET that reaching VICTIM requires tiny packets.
# The quoted inner packet must look like traffic TARGET sent to VICTIM.
inner = IP(src="10.10.0.20", dst="10.10.0.30")/TCP(sport=12345, dport=80)
forged = IP(dst="10.10.0.20")/ICMP(type=3, code=4, nexthopmtu=296)/inner
send(forged)

# on TARGET
ip route get 10.10.0.30
MTU TARGET now caches for VICTIM Were you either TARGET or VICTIM? ☐ no

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• TARGET believed a complete stranger's claim about a path it is not on, and shrank its packets to VICTIM accordingly. You never touched VICTIM.
  • It worked because the forged error quoted a plausible inner packet — the source, destination and ports of traffic TARGET might really have sent. That quoted header, from A6, is how a host decides an error is "about" one of its connections. Here it is the whole attack surface: guess the four-tuple, and the error is accepted.
  • This is why real stacks now sanity-check the quoted bytes — does this connection exist, is that sequence number in a window I actually sent — before acting on an ICMP error. A6's structural detail and A7's PMTU mechanism were the two halves of a live security problem, and you just assembled it.

Restore: ip route flush cache on TARGET.

items.title: Do this — options ping cannot make
items.text:
# on ATTACK — an IP option set by hand, and a deliberately wrong checksum
send(IP(dst="10.10.0.20", options=[IPOption_RR(length=39, pointer=4)])/ICMP())
send(IP(dst="10.10.0.20", chksum=0xdead)/ICMP()/b"bad checksum")

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• You built a Record Route option directly, choosing its size — something ping -R fixes for you. Compare its handling to A8: the lab honours it, and a real path would not.
  • The bad-checksum packet was silently discarded by TARGET's IP layer. No error, no reply — a corrupt header has no trustworthy return address to complain to, so the only safe action is to drop it. That is why a checksum failure is invisible from the sending side.

items.title: Shape of the week
items.text:
Session Do Note 1 A1, start A2 build A1 is short; getting w04-base cabled takes longer than expected 2 A2, A3 the two anchors; same project, do not delete between them 3 A4, A5 A5 pays off week 3's cliffhanger — do not drop it 4 A6, A7 same w04-base; A6 must precede A7 — A8, A9 + the reading extensions: homework, or drop

Compressed: A2, A3 and A6. A1 can be a ten-minute demonstration; A4, A5 and A7 can be homework; A8 and A9 are already optional.

A9 is the most droppable and the most rewarding. It is the only place students build ICMP rather than read it, and the forged-error section is the security payoff of A6. Treat it as an enrichment activity for students who finish A6/A7 early, or as a bridge into the network_sec/ module, which is its other natural home.

If the week is only three sessions, the honest trade is A5 or A6 — not both — and A6 is the one that changes how students diagnose everything afterwards. A5 can move to week 5 alongside subnetting; A6 cannot move without breaking A7.

items.title: RAM
items.text:
w04-base is four OL9 nodes, ~3 GB — two Routers at 1 GB, two PCs at 512 MB — plus two Ethernet switches, which are free. A3 wants three simultaneous Wireshark windows on top. This is the term's peak so far.

If students build PC1 and PC2 from the Router template out of habit, the project costs 4 GB instead of 3. Worth checking before the session.

For 8 GB machines running the GNS3 VM (itself pinned at 8 GB — Appendix A4), this does not fit. Two workable options:

  • Pairs. One build per pair of students, both watching. A3 genuinely benefits from two people reading two captures.
  • Demonstration. Project A2 and A3 and have students fill in the same worksheet from your captures. They lose the build, not the observation.

A1 needs 2 nodes and A5 needs 2; both fit anywhere.

items.title: What actually goes wrong
items.text:
• firewalld blocks ICMP errors, which silently ruins A4 — no Time to live exceeded, and tracepath shows nothing but *. If you have not disabled it in the image, put systemctl stop firewalld on the board for the whole week.
  • The /30 transit trips people up. 10.0.0.0/30 has exactly two usable addresses. Students assign .3 or .0 and are confused. This is deliberate foreshadowing of week 5 — let it happen, then name it.
  • A2 part 1 only works if students resist adding both routes. Some will add the return route from habit and see success, destroying the activity. Have them run ip route show on R2 and read it aloud before pinging.
  • A2 part 4's loop route may be rejected by some kernels as invalid. The fallback is in the activity's troubleshooting table.
  • A3 requires all twelve addresses collected first. Students who start capturing before building the address table cannot interpret anything they see, conclude the captures are wrong, and rebuild the topology. Insist on the table.
  • A5: modprobe 8021q may be needed. Check on the image before the session.
  • firewalld now ruins three activities, not one. It swallows ICMP errors, so A4 shows nothing but *, A6's five cases collapse into five timeouts, and A7's path MTU discovery silently fails. If it is not disabled in the image, this belongs on the board for the whole week, not just A4's session.
  • A6 case 1 is the one students misread. They see "Network is unreachable" and assume a packet went out and something answered. Make them look at the empty capture. If they skip that, the rest of the activity has no anchor.
  • A6's reject needs the explicit form. A bare nft ... reject returns port unreachable, not admin prohibited, and the distinction is the point of the case. The activity spells it out; students copying from memory will not.
  • A6's redirect section modifies w04-base — one extra link and a repointed route on R1. The restore commands are at the end of the activity and A7 will fail confusingly without them. Check the class has run them before dismissing.
  • A7's black-hole demonstration needs the rule on R1's output chain, not forward. R1 generates those errors itself. Students who put it on forward see nothing happen and conclude the demonstration is broken.
  • A8 needs a NAT node and working egress from the GNS3 host. Test it yourself before the session — if the room's network blocks outbound ICMP, part 4 produces the right answer for the wrong reason, and the comparison is worthless. Have a screenshot ready as a fallback.
  • A8's source-routing section needs accept_source_route=1 on both routers. Setting it on one produces a confusing partial result.
  • A9's forged MTU may be ignored by a kernel with a high min_pmtu, or if the quoted inner packet is implausible. The activity's troubleshooting table covers both; the fix that usually works is lowering nexthopmtu toward 552 and matching a four-tuple the target would actually use.
  • A9 must run as root (sudo scapy) — raw sockets. Students who launch scapy unprivileged get a permission error on the first send.

items.title: Things to say out loud
items.text:
• Before A2 part 1: "Everything you can check from either end will pass. Notice how strong the urge is to start changing settings. That urge is what this activity is inoculating you against."
  • After A2: "Two devices, one conversation, two routes — and neither router is wrong on its own. Correctness here is a property of the pair, not of either configuration."
  • After A3: "Your IP address is who you are. Your MAC address is who is standing next to you."
  • After A4's loop: "Week 3's loop destroyed the network. This one killed one packet. One field."
  • After A5 part 3: "Those two frames were on the same wire, half a millisecond apart, in different broadcast domains — because both ends agreed to respect a number. That is all a VLAN is."
  • Before A6: "Every failure you have had this week said the same thing on screen. The network has been telling you far more than that, in every single case, and you have not been reading it."
  • After A6's redirect: "Nothing failed. The ping worked. And ICMP still had something to say — so whatever ICMP is, it is not the thing that shows up when you break something."
  • After A7's black hole: "Somebody blocked ICMP to be safe. What they actually did was remove the message that would have told them what was wrong."
  • After A8 part 4: "Nobody on that path is misconfigured. Every one of them made a reasonable decision. Between them they deleted a feature from the internet without changing a single standard."
  • After A9's forged error: "You are not either end of that connection, and you just changed it. The network believed a stranger because nothing in ICMP asks who is speaking. That is the whole reason the next section of the course exists."
