items.title: Reading — Why protocol extensions die
items.text: Not an activity. Background for W4·A8, best read after it. No commands, nothing to submit. It takes one dead header field and turns it into the single most useful thing you can know about how the internet actually changes.

items.title: The room that was left on purpose
items.text:
The people who designed the internet's addressing in the 1970s knew they could not foresee what it would need. So they left room. Every packet carries a header — a small block of bookkeeping at the front — and they made that header able to grow. A packet could carry extra instructions: record the address of every router you pass through, or stamp the time at each hop, or take this specific route rather than the one you would normally choose.

This was good design. It meant the network could gain new abilities later without replacing everything that already existed.

And it worked, for a while. Those extras were real, useful, and used.

Today they are effectively dead. Not removed from the standard — the standard still describes them, and the lab network you built in A8 handles them perfectly. They died in the real world, and how they died is worth more than the features themselves.

items.title: Three forces
items.text:
Speed. Routers became fast by making the common case predictable. An ordinary packet header is always the same size and always laid out the same way, so the decision about where to send it can be made by dedicated hardware in a fraction of a microsecond. A packet carrying extras is a different shape — variable length, requiring interpretation. It cannot take that fast path. It is handed to a general-purpose processor instead, which is not slightly slower but thousands of times slower.

So a packet using the extension mechanism costs the network far more to carry than a normal one. Multiply that by the volume a backbone router handles and it stops being an inefficiency and becomes a way to overwhelm expensive equipment using very little effort.

Space. The room left for extras was capped at 40 bytes. Record Route spends four bytes per router plus a little bookkeeping — nine routers, maximum, which you calculated yourself in A8. When the design was written, nine was generous. On today's internet a path of fifteen or twenty hops is unremarkable. The feature could not describe the network it was meant to describe.

Trust. One of the extras let the sender dictate the route its packet would take. That sounds harmless. It is not. Nearly every protection a network has rests on an assumption about where traffic came from — this arrived on the outside link, so treat it as untrusted; that arrived on the inside link, so trust it more. If the sender controls the path, the sender controls which link the packet appears to arrive on, and every one of those assumptions can be deliberately arranged to be wrong. Once people noticed, operators switched it off everywhere.

items.title: The loop that finished them off
items.text:
Now follow the incentives.

Each of those three forces gives a network operator a good reason to discard packets carrying extras. None of them is a conspiracy. Each is an entirely local, entirely sensible decision made by someone with a network to run.

But once enough operators make it, a packet using extras is no longer reliably deliverable. So software stops using them — because software that depends on something unreliable is software that fails.

And once nothing uses them, discarding them costs nothing. There is no longer any traffic to break. Which makes the decision easier still for the next operator.

That loop is the whole story. The capability was never withdrawn. It was written out of reality by a million independent, individually reasonable choices. The document still says it works. The network says otherwise, and the network wins.

items.title: The general law
items.text:
This generalises far beyond one header:

Anything a protocol permits but rarely uses will eventually stop working.

Not by decision. By disuse. Equipment sitting between two computers — firewalls, load balancers, carrier gear, home routers — only reliably handles what it sees every day. Anything rare is anything untested, and anything untested is, sooner or later, broken. Rarity is not a symptom of the failure. It is the cause.

The name for this is ossification: the protocol hardens into the shape of whatever traffic is common, and the written specification drifts away from the working one. The internet is not what its standards say. It is the intersection of what its standards say and what the equipment in the middle happens to tolerate.

items.title: It happened again
items.text:
When IPv6 was designed, all of this was already understood. The response was structural: make the main header a fixed size — always the same, always fast — and move every extension into a separate chain behind it, so the fast path stays fast no matter what a packet is carrying.

Extensions of that kind are now widely discarded in transit. Measurement studies keep finding that a meaningful share of the internet simply drops packets that carry them.

The redesign did not help, and the reason is the important part: the format was never the problem. The problem was the incentive. Equipment in the middle gains nothing from handling rare traffic and loses nothing by discarding it. Change the format and that incentive is untouched.

items.title: What actually worked
items.text:
Given all that, only two strategies have succeeded, and both rest on the same insight: stop asking the middle of the network to cooperate.

Hide the change. If equipment in the middle cannot see a field, it cannot object to it. So encrypt everything you intend to keep evolving. The newest transport protocols encrypt not only your data but almost all of their own bookkeeping. Privacy is part of the motivation; the larger part is preserving the ability to change things later without needing permission from hardware nobody controls.

Wear a familiar shape. Build the new thing so it looks exactly like something the network already carries in enormous volume and passes without inspection. QUIC — the transport protocol that now carries a large share of the web — is a genuinely new design that deliberately presents itself as ordinary, unremarkable traffic of a kind every network already forwards without a second look. It did not win an argument about what networks ought to support. It arranged for the argument never to happen.

items.title: Back to the two traceroutes
items.text:
You built the same tool twice. Once as the designed feature — ask the network to record its own path — and once as the workaround from A4: send packets rigged to expire one hop earlier each time, and collect the complaints.

The designed feature is elegant, purpose-built, and dead. The workaround is a hack, and it is what every network engineer on earth uses.

The workaround won because it asks the network for nothing new. No cooperation, no capability, no permission. It needs routers to do the one thing they already do when a packet runs out of hops: complain about it. So it works through equipment that has never heard of traceroute and would refuse it if asked.

That is the lesson, in one line:

Mechanisms that require the network to cooperate die. Mechanisms that exploit what the network already does survive.

It is why the internet is so hard to improve, and why the improvements that do succeed almost always arrive disguised as something that was already there.

items.title: Week 4 topologies
items.text: Activity Project Notes A1 w04-a1-routing-table 2 nodes A2, A3, A4, A6, A7, A8 w04-base one project, six activities — do not delete between sessions A5 w04-a5-intervlan rebuilds W3·A4's network on a plain switch, adds a router A9 w04-a9-forge 3 OL9 PCs on one switch; extension

items.title: A6–A8 add no nodes, but they do change w04-base
items.text:
• A6's redirect section adds a second link from R2 to LAN1's switch and repoints R1's route to 192.168.200.0/24 via 192.168.100.2. The activity ends with restore commands. A7 will behave strangely if they are skipped — verify before the next session.
  • A8 part 4 attaches a NAT node to LAN1's switch so PC1 can reach a public address. It costs no RAM, but it needs working egress from the GNS3 host. Test it before class. A8 also has students store PC1's address as an nmcli connection first — a NAT node hands out addresses, and PC1's has only ever been set with ip addr add. That connection persists in the exported project.
  • A6, A7 and A8 all install nft rules and each activity ends with nft flush ruleset. A forgotten rule is the most likely cause of a later activity "not working".

Consider a third export, w04-base-restored.gns3project, taken after A6's restore step — it saves a session when a class leaves the redirect wiring in place.

items.title: w04-base is the week's spine — export it
items.text:
Four OL9 nodes — two OL9 Routers, two OL9 PCs — plus a switch on each LAN, three subnets. It takes a full session to cable and address, and A3 and A4 both depend on it being correct.

Export two states:

Export State For w04-base-broken.gns3project R1 has the route to LAN2; R2 has no return route A2 part 1 — this is the activity's starting point w04-base-working.gns3project both routes present recovery, and the starting point for A3 and A4

Handing out the broken one saves a session and loses nothing: the fault is the subject of A2, not something students should have to construct.

items.title: Verify before distributing
items.text:
The nmcli device set ethN managed no lines are ip-level and do not travel in an export — they are runtime state, not configuration. A student importing w04-base still has to run them, or NetworkManager will claim the interfaces on boot and the addressing will evaporate.

Either say so when you hand it out, or configure the export with nmcli connection profiles, which do persist inside the node's disk image. The second is more work and more realistic.

items.title: A5 depends on the 8021q module
items.text: Confirm modprobe 8021q succeeds on the OL9 image before the session. If it is absent from the image, A5 cannot run and milestone 2's R2 requirement is unbuildable — that is a rebuild-the-image problem, not a lab-day problem, so check it early.

items.title: Week 5 — Subnetting
items.text:
Assumes: weeks 1–4. Students can build routers, read routing tables, and have already met a /30 transit link and a /25 that broke a working network in week 1.

Leaves students able to: state what a mask actually does to a host's behaviour; recognise a mask mismatch from its one-directional symptom; locate a subnet's boundaries by measurement rather than arithmetic alone; and produce a VLSM plan that survives being built by somebody else.

items.title: The arc
items.text:
Subnetting is normally taught as arithmetic and assessed on paper, which is why students who can convert masks flawlessly still cannot fix a network. This week keeps the arithmetic — there is no substitute — but every answer is checked by building it, so a wrong bit-count shows up as a failed ping rather than a red mark.

The week is ordered by consequence, not by mechanics: what a mask does to one host → what happens when two hosts disagree about it → where the edges are → splitting a block → design something real.

# Activity Time Needs A1 The mask is a claim 35 min 2 PCs, 1 switch A2 The asymmetric mask ★ 45 min 1 router, 2 PCs, 1 switch A3 Boundaries, measured 40 min 3 PCs, 1 switch A4 Splitting a block 45 min 1 router, 4 hosts, 4 switches A5 Design it, then build it ★ 90 min 1 router, 4 hosts, 4 switches

★ = keep if compressed.

items.title: Why A2 is the anchor
items.text: A mask mismatch is the failure that paper cannot teach. Two hosts on one wire, one with /24 and one with /25, produce a network where traffic flows one way directly and the other way via a router — which works, or half-works, or works until the router is removed, and looks like nothing else. Students who have seen it once recognise it for the rest of their careers.

items.title: Deliverable
items.text: worksheet.md, plus A5's design document, which is graded as a lab (not part of the running project — see below).

items.title: Relationship to the running project
items.text:
Milestones 1 and 2 are already built and graded, on addressing you handed out. A5 is where students choose addressing for the first time, on a separate topology, so that a bad plan costs a lab rather than the project.

A future milestone 3 would re-address the project network from a block the students subnet themselves — which is exactly what A5 rehearses. See ../../project/README.md.

items.title: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim
items.text:
Time: 35 min · Needs: two OL9 PCs on an Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: w05-a1-mask

The question: you have typed /24 after every address for four weeks. What does the host actually do with it?
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Build it
items.text:
H1 and H2, both OL9 PCs, on an Ethernet switch. nmcli device set eth0 managed no on both.

# H1
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
# H2
ip addr add 192.168.10.200/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up

Confirm they ping.
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
You will change only H1's mask, from /24 to /25. Nothing else — not its address, not H2, not the cable.

  1. Can H1 still reach H2? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. Can H2 still reach H1? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. Are those the same question? ☐ yes ☐ no
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Do this — watch the table change with the mask
items.text:
# on H1
ip route show
ip route get 192.168.10.200

ip addr del 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/25 dev eth0

ip route show
ip route get 192.168.10.200
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The connected route changed from 192.168.10.0/24 to 192.168.10.0/25. The mask's only direct effect is on the routing table — it decides the size of the one route you get for free.
  • ip route get went from a direct answer to Network is unreachable. 192.168.10.200 is above .127 and therefore outside H1's new claim.
  • So a mask is a claim about which addresses are reachable without help. Change the claim and you change what the host considers to be its neighbours — and nothing else at all. No packet was affected, no interface reset, no negotiation with anyone.
  • H2 was not consulted and does not know. Masks are configured per host, never announced, and never checked for agreement. That is A2's subject.
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Do this — the boundary, one address at a time
items.text:
Still on H1 with /25:

ip route get 192.168.10.126
ip route get 192.168.10.127
ip route get 192.168.10.128
ip route get 192.168.10.129
Address Reachable directly? Why .126 .127 .128 .129
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The behaviour changes between .127 and .128, and nowhere else. 192.168.10.0/25 covers .0–.127; the next address begins a different subnet.
  • .127 is inside the claim but is the broadcast address of that subnet, and .128 is the network address of the next. A3 measures what those two actually do.
  • The boundary is a property of the number, visible only in binary: /25 means "the first 25 bits must match". .127 is 0111 1111 and .128 is 1000 0000 — the 25th bit is the one that flips. Write out both and confirm.
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Do this — restore the claim by widening it
items.text:
ip addr del 192.168.10.11/25 dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0
ip route get 192.168.10.200
ping -c1 192.168.10.200
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Working again, with no change anywhere except one number on one host.
  • Nothing was ever broken. The link, the switch, both NICs and H2 behaved identically throughout. A subnet is not a thing that exists in the network; it is a shared belief held by the hosts, and the network has no opinion about it whatsoever.
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: Record
items.text:
Connected route with /24 / with /25 ip route get 192.168.10.200 under each Address where the behaviour changes The bit that flips there What was reconfigured on H2

One sentence: what does a subnet mask actually do?
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Both addresses present after ip addr add you added without deleting ip addr show; delete the old one Route unchanged you changed the address, not the mask the address must stay .11 ip route get still succeeds under /25 a default route is present ip route del default for this activity Ping works despite Network is unreachable ARP cache still warm ip neigh flush all
path: W5·A1 — The mask is a claim

items.title: W5·A2 — The asymmetric mask ★
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Router, two OL9 PCs, one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: w05-a2-asymmetric

The question: A1 changed one host's mask and broke it in one direction. What does a network look like when two hosts on the same wire disagree about the mask — and it still works?

This is the failure that a subnetting worksheet cannot teach you and that you will meet in the field.

items.title: Build it
items.text:
192.168.10.0/24
   H1 ────┐
          SW1 ──── R1:eth0  192.168.10.1/24
   H2 ────┘        R1:eth1  203.0.113.1/24 ── (nothing; it exists to be a gateway)

# R1 — correct, and it is the only device that is
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done
ip addr add 192.168.10.1/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 203.0.113.1/24  dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0        # so the symptom is not hidden

# H1 — correct
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/24 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.10.1

# H2 — the mistake: /25, everything else identical
ip addr add 192.168.10.200/25 dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip route add default via 192.168.10.1

H2's mask is wrong. Nothing else in this network is.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. H1 pings H2. Works? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. H2 pings H1. Works? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. If both work, is anything wrong?

items.title: Do this — test both directions
items.text:
# on H1
ping -c2 192.168.10.200

# on H2
ping -c2 192.168.10.11

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Both directions work. A network with a definite misconfiguration, passing every test anyone would normally run.
  • This is why the fault survives to production. ping says yes, users say yes, and the mask stays wrong for years.

items.title: Do this — find it anyway
items.text:
Capture the R1↔SW1 link — the router's link, which nobody would think to watch for traffic between two hosts on the same switch. Then run both pings again.

Appears on R1's link? H1 → H2 H2 → H1

And ask each host what it thinks it is doing:

# on H1
ip route get 192.168.10.200
# on H2
ip route get 192.168.10.11

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• H1 → H2 never touched the router. H1 believes .200 is local — under /24 it is — so it ARPs for it and sends directly.
  • H2 → H1 went through the router. Under /25, H2's subnet is 192.168.10.128–.255, and .11 is outside it. H2 classified its own next-door neighbour as a foreign network and sent the packet to its gateway, which sent it straight back out of the same interface to H1.
  • ip route get confirms it in one line per host: H1 reports a direct route, H2 reports via 192.168.10.1.
  • The two directions of one conversation took different paths. That is the signature of a mask mismatch, and it is visible from neither endpoint — it took a capture on a third device, exactly as in W4·A2.
  • Note what the router did: it forwarded the packet back out of the interface it arrived on, which is a strong hint that something upstream is confused. Real routers send an ICMP redirect here, saying "you did not need me". send_redirects=0 above suppresses that so you could see the raw symptom; turn it back on and watch the redirect appear.

items.title: Do this — make it hurt
items.text:
The fault is invisible while the router is available. Remove that:

# on R1
ip link set eth0 down

Then, from H1: ping -c2 192.168.10.200, and from H2: ping -c2 192.168.10.11.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• H1 → H2 still works. It never needed the router.
  • H2 → H1 fails completely. Its path depended on a device that has nothing to do with a conversation between two hosts three feet apart on the same switch.
  • The misconfiguration was latent. It cost nothing until an unrelated component failed, and then it produced a failure whose obvious explanation ("the router is down") is wrong — the router was never supposed to be involved.
  • Half-working networks are worse than broken ones. A broken network gets fixed on the day it breaks.

Bring it back: ip link set eth0 up.

items.title: Do this — find it the fast way
items.text:
If you suspected this on a real network, the diagnosis is two commands, not a capture:

# on every host on the segment
ip addr show eth0 | grep inet

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The masks are right there and they do not match. The check is trivial once you know to make it, and impossible to stumble on if you do not — which is the entire value of having seen the symptom.
  • Add it to your own checklist: when traffic between two hosts on one segment behaves asymmetrically, compare the masks before anything else.

items.title: Record
items.text:
H1 → H2 H2 → H1 H1 → H2 on the router's link H2 → H1 on the router's link ip route get on H1 / on H2 Both directions with R1's eth0 down

Two sentences: why did every normal test pass, and what is the one-command check?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Both directions bypass the router H2's mask is not actually /25 ip addr show — delete the old address first H2 → H1 fails from the start no default route on H2, or forwarding off on R1 add the route; sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward Traffic stops matching after a while ICMP redirects taught H2 a host route sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0 on R1, ip route flush cache on H2 Router's link shows nothing at all wrong link captured capture R1↔SW1, not a host link Both directions fail .200 is outside /25's range in your build /25 covers .128–.255; .200 must be in it and .11 must not

items.title: W5·A3 — Boundaries, measured
items.text:
Time: 40 min · Needs: three OL9 PCs on an Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: w05-a3-boundaries

The question: every subnetting exercise says "subtract two — the network address and the broadcast address". Subtract two what, and what happens if you use them anyway?

items.title: Build it
items.text: H1 .11, H2 .12, H3 .13 — three OL9 PCs, all in 192.168.10.0/24, on one Ethernet switch. nmcli device set eth0 managed no on each. Confirm they ping.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
For 192.168.10.0/24:

Address Usable by a host? Network address Broadcast address First usable Last usable Total usable

Then: what do you expect to happen if you assign a host the broadcast address anyway?

items.title: Do this — the broadcast address is not a name, it is a behaviour
items.text:
# on H2 and H3
sysctl -w net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts=0

# on H1
ping -b -c1 192.168.10.255

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two replies to one packet, from two different hosts, reported as DUP!. You met this in W3·A3 as a measurement of the broadcast domain; here it is a measurement of the address.
  • .255 is not owned by anybody. It is a value that every host in the subnet recognises as "also me", which is precisely why nobody can be assigned it — an address that means "everyone" cannot also mean "one particular machine".
  • The rule is not arithmetic, it is behaviour. "Subtract two" is a consequence, not a definition.

items.title: Do this — use it anyway
items.text:
# on H3
ip addr flush dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.10.255/24 dev eth0
ip addr show eth0

Record whether the command was accepted. Then from H1:

ping -c2 192.168.10.255
ip neigh show

And try the network address:

# on H3
ip addr flush dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.10.0/24 dev eth0
ip addr show eth0

From H1: ping -c2 192.168.10.0.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
Record what you observed rather than what you expected — behaviour here varies with the stack, and that variation is itself the finding.

  • Linux is permissive about assigning these addresses; the trouble starts with everything else. The broadcast address is interpreted as a broadcast by every other host on the segment, so replies come from machines you did not address, and the ARP cache fills with contradictions.
  • Nothing enforced the rule. No error, no warning from the switch, no complaint from the other hosts. The convention lives in how the other machines interpret the address, and they will all keep interpreting it that way regardless of what H3 believes.
  • That is why "unusable" is a stronger word than the tooling suggests: you can configure it, and it will fail in ways that look like a hardware fault.

Restore H3: ip addr flush dev eth0; ip addr add 192.168.10.13/24 dev eth0.

items.title: Do this — move the boundary and find it again
items.text:
# on all three hosts — same addresses, narrower mask
ip addr flush dev eth0
ip addr add 192.168.10.11/28 dev eth0      # .12 and .13 on the others
ip route show

Now, from H1, find the edges by measurement:

ip route get 192.168.10.14
ip route get 192.168.10.15
ip route get 192.168.10.16
ping -b -c1 192.168.10.15
Address How you determined it Network address Broadcast address First / last usable Usable count

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• /28 gives 16 addresses and 14 usable. The boundary moved from .255 to .15, and every host agreed instantly because they all did the same arithmetic on the same mask.
  • The broadcast ping to .15 produced DUP! replies — the broadcast address moved with the mask, and nothing was configured to make that happen. It is derived, not stored.
  • ip route get located the edge without any binary arithmetic. Use it to check your arithmetic, never to replace it: on paper you must still be able to say why .16 starts a new subnet.

items.title: Do this — the sizes where the rule bends
items.text:
The /30 you used for every transit link in week 4 gives 4 addresses, 2 usable — 50% waste, on every point-to-point link in the network. Linux supports the fix:

# on H1 and H2 — remove H3 from the switch, or ignore it
ip addr flush dev eth0
ip addr add 10.0.0.0/31 dev eth0        # H1
ip addr add 10.0.0.1/31 dev eth0        # H2
ip link set eth0 up
ip route show
ping -c1 10.0.0.1                       # from H1

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Both addresses are usable. 10.0.0.0 is assigned to a host and works, on a prefix where "the network address" would leave nothing at all.
  • A /31 (RFC 3021) is defined for point-to-point links only, where broadcast is meaningless: there is exactly one other machine, so a frame sent to "everyone" and a frame sent to "the other end" are the same frame. With the concept gone, the reserved addresses are unnecessary.
  • So "subtract two" is a rule with a reason, and where the reason does not apply the rule does not either. Learn the reason; the arithmetic follows from it.
  • A /32 has no network at all — one address, no neighbours. It is used for loopbacks and host routes, and you will meet it again in any routing protocol.

items.title: Record
items.text: Prefix Total Usable Network addr Broadcast addr /24 /28 /30 /31 Did Linux accept the broadcast address on a host? What went wrong when you used it What enforced the rule Why a /31 needs no reserved addresses

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix ping -b returns nothing icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is 1 set it to 0 on the responders /31 refused not a point-to-point pair, or a third host is on the switch only two hosts; remove or ignore the third Cannot remove an address wrong prefix in the del ip addr flush dev eth0 ip route get disagrees with your arithmetic trust neither yet write out the binary; one of them is a typo Assigning .0 or .255 produces no visible trouble your topology is too quiet ping from a third host, which is where the contradiction shows

items.title: W5·A4 — Splitting a block
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Router, 4 hosts (VPCS is fine), 4 Ethernet switches · GNS3 project: w05-a4-splitting

The question: you are given one /24 and told to build four separate networks out of it, without asking for more addresses. Do it.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
You have 192.168.50.0/24 and need four equal subnets.

  1. What prefix length? _
  2. How many addresses per subnet? _ How many usable? _
  3. Write out all four:
# Network First usable Last usable Broadcast 1 2 3 4

Do the arithmetic before building. The build is the check, not the method.

items.title: Do this — build what you calculated
items.text:
R1 is an OL9 Router. Each of its four interfaces is a separate subnet, and each subnet gets its own switch with one host on it:

   PC1 ─── SW1 ─── R1:eth0     192.168.50.1/26
   PC2 ─── SW2 ─── R1:eth1     192.168.50.65/26
   PC3 ─── SW3 ─── R1:eth2     192.168.50.129/26
   PC4 ─── SW4 ─── R1:eth3     192.168.50.193/26

Four switches for four hosts is more than this lab strictly needs. It is what the real thing looks like, though — a subnet is a LAN, and a LAN has a switch in it — so from here on the diagrams match what you would actually build.

# on R1 — use YOUR numbers, not these
for i in eth0 eth1 eth2 eth3; do nmcli device set $i managed no; done
ip addr add 192.168.50.1/26   dev eth0 ; ip link set eth0 up
ip addr add 192.168.50.65/26  dev eth1 ; ip link set eth1 up
ip addr add 192.168.50.129/26 dev eth2 ; ip link set eth2 up
ip addr add 192.168.50.193/26 dev eth3 ; ip link set eth3 up
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
ip route show

Each host gets an address in its own subnet, with the router's address on that interface as its gateway:

# PC1 (VPCS)
ip 192.168.50.10/26 192.168.50.1
# PC2
ip 192.168.50.70/26 192.168.50.65
# PC3
ip 192.168.50.140/26 192.168.50.129
# PC4
ip 192.168.50.200/26 192.168.50.193

Then, from PC1, ping all three others and the router.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• ip route show holds four connected routes, and you typed none of them. Every one is a restatement of an address-plus-mask you assigned.
  • The arithmetic is checked by the build. An off-by-one in a boundary produces a host that cannot reach its own gateway — an immediate, unambiguous failure, in the same session, with no marker involved.
  • Four subnets came out of one /24 by borrowing 2 bits from the host portion: /24 → /26. Those two bits give exactly four combinations, which is why four subnets and not three or five.
  • The cost is visible: 256 addresses became 4 × 62 = 248 usable. Eight addresses vanished into network and broadcast addresses — two per subnet, and you now have four subnets instead of one. Subnetting always costs addresses, and the finer you cut, the more it costs.

items.title: Do this — prove the separation
items.text:
Capture on PC2's link. From PC1, run a broadcast ping and an ARP:

# on PC1 (or an OL9 host in its place)
ip neigh flush all
ping -c1 192.168.50.70
ping -b -c1 192.168.50.63

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC2's cable carried the routed unicast only — no ARP from PC1, no broadcast.
  • PC1's broadcast to 192.168.50.63 reached its own subnet and stopped at the router. Routers do not forward broadcasts, and that is a large part of what you bought with the split.
  • Compare with week 3: VLANs split a broadcast domain inside one subnet, at layer 2. Here the split is at layer 3, using different subnets and a router. Two mechanisms, similar effect, different layer — and real networks use both together, which is exactly what W4·A5 built.

items.title: Do this — the wrong split
items.text:
Deliberately mis-size one subnet and watch what it does to a neighbour:

# on R1 — eth1 claims a /25 that overlaps eth2's block
ip addr del 192.168.50.65/26 dev eth1
ip addr add 192.168.50.65/25 dev eth1
ip route show
ip route get 192.168.50.140

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two connected routes now overlap: 192.168.50.0/25 on eth1 covers addresses that 192.168.50.128/26 on eth2 also claims — check the arithmetic and see exactly which.
  • ip route get 192.168.50.140 reveals the winner. Longest prefix decides (W4·A1), so the more specific /26 still wins for PC3 — but the router now believes part of eth2's range is reachable via eth1, and any address in the overlap that is not covered by a longer prefix is sent to the wrong port.
  • No error was reported at any point. Overlapping subnets are accepted silently and fail selectively, which is why an address plan is a document you check before you configure, not after.

Restore: ip addr del 192.168.50.65/25 dev eth1; ip addr add 192.168.50.65/26 dev eth1.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Your four-subnet table, plus:

Bits borrowed Usable addresses per subnet Total usable, before / after the split Addresses lost to the split Did PC2's cable carry PC1's broadcast? Route chosen for .140 during the overlap

One sentence: what does subnetting cost, and what does it buy?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix A host cannot reach its own gateway address outside its subnet recheck the boundary; ip route get from the host Everything reachable from everywhere all interfaces still /24 the masks must be /26 on both router and hosts VPCS rejects the gateway gateway outside the host's subnet ip <addr>/<mask> <gw> — the gateway must be inside Router pings work, host-to-host does not forwarding off sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward Broadcast crosses to another subnet it should not check you are watching a link on a different subnet

items.title: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★
items.text:
Time: 90 min, or one session plus homework · Needs: 1 OL9 Router, 4 hosts, 4 Ethernet switches · GNS3 project: w05-a5-design · Graded as a lab

The question: everything so far gave you the addresses. Now you choose them, and somebody else has to be able to build your network from what you wrote down.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: The brief
items.text:
You have been allocated one block: 172.16.40.0/24. Nothing else. You may not request more.

Segment Hosts required now Growth expected OFFICE 50 to 60 LAB 20 to 25 SERVERS 6 none MGMT 2 none Transit to the upstream router 2 none

Constraints:

  1. No overlap. Every subnet disjoint from every other.
  2. Each subnet must fit its growth figure plus the router's own address, and be the smallest prefix that does. A segment planned for 6 hosts needs 7 usable addresses — the router lives in the subnet too. Being off by one here is the most common error in this exercise, and it is invisible until the day the last host is added.
  3. Contiguous from the bottom of the block. State the unused remainder as the smallest set of CIDR blocks that covers it exactly — it will not be one block, and working out why is part of the question.
  4. .1 of each subnet is the router. Hosts start at .10 except where the subnet is too small.
  5. The transit subnet has a router at each end and no hosts, so 2 usable addresses is enough.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Part 1 — The plan (do this before touching GNS3)
items.text:
Allocate largest first. This is not a style preference: allocating a small subnet into the middle of the block fragments it and can make a later large one impossible even when enough addresses remain.

Segment Hosts needed + router Prefix Network First usable Last usable Broadcast Spare OFFICE 60 61 LAB 25 26 SERVERS 6 7 MGMT 2 3 Transit 2 2 Unused remainder — — — — — —

Check before you build:

  • [ ] Every prefix is the smallest that fits its growth number plus one for the router
  • [ ] No two ranges overlap — check each boundary against the next network address
  • [ ] Total allocated + remainder = 256 addresses exactly
  • [ ] Each usable count ≥ the "+ router" column, not the "hosts needed" column
  • [ ] The remainder is expressed as properly aligned CIDR blocks, not as a range

Answer in writing: why does allocating largest-first matter? Give a specific ordering of these five subnets that would waste addresses or fail outright.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Part 2 — Build it
items.text:
One OL9 Router. Each segment — OFFICE, LAB, SERVERS and MGMT — gets its own Ethernet switch, named SW-OFFICE, SW-LAB, SW-SERVERS and SW-MGMT, with one host on it. (The transit subnet has no hardware in this lab — configure it on a spare interface or record it as reserved, and say which you did.)

Use nmcli, not ip. The project expects configuration that survives a reboot, and this is the rehearsal:

# on the router, per segment
nmcli device set eth0 managed no
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name office \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 172.16.40.1/26
nmcli con up office

Then hosts, then sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Part 3 — Prove it
items.text:
Evidence, not assertion. For each claim, the command output that supports it:

Claim Evidence to attach Every host reaches its own gateway ping from each host Every host reaches every other segment ping matrix, 4 × 4 The router has exactly the intended connected routes ip route show Each host agrees with your plan about its own subnet ip route get for an address just outside it A broadcast does not leave its segment capture on another segment's link during ping -b Boundaries are where you said ip route get for the last address in each subnet and the first of the next

../../scripts/collect-report.sh gathers most of this into one text file per node. Use it.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Part 4 — Peer review (the part that teaches the most)
items.text:
Swap plans with another student. Build their network from their document only — no conversation, no clarifying questions. Then report:

Could you build it without asking anything? Anything ambiguous, and how you resolved it Anything wrong — overlap, wrong size, wrong boundary One thing their document did better than yours
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Almost every plan is unambiguous to its author. The gaps show up only when someone else builds it — a missing gateway convention, a prefix stated in one notation in one row and another notation elsewhere, a "spare" range whose ownership is unstated.
  • That is why address plans are documents with conventions, not just tables of numbers. On a real network the person building it is you, eighteen months later, and you will remember none of this.
  • A plan that requires a conversation has failed, even if the arithmetic is perfect.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Marking
items.text:
Marks Plan: arithmetic correct, no overlaps, smallest fitting prefixes 30 Plan: written justification of largest-first allocation 10 Build matches the plan exactly 20 Evidence: all six claims supported by command output 25 Peer review completed, specific and fair 15

Note where the marks are: half of them are for the plan and the evidence, not the build. A working network you cannot document or prove is worth less than a documented one with a fixable fault.
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Subnets do not add up to 256 a boundary is off by one recompute each network address as previous + block size A host cannot reach its gateway host outside its own subnet ip route get from the host nmcli con up fails device still managed, or name collision nmcli device set ethN managed no; nmcli con show The remainder is fragmented you allocated smallest-first reallocate largest-first; this is Part 1's question, answered the hard way Peer's network will not build ambiguity, not necessarily error record exactly where you had to guess — that is the deliverable
path: W5·A5 — Design it, then build it ★

items.title: Shape of the week
items.text:
Session Do Note 1 A1, A2 A2 is the week's anchor; give it the time 2 A3, A4 both are arithmetic checked by building 3 A5 parts 1–3 part 4 (peer review) as homework, due next week

Compressed: A2 and A5. A1 is a good ten-minute demonstration; A3 and A4 can be homework with the worksheet as the deliverable.

items.title: The pedagogical bet of this week
items.text:
Subnetting arithmetic still has to be learned and practised on paper — nothing here replaces that. What changes is where the feedback comes from. A wrong boundary produces a host that cannot reach its gateway, in the same session, unambiguously. Students correct themselves before a mark is involved.

Keep worksheet problems as homework if you already have a bank of them. The activities are the check, not the substitute.

items.title: What actually goes wrong
items.text:
• A2 is invisible unless redirects are suppressed. sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0 on R1 is in the build for a reason: with redirects on, H2 learns a host route after the first ping and the asymmetry disappears mid-activity. Have them turn redirects back on afterwards and watch the ICMP redirect arrive — it is a good second half.
  • A2's addresses are load-bearing. .11 must fall outside the /25 and .200 inside it. Students who pick their own numbers often choose two that are both in the upper half, and nothing happens.
  • A3's /31 needs exactly two hosts on the segment. A third node on the switch will make it fail confusingly.
  • A3's "use the broadcast address anyway" has genuinely variable outcomes across stacks. The activity asks students to record what they see rather than confirm a prediction; mark it that way. A student who reports "it was accepted and nothing obvious broke" has observed correctly.
  • A4's overlap section: the point is that no error appears. Students will hunt for one. Tell them in advance that silence is the finding.
  • A5 part 1 must be finished before anyone opens GNS3. Students who build first and calculate afterwards get a working network by trial and error and learn nothing. Collect the plans, or at least sight them, before the build starts.

items.title: Things to say out loud
items.text:
• After A1: "The switch, the cable and the other host were never consulted. A subnet is a belief held by hosts, and the network has no opinion about it."
  • After A2: "This network passes every test you would run and is wrong. It will keep working until something unrelated fails, and then the obvious explanation will be the wrong one."
  • After A3's /31: "'Subtract two' has a reason. When you know the reason you can tell when it stops applying, and that is the difference between knowing a rule and understanding it."
  • Before A5 part 4: "Your plan is perfectly clear to you. That is not the test."

items.title: Assessment
items.text:
• A1–A4: worksheet, ungraded or lightly graded.
  • A5 is graded as a lab, with its own rubric in the activity file. Half the marks are on the plan and the evidence, not the build.
  • The running project is not re-addressed this week. Milestones 1 and 2 use addressing you supplied, deliberately: a bad subnet plan should cost a lab, not cascade into the project. If you later add a milestone 3 that re-addresses the project network from a student-chosen block, A5 is its rehearsal — see ../../project/README.md.

items.title: Prep checklist
items.text:
• [ ] Paper subnetting practice available for students who need more repetition
  • [ ] A2's exact addresses on the board (.11 with /24, .200 with /25)
  • [ ] A5 briefs printed; peer-review pairings decided in advance
  • [ ] Milestone 2 progress checked — week 5 is when a struggling student becomes visible
  • [ ] Decision recorded on whether a milestone 3 will re-address the project network

items.title: Week 5 worksheet — Subnetting
items.text:
Name: ____ Date: ______

A5 has its own deliverable and its own marks. This sheet covers A1–A4.

items.title: 1 — The mask is a claim
items.text:
Predict. Change only H1's mask, /24 → /25. H1 → H2 ☐ works ☐ fails · H2 → H1 ☐ works ☐ fails

Are those the same question? ☐ yes ☐ no

Observe.

Connected route under /24 / /25 ip route get 192.168.10.200 under each Address where behaviour changes Which bit flips there (show the binary) What was reconfigured on H2

Explain. What does a subnet mask actually do? One sentence, mentioning the routing table.

items.title: 2 — The asymmetric mask
items.text:
Predict. H2's mask is wrong. H1 → H2 ☐ works ☐ fails · H2 → H1 ☐ works ☐ fails

Observe.

H1 → H2 H2 → H1 H1 → H2 seen on the router's link H2 → H1 seen on the router's link ip route get on H1 / on H2 Both directions with the router's LAN interface down

Explain. Every normal test passed. Why?

Apply. Two hosts on one switch behave asymmetrically. What is your first command, and what are you looking for?

Connect. In W4·A2 a fault was invisible from both endpoints and needed captures at two points. What did this week's fault have in common with it?

items.title: 3 — Boundaries, measured
items.text:
Predict, then observe.

Prefix Total Usable Network addr Broadcast addr /24 /28 /30 /31 Did Linux accept the broadcast address on a host? What went wrong when you used it What component enforced the rule Why a /31 needs no reserved addresses

Explain. "Subtract two" is a rule with a reason. State the reason, then state the case where it does not apply.

items.title: 4 — Splitting a block
items.text:
Predict. 192.168.50.0/24 into four equal subnets. Prefix: _ Usable each: _

# Network First usable Last usable Broadcast 1 2 3 4

Observe.

Bits borrowed Total usable, before / after the split Addresses lost to the split Did PC2's cable carry PC1's broadcast? Route chosen for .140 during the overlap

Explain. The overlapping-subnet mistake produced no error at all. Why is that dangerous, and what decided which route won?

Apply. Week 3 split a broadcast domain with VLANs; this week split one with subnets and a router. Name the layer each works at, and one thing each can do that the other cannot.

VLANs Subnets + router Layer Can do that the other cannot

items.title: 5 — Five weeks of failures
items.text:
Each week produced a network that was configured correctly at every visible point and did not work. Name them, and what was needed to find each.

Week The failure What located it 1 2 4 5

What do they have in common?

items.title: Week 5 topologies
items.text: Activity Project Export? A1 w05-a1-mask no — two nodes and a cable A2 w05-a2-asymmetric yes A3 w05-a3-boundaries no A4 w05-a4-splitting no — building it is the activity A5 w05-a5-design the shell only — see below

items.title: Export w05-a2-asymmetric
items.text:
The addressing has to be exact for the activity to work: .11 with /24 must fall outside the /25, and .200 with /25 must fall inside it. Students who pick their own numbers often choose two that land in the same half, and then nothing happens and the activity appears broken.

Export it with the fault already in place, including send_redirects=0 on R1 — with redirects on, H2 learns a host route after the first ping and the asymmetry vanishes mid-activity.

items.title: A5: export the shell, never the addressing
items.text:
w05-a5-design should contain the nodes and cabling only — one OL9 Router, four hosts, four Ethernet switches, no addresses anywhere.

Choosing the addressing is the entire assignment. An export with any address in it hands out the answer, including to the students who would have got there themselves.

items.title: A4 is deliberately not exported
items.text: Calculating four /26 boundaries and then discovering an off-by-one when a host cannot reach its own gateway is the activity. A pre-built version removes the feedback loop that makes this week work at all.

items.title: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: three OL9 PCs on one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: v6-a2-ndp

The question: IPv6 has no ARP. It also has no broadcast. Both statements are true, and yet a host still has to turn an address into a MAC before it can send anything. Find out what replaced it, and what the replacement bought.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. H1 wants to reach H2 on the same wire. Something must resolve the address to a MAC. What? ___
  2. In IPv4, how many hosts on the segment have to process an ARP request? _
  3. In IPv6, how many should have to? _
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Topology
items.text:
H1 ───────── SW ───────── H2
                   │
                   H3   (does nothing — it is the control)

Three OL9 PCs on one Ethernet switch, all with IPv4 addresses .11, .12, .13 and their automatic link-local IPv6 addresses from the previous activity. H3 is here only to be counted; it sends nothing all session.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Do this — the IPv4 baseline, one more time
items.text:
Capture H3's link. On H1:

# on H1
ip neigh flush all
ping -c1 192.168.10.12
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• H3 saw the ARP request, even though the conversation had nothing to do with it. You measured this cost in W3·A3: a broadcast is delivered to every host in the segment, and every one of them spends a little CPU deciding it is not the intended recipient.
  • The destination MAC was ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. There is no way to be more specific, because at the moment ARP is sent the sender does not yet know any MAC to aim at. That is the trap ARP is stuck in, and it is why the request has to go to everyone.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Do this — the same job in IPv6
items.text:
Keep the capture on H3 running. On H1:

# on H1
ip -6 neigh flush all
ping -c1 fe80::<H2's interface ID>%eth0

Now stop the capture and compare the two halves.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• H3 did not see it. Its capture has the ARP exchange from before and nothing from the IPv6 ping. The two hosts resolved each other's addresses without H3 being involved at all.
  • In the capture on the H1–H2 link you will find two ICMPv6 messages doing exactly ARP's job:
ICMPv6 type Asks / answers Neighbour Solicitation 135 who has this address? Neighbour Advertisement 136 I do, and here is my MAC
  • This is NDP — Neighbour Discovery Protocol. So "IPv6 has no ARP" is true in the narrow sense that the ARP protocol is gone, and misleading in every other sense: the job still exists and is still done, just by ICMPv6 messages instead of by a protocol of its own.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Do this — read the destination address
items.text: In the capture, find the Neighbour Solicitation and read its destination, at both layers.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The IPv6 destination is not H2's address — H1 does not know it is reachable yet. It is something like ff02::1:ff00:12, a solicited-node multicast address, built by taking the last 24 bits of the address being looked for and pasting them onto a fixed prefix.
  • The Ethernet destination is not broadcast either. It is 33:33:ff:00:00:12 — a multicast MAC derived from the multicast IPv6 address in the same mechanical way.
  • Here is why that matters, and it is the whole point of the activity: a NIC that has not joined that multicast group discards the frame in hardware. H3's operating system was never interrupted, never scheduled, never asked to look at anything. The frame did not reach software.
  • Any host whose address happens to end in the same 24 bits will join the same group and will see the solicitation — so it is not perfectly targeted. But that is a handful of machines out of a segment of forty, instead of all forty.
  • IPv6 has no broadcast address at all. It was removed on purpose and multicast does its work, because "interrupt every host on the segment" turned out to be an expensive default. W3·A3 is the activity where you measured exactly how expensive.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Do this — the neighbour table has states
items.text:
# on H1
ip -6 neigh show
ping -c1 fe80::<H2's interface ID>%eth0
ip -6 neigh show          # again, immediately

Wait a minute with no traffic, then run ip -6 neigh show once more.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The entry moved between states: REACHABLE just after you used it, then STALE, and it will pass through DELAY and PROBE if it is used again after going stale.
  • Compare ip neigh show for IPv4, where entries are mostly REACHABLE or STALE and the machinery is far thinner. NDP actively tracks whether a neighbour is still there, rather than caching an answer and hoping.
  • That is called neighbour unreachability detection, and it is a second job ARP never did. When a machine is unplugged, an IPv6 host notices; an IPv4 host keeps sending into the void until its ARP entry ages out.
  • So NDP did not merely replace ARP. It absorbed ARP's job, dropped broadcast, and added a liveness check — three changes in one protocol.
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: Record
items.text:
ICMPv6 types for solicitation / advertisement H3's capture: ARP seen? NDP seen? Layer-2 destination of an ARP request / of an NS How a solicited-node multicast address is built Why H3's CPU was not involved Two neighbour states you observed, and what they mean

Two sentences: "IPv6 has no ARP" — in what sense is that true, and in what sense is it misleading?
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix H3 sees the NDP traffic too its address ends in the same 24 bits, or the capture is on the wrong link check the last 24 bits of all three addresses; renumber H3 No NS in the capture at all the neighbour entry was still cached ip -6 neigh flush all before pinging, and capture first Ping fails with "invalid argument" missing %eth0 link-local always needs the scope identifier Neighbour state never leaves STALE nothing is using the entry states only advance when traffic is sent; ping again Only one ICMPv6 message appears you captured after the advertisement flush and repeat with the capture already running
path: IPv6 — NDP does ARP's job, and stops waking everyone up

items.title: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Router, one OL9 PC, one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: v6-a3-slaac

The question: the previous two activities gave you an address that works on one wire and goes no further. Getting a routable address in IPv4 means either typing one or running a DHCP server. IPv6 has a third answer that needs neither. Watch a host build its own address out of thin air, and work out who told it what.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. A host with no IPv6 configuration is plugged into a network with a router on it. Does it end up with a routable address? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. If it does, does a server anywhere record that it handed that address out? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. Where does its default route come from? _
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Topology
items.text:
fd00:10::/64

   R1 ───────── SW ───────── CLIENT
   ::1                       (configure nothing)

R1 is an OL9 Router. CLIENT is an OL9 PC you will not configure at all — that is the entire point. Leave it running with its automatic link-local address and nothing else.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Do this — before the router speaks
items.text:
# on CLIENT
ip -6 addr show dev eth0
ip -6 route show

Write down what is there: one fe80:: address, and a route for fe80::/64 and nothing else. No way off this wire.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Do this — give the router something to announce
items.text:
# on R1
nmcli con modify <connection> ipv6.method manual \
      ipv6.addresses fd00:10::1/64
nmcli con up <connection>

sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1

Forwarding matters here for a reason beyond routing: a Linux box will not send router advertisements unless it believes it is a router, and this is the switch that decides.

Now start a capture on the link, and turn on advertisements:

# on R1
nmcli con modify <connection> ipv6.method shared
nmcli con up <connection>

Watch CLIENT — without touching it:

# on CLIENT
ip -6 addr show dev eth0
ip -6 route show
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• CLIENT now has a second IPv6 address, a routable one, and a default route. Nobody logged into it. Nobody configured it. Nothing was requested from a server.
  • This is SLAAC — stateless address autoconfiguration — and the word doing the work is stateless.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Do this — read the message that caused it
items.text:
Find the ICMPv6 messages in the capture:

ICMPv6 type Sent by Says Router Solicitation 133 the host is there a router here? Router Advertisement 134 the router yes, I am one, and this link uses this prefix

Expand the Router Advertisement and find the Prefix Information option inside it.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The router announced a prefix — the first 64 bits — and its own presence. That is all it said. It did not name CLIENT, did not choose an address for it, and does not know what address CLIENT ended up with.
  • Compare the prefix in the capture with CLIENT's new address. The first half is the router's prefix; the second half is the interface ID CLIENT already had. The host did the arithmetic itself: here is the network, and I already know who I am, so here is my address.
  • The default route came from the RA too — specifically from the fact that a router sent it. The source address of the advertisement, a link-local address, is what CLIENT installed as its gateway. Check with ip -6 route show and note that your default route points at an fe80:: address, which is why link-local had to exist first.
  • Routers send these unsolicited, every few minutes. The Router Solicitation exists so a host that has just booted does not have to wait for the next one.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Do this — find the lease
items.text:
Try to find, anywhere on R1, a record of the address CLIENT is using.

# on R1
ip -6 neigh show
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The neighbour table knows CLIENT exists, because they have spoken — that is NDP from the previous activity, not SLAAC. There is no lease, no database, no allocation record, and no server.
  • That is the trade. DHCP knows exactly which machine holds which address, when it expires, and can hand out a different answer per client — at the cost of running a server that must be available, backed up, and made redundant. SLAAC needs nothing but a router that already had to be there, and in exchange nobody can tell you who has which address.
  • Neither is better. Real networks frequently run both: SLAAC for addressing, and DHCPv6 for the things an RA cannot express. The RA has flag bits (M and O in the capture) whose entire job is to tell hosts which combination this network expects.
  • Notice also that CLIENT kept its link-local address. A host does not swap one address for another; it accumulates them, and normal IPv6 machines have several at once.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Do this — take it away again
items.text:
# on R1
nmcli con modify <connection> ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses fd00:10::1/64
nmcli con up <connection>

Wait, then check CLIENT again.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The address does not vanish immediately. Every prefix in an RA carries a valid lifetime and a preferred lifetime, and the host holds the address until those run down.
  • So SLAAC is stateless but not timeless. The router controls how long its announcements are trusted, which is the only lever it has over addresses it never assigned.
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: Record
items.text:
CLIENT's addresses before / after ICMPv6 types for solicitation / advertisement Which half of the address came from the router Which half came from the host Where the default route came from, and what kind of address it points at Where the allocation is recorded

Two sentences: what does SLAAC cost an administrator, and what does DHCP buy that it cannot?
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No RA in the capture forwarding off, so the box does not consider itself a router sysctl net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding=1 before enabling advertisements ipv6.method shared not supported older NetworkManager install and configure radvd with a prefix fd00:10::/64 block on that interface — the observations are identical CLIENT gets no address RAs are being ignored sysctl net.ipv6.conf.eth0.accept_ra must be 1; on a forwarding host it defaults to 0, so check CLIENT is not itself set up as a router Address appears but no default route accept_ra is 1 but accept_ra_defrtr is 0 check both sysctls Two addresses from the same prefix temporary privacy addresses are enabled that is correct behaviour — ip -6 addr marks one temporary; it is a third scheme worth reading about Address never expires after removing the RA lifetimes not yet elapsed they are minutes, not seconds; check ip -6 addr for the countdown
path: IPv6 — The host that addresses itself

items.title: IPv6 — The address you already have
items.text:
Time: 40 min · Needs: two OL9 PCs on one Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: v6-a1-linklocal

The question: you have not configured IPv6 anywhere in this course. Before you type anything, find out whether your machines already have IPv6 addresses — and if they do, where those came from and what they are for.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Does an interface you never configured for IPv6 have an IPv6 address? ☐ yes ☐ no
  2. If it does, who assigned it? _
  3. Two machines on one switch, neither configured. Can they ping each other over IPv6? ☐ yes ☐ no
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Topology
items.text:
192.168.10.0/24  (IPv4, for contrast only)

     H1 ───────── SW ───────── H2
     .11                       .12

An OL9 PC at each end of a GNS3 Ethernet switch. Give them IPv4 addresses as usual, so you have something familiar beside the new thing. Configure no IPv6 at all.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Do this — look before you build
items.text:
# on H1
ip -6 addr show dev eth0
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• There is an address there, and you did not put it there. It begins fe80:: and it appeared when the interface came up.
  • Every IPv6 interface gets one of these automatically, always, for as long as the link is up. It is called a link-local address, and IPv6 is not willing to operate without one.
  • Note the two words in the name. Link: it is valid on this one cable and nowhere else. Local: no router will ever forward it. It exists so that two machines sharing a wire can talk before anybody has been given a real address — which turns out to be a prerequisite for almost everything else IPv6 does.
  • Compare this with IPv4, where an interface with no configuration has no address at all and can do nothing. That difference is deliberate and it is the foundation of the next two activities.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Do this — use it
items.text:
Read H2's link-local address the same way, then from H1:

# on H1 — this will fail
ping -c2 fe80::XXXX:XXXX:XXXX:XXXX

It fails, and the error is the lesson. Now try again with the interface named on the end:

# on H1 — this works
ping -c2 fe80::XXXX:XXXX:XXXX:XXXX%eth0
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Invalid argument, or "no route to host". The address alone was not enough information to send a packet, which is not something IPv4 ever does to you.
  • The reason is that fe80::/64 is not one network — it is the same network on every interface at once. Your machine has that prefix on eth0, and would have it on eth1, eth2 and every other link as well. So "send this to fe80::1234" is genuinely ambiguous: out of which cable?
  • %eth0 is the answer to that question. It is called a zone index or scope identifier, and it is not part of the address — it is a note to your own machine about which door to use. It never appears in the packet.
  • This is the one piece of IPv6 syntax that catches everybody, and now you know it is not a quirk. It is the direct consequence of having an address range that is deliberately reused on every link.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Do this — where did the last 64 bits come from?
items.text:
# on H1
ip link show dev eth0 | grep ether        # your MAC address
ip -6 addr show dev eth0 | grep fe80      # your link-local

Compare the two. On a current OL9 system they will look unrelated.

Now watch what the older scheme looked like:

# on H1
nmcli con modify <your-connection> ipv6.addr-gen-mode eui64
nmcli con up <your-connection>
ip -6 addr show dev eth0 | grep fe80
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• With eui64, the last 64 bits are built directly from the MAC address: split the six bytes in half, insert ff:fe in the middle, and flip one bit in the first byte. Find your MAC inside your address and you have decoded it.
  • That was the original scheme, and it has an obvious problem. Your interface ID would then be the same on every network you ever joined — a permanent, globally unique serial number, broadcast by every packet you sent. Change coffee shops, keep the same second half of your address.
  • So modern systems default to stable-privacy: an interface ID that is stable per network but different on each one, computed from a secret key rather than from hardware. Same address size, same rules, no tracking identifier.
  • Put it back with nmcli con modify <your-connection> ipv6.addr-gen-mode stable-privacy. Note that you have just changed an address without changing any hardware, which is the point.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Do this — one wire, two protocols
items.text: Start a capture on the link and, from H1, ping H2 over IPv4 and then over IPv6 link-local.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Both conversations are on the same cable, in the same switch, at the same time. Nothing had to be chosen between them. A host runs both protocols side by side, and this is how essentially every real network operates today — the phrase for it is dual stack.
  • In the capture, the two look like completely different animals above Ethernet, and completely identical below it. The switch forwarding them has no opinion about either, because it is reading MAC addresses, exactly as in week 3.
  • Look at the EtherType field on each frame: 0x0800 for IPv4 and 0x86DD for IPv6. That single field is how one wire carries two incompatible protocols without ambiguity, and it has been in the Ethernet header since week 1.
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: Record
items.text:
Prefix of an address you never configured What "link" and "local" each mean in the name Why ping fe80::… fails without %eth0 Where the interface ID comes from under eui64 Why stable-privacy replaced it EtherType for IPv4 / for IPv6

One sentence: why does IPv6 insist on an address before you have configured anything, when IPv4 is happy with none?
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No fe80:: address at all IPv6 disabled on the interface or at boot sysctl net.ipv6.conf.eth0.disable_ipv6 must be 0; check for ipv6.disable=1 on the kernel command line ping says "invalid argument" missing %eth0 the scope identifier is not optional for link-local %eth0 given but still unreachable you used H1's own address read H2's address on H2, not on H1 Address unchanged after addr-gen-mode the connection was not brought back up nmcli con up <name>; the address is generated at activation nmcli reports no such connection the interface is unmanaged from an earlier activity nmcli device set eth0 managed yes, or configure it with a fresh connection Capture shows no IPv6 you pinged the IPv4 address twice check the target begins fe80::
path: IPv6 — The address you already have

items.title: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible
items.text:
Time: 60 min · Needs: one OL9 PC (PC1), one OL9 Router (R1), one OL9 Server (SRV), 2 Ethernet switches, Wireshark · GNS3 project: dh-a2-relay

The question: DHCP works by broadcasting. Routers do not forward broadcasts — you proved that in week 3 and relied on it in week 4. So a building with twenty subnets needs twenty DHCP servers. It does not have twenty. Find out why not.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. PC1 broadcasts a DISCOVER. R1 is between it and the server. What reaches the server? _
  2. If something did carry it across, how would the server know which subnet to allocate from? _
  3. And how would the reply get back to a client that still has no address? _
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Topology
items.text:
10.0.10.0/24                        10.0.30.0/24

  PC1 ──── SW1 ──── R1 ──── SW2 ──── SRV
  (dhcp)          .1  │  .1          .5
                  eth0│eth1
Node Configuration R1 eth0 10.0.10.1/24, eth1 10.0.30.1/24, both stored (below), sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 SRV 10.0.30.5/24 stored, and a route back: ip route add 10.0.10.0/24 via 10.0.30.1 PC1 nothing — ipv4.method auto

Store R1's and SRV's addresses rather than setting them with ip addr add. A DHCP server is about to start serving this network, and R1:eth0 sits on the very wire the offers cross — a card there with nothing stored can ask for an address and be handed one out of the pool it is supposed to be relaying. PC1 is the exception, and having nothing stored is the entire point of it.

# on R1
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name client-side \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.0.10.1/24
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth1 con-name server-side \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.0.30.1/24
nmcli con up client-side ; nmcli con up server-side

# on SRV
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name srv \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.0.30.5/24
nmcli con up srv

That distinction — a change to the running machine, versus a stored configuration NetworkManager keeps the running machine matching — is W3·A8, part 1.

That route on SRV is not an afterthought. The server is going to have to answer a client on a network it is not attached to, and it needs a way back.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Do this — try it without help
items.text:
Put the Kea config from the previous activities on SRV, but for the client's subnet, not its own:

{
  "Dhcp4": {
    "interfaces-config": { "interfaces": [ "eth0" ] },
    "lease-database": { "type": "memfile", "name": "/var/lib/kea/kea-leases4.csv" },
    "valid-lifetime": 600,
    "subnet4": [
      {
        "id": 1,
        "subnet": "10.0.10.0/24",
        "pools": [ { "pool": "10.0.10.100 - 10.0.10.110" } ],
        "option-data": [ { "name": "routers", "data": "10.0.10.1" } ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

# on SRV
systemctl restart kea-dhcp4

Capture both links — PC1–SW1 and SW2–SRV — and:

# on PC1
nmcli con up dh
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC1's capture has DISCOVERs, repeated, getting no answer. SRV's capture has nothing at all.
  • R1 did exactly what a router does: the destination was 255.255.255.255, which is not an address on any network it forwards to, so it dropped it. This is not a misconfiguration and there is no setting called "forward broadcasts" that you should be looking for.
  • The server, meanwhile, is running correctly, holding a perfectly good pool for 10.0.10.0/24, and will never hear anyone ask for it.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Do this — put a listener on the client's wire
items.text:
The thing that is missing has to be on PC1's segment, because that is where the broadcast is audible. It is called a relay agent, and its job is to hear DHCP broadcasts locally and forward them as ordinary unicast packets to a server somewhere else.

R1 already has a leg on that segment, so R1 is the natural place for it:

# on R1
dnsmasq --dhcp-relay=10.0.10.1,10.0.30.5 --keep-in-foreground --log-dhcp

Two addresses, and the order matters: the interface to listen on, then the server to forward to. Leave it running in that console.

With both captures still going:

# on PC1
nmcli con down dh && nmcli con up dh
ip addr show dev eth0 | grep 'inet '
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• PC1 has an address from a server two networks away, and nothing about PC1 changed. It broadcast, exactly as before, and was not aware that anything unusual happened.
  • Compare the two captures side by side. This is the whole activity:
On PC1's wire On SRV's wire Source 0.0.0.0 10.0.10.1 Destination 255.255.255.255 10.0.30.5 Delivery broadcast unicast
  • The relay did not tunnel or encapsulate anything. It re-sent the request as its own, from its own address, to a specific server. On SRV's wire this is an ordinary routable packet that any network can carry.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Do this — find giaddr
items.text: Expand the DISCOVER as it arrives at SRV and find the field named gateway IP address, giaddr.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It contains 10.0.10.1 — the address of the relay's interface on the segment the client is on. Not the relay's other address, and not the server's.

  • That single field does two jobs at once, and both are indispensable:

  • It tells the server which subnet to allocate from. SRV has no idea where the client is — the packet arrived on its 10.0.30.0/24 interface like everything else. It looks at giaddr, finds 10.0.10.1 inside its declared 10.0.10.0/24 subnet, and picks from that pool. This is why the config declares the client's subnet and not the server's.

  • It tells the server where to send the reply. The client still has no address, so the answer goes back to giaddr, and the relay does the last step — broadcasting it onto the client's wire, where a machine with no address can receive it.

  • So the relay's address is not a routing detail. It is the client's location, written into the packet, and it is the only thing that lets one server serve twenty subnets correctly.

  • Add a second subnet to the Kea config and a second relay on another segment, and nothing else has to change. That is how a building with twenty networks has one DHCP server and not twenty.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Do this — break it in the instructive way
items.text:
Change the relay to announce the wrong interface:

# on R1 — stop the relay, then
dnsmasq --dhcp-relay=10.0.30.1,10.0.30.5 --keep-in-foreground --log-dhcp

Try PC1 again.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The request reaches the server and is refused, or answered from the wrong pool — because giaddr now claims the client is on 10.0.30.0/24, and the server believes it.
  • The server has no independent way to check. It cannot see the client, cannot see the topology, and has exactly one piece of evidence about where the request came from. giaddr is trusted absolutely, which is worth remembering the next time you see a DHCP problem that looks like the server has gone mad.

Put it back the way it was.
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: Record
items.text:
What R1 did with the broadcast, and why that is correct Where a relay agent has to run, and why there Source and destination of the request on each of the two wires The two jobs giaddr does Which subnet the config declares, and why not the server's own What happened when giaddr was wrong

One sentence: a campus has forty subnets and one DHCP server. What has to exist on each of the forty?
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Relay starts but nothing is forwarded wrong first address it must be the relay's address on the client's segment Server receives the request, sends nothing no matching subnet for giaddr the subnet4 entry must contain the giaddr address Server replies, client never sees it no route back to 10.0.10.0/24 on SRV ip route add 10.0.10.0/24 via 10.0.30.1 dnsmasq refuses to start it is already running as a service systemctl stop dnsmasq first; this activity runs it in the foreground on purpose so you can read its log Kea ignores the relayed packet not listening on the right interface interfaces-config must name the interface facing R1 Client gets an address from R1 itself you started a DHCP server rather than a relay --dhcp-relay and --dhcp-range are different things; do not set both Everything works but the client has no gateway option-data missing the routers option is what supplies the default route
path: DHCP — Crossing a router, and the field that makes it possible

items.title: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: one OL9 Server (SRV), one OL9 PC (PC1), one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: dh-a1-dora

The question: a machine that has just booted has no IP address. To ask for one it must send a packet. But every packet needs a source address and a destination address, and it has neither. Work out how it asks.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. What source address can a machine use before it has one? _
  2. What destination address, given that it does not know where the server is? _
  3. How many packets does it take to get an address? _
  4. Why more than two?
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Topology
items.text:
192.168.10.0/24
