   SRV ───────── SW ───────── PC1
   .5 (static)               (nothing)

SRV is an OL9 Server, PC1 an OL9 PC, both on one Ethernet switch. SRV gets 192.168.10.5/24 by hand. PC1 gets nothing — you are going to watch it ask.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Do this — a DHCP server, in eleven lines
items.text:
On SRV, replace /etc/kea/kea-dhcp4.conf with:

{
  "Dhcp4": {
    "interfaces-config": { "interfaces": [ "eth0" ] },
    "lease-database": { "type": "memfile", "name": "/var/lib/kea/kea-leases4.csv" },
    "valid-lifetime": 600,
    "subnet4": [
      {
        "id": 1,
        "subnet": "192.168.10.0/24",
        "pools": [ { "pool": "192.168.10.100 - 192.168.10.110" } ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

Every line of that is one decision, and none of them is boilerplate:

Setting The decision it records interfaces-config which wires this server answers on — it will ignore every other one lease-database where the record of who-has-what is kept, on disk valid-lifetime how long an address is good for, in seconds — 600 is ten minutes subnet the network this server believes it is serving pools the range it is allowed to hand out — eleven addresses, deliberately few

Before you start it, pin SRV's own address. Right now 192.168.10.5 exists only in the running kernel: you typed it with ip addr add, and nothing recorded that you meant it. The moment a DHCP server is running on this wire, SRV's own card can ask for an address and be given one — and the .5 you typed disappears with no warning at all. Write it down instead:

# on SRV
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name srv \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.5/24
nmcli con up srv

ipv4.method manual is the part doing the work. It tells NetworkManager where this card's address comes from, so the card never asks the network. That distinction — a change to the running machine, versus a stored configuration NetworkManager keeps the running machine matching — is W3·A8, part 1.

Check it before starting it, then start it:

# on SRV
kea-dhcp4 -t /etc/kea/kea-dhcp4.conf     # parse only — catches a missing comma before it matters
systemctl enable --now kea-dhcp4
systemctl status kea-dhcp4

Note the subnet is /24 but the pool is eleven addresses. A pool is not a subnet. The server hands out only what is in the pool; everything else in the subnet is left for machines like SRV that are addressed by hand. Overlapping those two is one of the most common ways to break a network.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Do this — watch a machine ask
items.text:
Start a capture on PC1's link first. Then:

# on PC1
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name dh ipv4.method auto
nmcli con up dh

ip addr show dev eth0

Filter the capture with bootp — the historical name Wireshark still uses for DHCP.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
You have four packets, and they have names:

# Name From To Meaning 1 DISCOVER 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 is there a DHCP server out there? 2 OFFER SRV broadcast yes — you may have 192.168.10.100 3 REQUEST 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 I accept 192.168.10.100 4 ACK SRV broadcast confirmed, it is yours for 600 seconds
  • The source address is 0.0.0.0, which is not an address — it is the absence of one, written down. This is the one situation where sending from it is legal, and the reason DHCP has to be specified so carefully.
  • The destination is 255.255.255.255, the all-hosts broadcast. PC1 cannot address the server directly because it does not know the server exists. So it shouts, and whichever servers are on the segment hear it. Remember from week 3 what a broadcast costs and who receives it — every host on the segment processed this.
  • Why four and not two? Because there might be more than one server, and both would offer. The DISCOVER may draw several OFFERs; the REQUEST names which offer the client is taking, and it is broadcast so that the servers whose offers were not taken hear the rejection and put their addresses back. Two packets would work only on a network you had promised never to grow.
  • Expand any of the four and find the client identifier and the client's MAC address. That is what the server keys its records on. The client has no IP to be identified by, so identity at this stage is a layer-2 identity.

Now look at the server's side of it:

# on SRV
cat /var/lib/kea/kea-leases4.csv

That file is the stateful half of DHCP, and it is the thing SLAAC does not have. The server knows exactly which machine holds which address and until when.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Do this — find out how it got back
items.text: Look at the OFFER again, at layer 2 this time.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The OFFER had to reach a machine that still has no IP address. It cannot be routed and it cannot rely on the client's IP stack accepting a unicast to an address it has not yet configured.
  • So the server broadcasts the reply too, and the client recognises it by matching the transaction ID in the packet against the one it generated for its DISCOVER. Find that field and confirm all four packets share a value.
  • Ports: server on 67, client on 68. Both fixed, both known in advance by every DHCP implementation ever written, because there is no way to discover them — the discovery mechanism is the thing being bootstrapped.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Do this — run out
items.text: Bring up nine more clients, or simply repeat on a handful of nodes, until the pool is exhausted. Then ask for one more.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The eleventh client gets nothing. No error dialog, no address, no route — the same outcome as an unplugged cable, from a completely different cause.
  • A DHCP pool is a fixed resource, and running out is a real and regular outage. It is also invisible from the client, which is why "some machines get on the network and some do not" is a symptom worth recognising immediately.
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: Record
items.text:
Source / destination address of a DISCOVER The four packet names, in order Why REQUEST is broadcast rather than sent to the chosen server What ties the four packets together UDP ports for server / client What the client is identified by, and why not by IP Where the server records the allocation

One sentence: why can a DHCP pool not simply be the whole subnet?
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix kea-dhcp4 will not start JSON syntax kea-dhcp4 -t /etc/kea/kea-dhcp4.conf names the line SRV loses .5 and picks up a pool address its card was never pinned nmcli con show — if there is no srv connection, the address was only ever in running state Server starts, client gets nothing wrong interface in interfaces-config it must list the interface facing the client Client gets an address from somewhere else another DHCP server on the segment — possibly the GNS3 host capture and read the OFFER's source; isolate the topology Only DISCOVERs, no OFFER firewalld on SRV blocking UDP 67 firewall-cmd --add-service=dhcp, or stop firewalld for this activity No packets at all in the capture capture started after nmcli con up DHCP completes in milliseconds; start the capture first Client keeps its old address NetworkManager reused a cached lease nmcli con down dh && nmcli con up dh, or delete /var/lib/NetworkManager/*.lease Wireshark shows nothing for filter dhcp older Wireshark the filter is bootp
path: DHCP — Four packets, and a client with no address

items.title: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: the previous activity's topology · GNS3 project: dh-a1-dora (continue in it)

The question: the previous activity ended with PC1 holding an address "for 600 seconds". Nobody took it away after 600 seconds. Find out what that number actually governs, and what happens when the server that granted it disappears.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. What does PC1 do when its lease is halfway through? _
  2. How many packets does renewing take? _
  3. The server is switched off. When does PC1 lose its address? _
  4. PC1 reboots. Does it get the same address back? ☐ yes ☐ no
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Do this — make time run faster
items.text:
Ten minutes is too long to watch and too short to be realistic, so shrink it. On SRV, change one value in /etc/kea/kea-dhcp4.conf:

    "valid-lifetime": 60,

# on SRV
systemctl restart kea-dhcp4

This is the same trick as shrinking the forwarding table in W3·A6: the mechanism you want to watch runs on a timescale built for real networks, so you compress the timescale rather than the mechanism. Nothing else about the behaviour changes.

On PC1, take a fresh lease and note the second it happened:

# on PC1
nmcli con down dh && nmcli con up dh
date; ip addr show dev eth0 | grep 'inet '
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Do this — watch it renew
items.text: Start a capture on PC1's link and leave it running for two minutes without touching anything.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• At about 30 seconds — half the lease — PC1 sent a REQUEST and got an ACK. Two packets, not four. There was no DISCOVER and no OFFER.
  • Look at the addresses on those two packets. The renewal is unicast, straight to the server. PC1 has an address now and knows exactly who granted it, so none of the shouting from the first activity is necessary any more.
  • That halfway point has a name: T1, the renewal timer. It is set to 50% of the lease by default, and the reason it is halfway rather than at the end is that it leaves the client another half a lease in which to keep trying if the server does not answer.
  • There is a second timer, T2, at 87.5%. If renewal has failed by then the client stops asking its server and starts broadcasting to any server that will listen — the state is called rebinding. Only when the full lifetime runs out does it give up the address.

So the lease is not a countdown to losing the address. It is a countdown with two alarm clocks before it, and in normal operation you never reach the end.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Do this — take the server away
items.text:
Leave the capture running.

# on SRV
systemctl stop kea-dhcp4

Now watch PC1 for the next two minutes. Keep pinging SRV from it and note when the address disappears:

# on PC1
watch -n1 'date; ip addr show dev eth0 | grep "inet "'
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Nothing happened immediately. PC1 kept its address and carried on working, because a lease is a grant with a deadline and the deadline had not arrived. This is why a DHCP server can be rebooted in the middle of the day without anybody noticing.
  • In the capture you will see renewal attempts at T1, then more of them, then the broadcast rebinding attempts after T2 — the client escalating from asking my server to asking anybody.
  • At the end of the 60 seconds, the address was removed. PC1 did not keep using it. That is the half of the contract clients are obliged to honour: when the lease expires without renewal, the address goes back, because something else may have been given it in the meantime.
  • Scale this back up mentally. With a realistic lease of 8 or 24 hours, a DHCP outage is invisible for hours and then takes down every client at roughly the same time. The failure is delayed and then sudden, which is a genuinely difficult shape to diagnose if you do not know the mechanism.

Start the server again and let PC1 recover:

# on SRV
systemctl start kea-dhcp4
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Do this — hand it back politely
items.text:
# on PC1
nmcli con down dh

# on SRV
cat /var/lib/kea/kea-leases4.csv

Then bring it back up and look again.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Shutting the connection down sent a RELEASE, and the server marked the lease as returned rather than waiting out the clock. Find it in the capture — it is a single packet with no reply, because there is nothing to agree about.
  • PC1 got the same address back. The server keyed the record on PC1's client identifier and offered the address it had before, which is why machines appear to have stable addresses on networks where nothing is static.
  • That stability is a courtesy, not a guarantee. It survives a reboot and usually a weekend; it does not survive the address being handed to someone else while you were away. Anything that genuinely must not move — a server, a printer, a switch's management address — gets a reservation on the DHCP server or a static address, and is kept out of the pool.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Record
items.text:
Packets in a renewal, and how it differs from the first four Unicast or broadcast, and why the answer changed T1 and T2 as fractions of the lease, and what each triggers How long PC1 survived with the server stopped What ended it Whether PC1 got the same address back, and what decided that

Two sentences: your DHCP server dies at 09:00 with an 8-hour lease. Describe the day.
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No renewal in the capture lease still long valid-lifetime must be short — 60 s; restart Kea and re-take the lease Address never disappears the client renewed successfully confirm Kea is actually stopped: systemctl status kea-dhcp4 Address disappears instantly you brought the connection down rather than waiting nmcli con down releases on purpose; to watch expiry, leave it alone No RELEASE packet NetworkManager skipped it on an already-dead link release only happens on a clean shutdown of the connection Different address on return the lease was reclaimed and reissued expected once the pool is under pressure; this is the point about reservations watch shows no change for minutes lease timers are in seconds but the capture is the better clock read the timing from the capture, not the shell
path: DHCP — The lease is a loan, with a deadline

items.title: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round
items.text:
Time: 55 min · Needs: the ring, with OSPF running on all four routers · GNS3 project: rp-a1-static-limits (continue in it)

The question: the first activity ended with a broken ring, an idle spare path, and a stopwatch running while you retyped routes. Do it again with OSPF on, and find out what changed. Then take control of which path the network picks, because "it works" and "it goes the way you intended" are different claims.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. The R1↔R2 link fails. How long until PC1 can reach PC3 again? _
  2. What decides whether traffic goes clockwise or anticlockwise around the ring? _
  3. Two paths of identical length. Which is used? _
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Do this — everyone knows everything
items.text:
Before breaking anything, look at what the four routers are holding:

# on R1, then on R3
birdc show ospf state
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The two outputs describe the same network. Not similar — the same. Every router in an area holds an identical database of who is connected to what, because each one floods a description of its own links to everybody and relays what it receives.
  • Each router then computes its own routes from that shared picture, by working out the shortest path from itself to everywhere. That is why the protocol family is called link-state: what gets distributed is the state of the links, not a list of routes.
  • This is the structural difference from static routing. You never described the topology to any router. They described themselves to each other, and every one of them derived the answer.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Do this — break the ring again
items.text:
Continuous ping from PC1 to PC3, then:

# on R1
ip link set <the R2-facing interface> down

Count the lost packets. Then bring it back and count again.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It recovered on its own, in about a second. Compare that with the number you wrote down in the first activity, where recovery was measured in minutes and required you to be present, awake and correct.
  • traceroute from PC1 to PC3 now and you will see the traffic going the other way round the ring, through R4. Nobody chose that. Every router recomputed, arrived at a consistent answer, and installed it.
  • You have seen this shape before. W3·A5 ended with a blocked port taking over automatically when a cable failed, and the argument was identical: the redundancy was already paid for, and the protocol removes the human from the recovery. This is the same bargain one layer up.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Do this — the two speeds of failure
items.text:
The recovery above was fast because the interface went down and the router noticed instantly. That is not the only way a link fails. Simulate the other kind — the link stays up, but the router at the far end stops answering:

# on R2
systemctl stop bird

Time it again.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• This took far longer — around 40 seconds, not one. The link never went down, so R1 had no event to react to. It had to wait until it had heard no hello from R2 for the dead interval, which defaults to four times the hello interval.
  • These are the two failure modes every network has, and they behave completely differently:
What the router sees Recovery Cable pulled, interface down carrier loss, immediately ~1 second Far end silent, link still up nothing — only the absence of hellos up to the dead interval
  • The second is why "the link is up" is not evidence that anything works, and why lowering hello and dead intervals is a normal tuning decision on links that matter. It is not free: shorter timers mean more hellos and a greater chance of declaring a neighbour dead during a brief hiccup.

Start BIRD on R2 again.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Do this — where the path preference comes from
items.text:
# on R1
birdc show ospf interface

Find the cost of each interface.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Each interface carries a number, derived by default from its bandwidth: a fast link gets a low cost, a slow link a high one. OSPF adds these up along each candidate path and picks the lowest total.
  • This is exactly the mechanism from W3·A5. There, each link had a cost from its speed, costs were summed along the path to the root, and the lowest total won. Same idea, same direction — lower is better — implemented independently at a different layer for a different purpose. Two protocols built decades apart reached for the same tool.
  • The difference is what the number is measured to. Spanning tree measures distance to one elected root. OSPF measures distance from each router to every destination, separately, which is why there is no root here and no blocked links.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Do this — take control of the path
items.text:
Right now PC1 → PC3 goes one way round. Make it go the other way, without unplugging anything.

On R1, raise the cost of the interface facing R2:

    area 0 {
        interface "eth1" { cost 500; };
        ...
    };

# on R1
birdc configure
traceroute 10.3.0.10        # from PC1
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The path moved, and every router agreed about it, because you changed a number that all of them were told about. You did not configure a route anywhere.
  • This is the layer-3 twin of setting the bridge priority in W3·A5. Left alone, the path is whatever the default costs happen to produce — which is to say, an accident of interface speeds. Set deliberately, it is a decision you can point at in a design document.
  • Real reasons to do this: one path is metered and the other is not; one crosses a link you are paying for by the gigabyte; one goes through a firewall you want traffic to pass. None of those are visible to a protocol that only knows bandwidth.
  • Set the two paths to equal cost instead and look at ip route show. You will get both next-hops in one route — equal-cost multipath — and traffic is shared between them. Note that this is a thing spanning tree specifically cannot do: at layer 2 the second path must be blocked, and at layer 3 it can be used. That is a real advantage of routing over bridging, and a reason large networks push the layer-3 boundary as close to the edge as they can.
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Record
items.text:
Are two routers' show ospf state outputs the same or different? Packets lost when the interface went down Packets lost when the far end went silent Why the two differ, and the timer responsible Default cost of your interfaces, and where it comes from Cost you set, and the path it produced What equal-cost paths do at layer 3 that blocked ports cannot at layer 2

Two sentences: compare this activity's recovery with the manual recovery you timed in the first activity. What exactly did the protocol replace?
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No recovery at all the other side of the ring was never adjacent birdc show ospf neighbors on all four — you need Full all the way round Recovery takes 40 s even for a cable pull the interface did not actually go down in GNS3, ip link set … down on the router is reliable; suspending the link may not be birdc configure reports no change you edited the file on the wrong router check the router id in the file you edited Cost change has no effect the other path is still cheaper raise it further, or read the totals with birdc show route all Equal-cost paths do not appear kernel multipath, or costs not actually equal birdc show ospf interface on both; the totals must match exactly Routes vanish after birdc configure a syntax error left the protocol down birdc show protocols, then bird -p -c /etc/bird.conf
path: Routing — Convergence, and choosing which way round

items.title: Routing — Neighbours come before routes
items.text:
Time: 60 min · Needs: the ring from the previous activity · GNS3 project: rp-a1-static-limits (continue in it)

The question: you are about to turn on a routing protocol and watch routes appear. Before that happens, something else has to happen first, and it is the part that breaks in the real world. Two routers on the same cable have to find each other and agree to exchange information. Watch them negotiate, then break the negotiation on purpose.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Two routers running OSPF on the same wire. What has to be true before either learns a route? ___
  2. What do they send each other before any route information moves? _
  3. If the two ends disagree about something, do you get wrong routes or no routes? _

items.title: Do this — clear the decks
items.text:
Remove every static route you wrote in the previous activity, on all four routers:

# on each router — delete the twenty statements
ip route flush proto static
ip route show

Confirm PC1 can no longer reach PC3. You are starting from a network that is correctly cabled, correctly addressed, and cannot deliver anything beyond its own segments.

items.title: Do this — the smallest possible OSPF
items.text:
The course image ships BIRD. It is configured by one file and controlled with birdc. On R1, replace /etc/bird.conf with:

log syslog all;
router id 10.255.12.1;

protocol device { }

protocol direct {
    ipv4;
    interface "eth*";
}

protocol kernel {
    ipv4 { export all; };
}

protocol ospf v2 {
    ipv4 { import all; export all; };
    area 0 {
        interface "eth0" { stub yes; };
        interface "eth1";
        interface "eth2";
    };
}

Six blocks, and none of them is decoration:

Block What it decides router id this router's name inside the protocol — an identifier, not an address it listens on protocol device keeps BIRD's view of local interfaces up to date; without it nothing notices a link change protocol direct brings the router's own connected networks into BIRD, so OSPF has something to advertise protocol kernel copies what OSPF learns into the kernel's routing table — the thing ip route show prints area 0 which OSPF area these interfaces belong to; everything here is in the backbone stub yes advertise this network, but send no hellos on it — correct for a LAN with no routers on it

stub yes on eth0 is worth pausing on. Without it, R1 sends OSPF hellos onto the LAN where the only listeners are PCs and, in a hostile network, anybody who fancies being told the topology.

Check the file parses before you commit to it, then start it:

# on R1
bird -p -c /etc/bird.conf
systemctl enable --now bird
birdc show protocols

Repeat on R2, R3 and R4, changing router id and the stub/non-stub interface names to match each router's wiring.

items.title: Do this — watch two routers meet
items.text:
Start a capture on the R1↔R2 link before starting BIRD on R2, then start it and run this on R1 repeatedly:

# on R1
birdc show ospf neighbors

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The neighbour moved through a sequence of states, and it is worth having seen them go past:
State What is happening Down / Init I have heard a hello, but it did not mention me 2-Way I have heard a hello that lists my router ID — we can both hear each other ExStart / Exchange agreeing who speaks first, then summarising what each of us knows Loading asking for the details I am missing Full we hold identical information about this area
  • No route is learned until Full. Everything before it is negotiation, and a neighbour stuck at any earlier state produces exactly the same symptom as no protocol at all: a router that looks configured and knows nothing.
  • In the capture, find the Hello packets. Note two things: they go to 224.0.0.5, a multicast address meaning all OSPF routers, and they are neither TCP nor UDP — the IP header's protocol field says 89, and OSPF rides directly on IP with no transport layer at all. It provides its own reliability, which is why it can afford to.
  • Read one hello. It carries the sender's router ID, its area, its hello and dead intervals, its network mask, and a list of neighbours it has heard from. Almost every field in it is a thing that has to match, which is the subject of the rest of this activity.

Now check the routes:

# on R1
birdc show route
ip route show

PC1 can reach PC3 again, and you typed no routes to make that true.

items.title: Do this — break it four ways
items.text:
Each of these is a real failure that occurs in real networks. Do them one at a time, and each time run birdc show ospf neighbors and note which state it sticks at.

1. A mismatched subnet. Change R2's address on the R1 link to 10.255.99.2/30.

2. A mismatched hello interval. On R2, set interface "eth1" { hello 5; }; — R1 is still using the default 10.

3. A mismatched area. On R2, put the R1-facing interface in area 1 instead of area 0.

4. A mismatched MTU. Put everything back, then: ip link set eth1 mtu 1400 on R2 only.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• 1, 2 and 3 never get past Init or fail to appear at all. The hello was heard and rejected. Two routers refuse to become neighbours unless they agree on the subnet, the timers and the area, because a disagreement about any of those means they disagree about what network they are on.
  • 4 is the interesting one. The adjacency reaches ExStart or Exchange and sticks there — the hellos matched perfectly, so the routers found each other, agreed to talk, and then failed while trying to exchange databases. Nothing about the symptom points at MTU.
  • That is the failure worth memorising. A neighbour stuck at ExStart/Exchange with correct addressing and correct timers is, in practice, almost always an MTU mismatch — often caused by a tunnel or a VLAN tag added somewhere in the middle by somebody else.
  • Note the general shape: the protocol fails safe. In every one of the four cases you got no routes rather than wrong routes. A router that cannot agree with its neighbour declines to learn from it, which is a much better failure than confidently forwarding into a black hole.

Put everything back and confirm all four neighbours reach Full.

items.title: Record
items.text:
Neighbour states you observed, in order The state at which routes begin to exist Destination address and IP protocol number of a hello Four things that must match, from reading one hello Which break stuck at ExStart/Exchange, and why that is hard to guess Wrong routes or no routes?

One sentence: what does stub yes prevent, and why would you want that on a LAN?

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix bird will not start config syntax bird -p -c /etc/bird.conf prints the line No neighbours at all interfaces not listed, or all marked stub birdc show ospf interface — the transit links must not be stub Neighbours Full, but ip route show unchanged no protocol kernel export ipv4 { export all; } inside protocol kernel Routes exist for transit links but not LANs protocol direct missing without it the router's own networks are never advertised Two routers share a router id copied the config without editing it IDs must be unique; BIRD will complain in the log MTU break does not stick some builds tolerate the mismatch check birdc show ospf interface for the MTU each side believes; the lesson stands either way Everything breaks after a reboot bird not enabled systemctl enable --now bird

items.title: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: four OL9 Routers, 2 VPCS, 2 Ethernet switches · GNS3 project: rp-a1-static-limits

The question: static routes work. You built them in week 4, they are predictable, they need no protocol and they never do anything surprising. So why does no real network of any size use them? Count, and find out.

No new commands in this activity. Everything here is week 4's ip route add. What is new is the arithmetic, and it is the arithmetic that makes the case for everything after it.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Four routers in a ring, each with a LAN. How many static route statements does the whole network need? _
  2. You add one new LAN. How many routers do you have to edit? _
  3. A link in the ring fails. There is another way round. How long until traffic uses it? _
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Topology
items.text:
LAN1                            LAN2
             10.1.0.0/24                     10.2.0.0/24
                 │                               │
                 R1 ─────── 10.255.12.0/30 ───── R2
                 │                               │
        10.255.14.0/30                    10.255.23.0/30
                 │                               │
                 R4 ─────── 10.255.34.0/30 ───── R3
                 │                               │
              LAN4                            LAN3
             10.4.0.0/24                     10.3.0.0/24

Four OL9 Routers in a ring, each carrying one LAN. The four links between routers are point-to-point cables with nothing else on them — that is what a /30 is for. Each LAN, though, is a switch with the router on one port, so put a switch on LAN1 and another on LAN3 and hang PC1 and PC3 off them — diagonally opposite, so their traffic has to cross the network. LAN2 and LAN4 have no hosts in this activity and need no switch. Every router needs sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1.

Address everything, but write no routes yet.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Do this — count before you type
items.text:
Before configuring anything, fill this in on paper:

Total networks in the topology (LANs + transit links) Networks each router is directly connected to Therefore, static routes needed per router Total static route statements for the network
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Eight networks: four LANs and four transit links. Each router touches three of them — its own LAN and two transit links — and needs a route for the other five.
  • Twenty route statements, on four routers, for a network with four sites. Every one of them is typed by a person, and every one of them is a chance to type 10.2.0.0 where you meant 10.3.0.0.
  • Now do the arithmetic for a real campus: thirty routers and sixty networks. You are not going to do that by hand, and more importantly you are not going to do it correctly by hand.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Do this — build it anyway
items.text:
Write the routes. All twenty. Time yourself.

# on R1 — example: reaching LAN3, the far side of the ring
ip route add 10.3.0.0/24 via 10.255.12.2

Confirm PC1 can reach PC3.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• It works, and it is completely deterministic. There is no protocol running, no packets exchanged between routers, no state to converge. Every forwarding decision in this network was made by you, in advance.
  • That determinism is a genuine virtue and it is why static routes still exist — on a default route out of a small office, on a link where you want no surprises. The problem is never that static routing is wrong. The problem is what happens next.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Do this — add one network
items.text: Add LAN5, 10.5.0.0/24, on R1. Count the edits.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• R1 gets it for free — a connected route appears the moment you address the interface, which you saw in W2·A2.
  • Every other router in the network needs a new statement. Three edits for one network, and none of them are on the device that changed.
  • That is the property that ends static routing: the work of adding a network is proportional to the size of the network, not to the size of the change. Adding one LAN to a thirty-router campus is twenty-nine edits, on twenty-nine devices, all of which have to be right.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Do this — break the ring
items.text:
Start a continuous ping from PC1 to PC3, then fail the link R1↔R2:

# on R1
ip link set <the R2-facing interface> down
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The ping stops, and it does not come back. There is a perfectly good path — R1 → R4 → R3 — and it is up, and it is idle.
  • Nothing is going to use it. R1's route to 10.3.0.0/24 says via 10.255.12.2 and that is what it will keep saying, because a static route is a statement about intent, not about reachability. It has no idea the link is gone.
  • Recover it by hand: change the route on R1, and on R2, and on any router whose path to anything went through that link. Time this too.
  • You have met this argument before. In W3·A5 you bought a redundant cable, watched it save you, and then noticed that a human had to notice the failure and act. This is the identical problem one layer up: the redundancy is real, the recovery is manual, and manual recovery means the outage lasts as long as it takes a person to arrive.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: The case, in one table
items.text:
Static routes What you want instead Adding a network edit every other router edit the router that changed A link fails outage until a person retypes routes the network finds another way Who knows the topology you, in your head and your notes the routers, from each other Chance of a typo proportional to network size one config per router, once Behaviour under change none — it is a fixed statement recomputed automatically

A routing protocol is what fills the right-hand column. Routers tell each other what they are connected to, each builds its own picture of the network, and each computes its own routes from that picture — continuously, so that a change anywhere is reflected everywhere without anybody typing.

The next activity is the first half of that: before any route can be learned, two routers have to discover each other and agree to talk. That turns out to be where most real problems live.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Record
items.text:
Networks / directly connected / routes per router / total Minutes to configure twenty static routes Edits required to add one LAN, and on which devices What happened to the ping when the ring broke Why the idle path was not used Minutes to recover by hand

Two sentences: static routing failed here for two different reasons. Name both, and say which one would hurt more in a building you are on call for.
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Ping works one way only a route exists outbound but not on the return path W4·A2 — every path needs a route in both directions Some pairs work, others do not a missing statement among the twenty ip route show on each router and check against your count Ping fails between directly connected routers forwarding off, or wrong mask on the /30 sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward; /30 gives exactly two usable addresses Ping recovers on its own after the break you left a route via R4 from an earlier attempt that is a redundant static route, which is worth noticing — but check it is deliberate PC has no route anywhere no default gateway on the VPCS ip 10.1.0.10/24 10.1.0.1
path: Routing — Why static routing stops scaling

items.title: Transport — The address inside the machine
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Server, one OL9 PC, one Ethernet switch · GNS3 project: tr-a0-ports

The question: an IP address gets a packet to a machine. That machine is running a web server, an SSH daemon, a DNS resolver and your shell. The packet arrives at one network card, once. Something has to decide which program gets it — and it is not IP, because IP has already finished.

This is the first transport activity. Do it before the three-way handshake.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Two programs on one machine, one IP address. What tells them apart? _
  2. You open two browser tabs to the same website. How many connections, and how does the machine keep the replies separate? _
  3. Is a connection identified by one number, or by more than one? _
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Topology
items.text:
192.168.10.0/24

   CLIENT ───── SW ───── SRV
     .11                 .12

An OL9 PC and an OL9 Server on one Ethernet switch. Capture the link for the last section.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Do this — two services, one address
items.text:
# on SRV — two terminals
python3 -m http.server 8080
python3 -m http.server 9090

# on CLIENT
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://192.168.10.12:8080/
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://192.168.10.12:9090/

Now look at what is waiting on SRV:

# on SRV
ss -tlnp
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two servers, one IP address, and every request reached the right one. The IP address was identical in both cases — the only difference in the packet was a 16-bit number, and that number is the port.
  • ss -tlnp lists listening sockets: -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p the process. Read the Local Address:Port column. Each program has claimed a port and the kernel will hand it anything addressed there.
  • So a port is not a networking concept so much as a delivery address inside one machine. IP gets the packet to the building; the port gets it to the right desk.
  • Two programs cannot claim the same port on the same address at the same time. Try it — start a third server on 8080 and read the error. That collision is why "address already in use" is one of the most common messages in all of computing.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Do this — where does the client's port come from?
items.text:
Hold two connections open at once. On SRV, make a file worth downloading slowly:

# on SRV
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/big.bin bs=1M count=50

# on CLIENT — two terminals, both at once
curl --limit-rate 20k -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.12:8080/big.bin
curl --limit-rate 20k -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.12:8080/big.bin

While both are running:

# on CLIENT
ss -tan '( dport = :8080 )'

# on SRV
ss -tan '( sport = :8080 )'
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Two connections, to the same server, on the same port, from the same client. Everything about them is identical except one field: the client's own port number, which is different for each.
  • The client never chose those numbers. The kernel allocated them from the ephemeral range — a block of high-numbered ports handed out temporarily for the life of a connection and returned afterwards. Check yours:
# on CLIENT
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range
  • So ports come in two kinds, and the difference is who has to know them in advance. A server port is fixed and published, because clients must be able to guess it — 80, 443, 22, 53. A client port is temporary and arbitrary, because only the two machines involved ever need to know it.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Do this — count the fields
items.text: Look at the ss output again and write out everything that distinguishes one of those connections from the other.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• A connection is identified by four things, not one:
Connection A Connection B Source IP 192.168.10.11 192.168.10.11 Source port e.g. 41022 e.g. 41024 Destination IP 192.168.10.12 192.168.10.12 Destination port 8080 8080
  • Three of the four are identical. The connections are distinct because the whole four-tuple is distinct, and that is the rule: two connections may share any three of those values, never all four.
  • This is what makes a web server serving ten thousand people simultaneously possible on one port. The port is not the connection. The port is one field of four.
  • Notice the listening socket in ss -tlnp is still there, unchanged, alongside the connected ones. A listening socket does not turn into a connection — it stays listening and spawns a separate connected socket for each client. That distinction is invisible until you look, and it explains how a server accepts a second visitor while the first is still reading.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Do this — see it in the packet
items.text: Capture the link and start one more curl. Expand the TCP header of any packet.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Source port and destination port are the first two fields of the TCP header — the very first four bytes, before sequence numbers, before flags, before anything else. They are that important.
  • Watch them swap between the request and the reply. 41022 → 8080 going out, 8080 → 41022 coming back. The pair reversed is how each end recognises the other's half of the conversation.
  • Look at where the TCP header sits: after the IP header, which is after the Ethernet header. Week 1 took that stack apart; this is the layer you had not yet needed. IP addresses the machine and TCP addresses the program, and both are in every single packet because both questions have to be answered on arrival.
  • UDP has the same two fields in the same place, for the same reason. The demultiplexing job is common to both, and it is arguably the only thing they have in common.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Record
items.text:
What distinguishes two servers on one IP address Command that lists listening sockets Where a client's own port number comes from The four fields that identify a connection How many of them differed between your two curls Position of the port fields in the TCP header

One sentence: a server has one IP address and one open port. Explain how it can serve ten thousand people at once.
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix Second http.server fails to start port already claimed that is the lesson — read the error, then use a different port ss shows nothing the connections finished too quickly --limit-rate 20k keeps them open long enough to look Both curls show the same client port you ran them one after the other, not together ports are reused once released; run them simultaneously ss -tlnp shows no process name not run as root sudo ss -tlnp Connections to 8080 refused server died with its terminal restart it, or background it with & No TCP header visible in Wireshark you expanded an ARP or ICMP frame filter with tcp.port == 8080
path: Transport — The address inside the machine

items.title: Transport — The receiver sets the pace
items.text:
Time: 50 min · Needs: one OL9 PC, one OL9 Server, one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: tr-a4-window

The question: a fast server sends a large file to a slow client. Nothing in IP prevents the server from sending as fast as its network card allows, and nothing in the network tells it not to. So why does the client not simply drown?

Do this after the three-way handshake and the UDP activity. It answers a question those two leave open: TCP does not merely deliver reliably, it delivers at a rate somebody agreed to.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. A 50 MB file is sent over TCP. How many packets? _
  2. What limits how much the sender may have in flight before hearing back? _
  3. The receiving application stops reading. What happens to the sender? _
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Topology
items.text:
CLIENT .11 (an OL9 PC) and SRV .12 (an OL9 Server) on one Ethernet switch. On SRV:

# on SRV
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/big.bin bs=1M count=50
cd /tmp && python3 -m http.server 8080
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Do this — how big is a piece?
items.text:
Capture the link, then:

# on CLIENT
curl -s -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.12:8080/big.bin

In the capture, find the SYN and look for the MSS option, then look at the size of the data packets that follow.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The file did not travel as a file. It was cut into thousands of segments, each one small enough to fit in a frame — around 1460 bytes of data apiece.
  • That number is not arbitrary: 1500 bytes of Ethernet payload, minus 20 for the IP header, minus 20 for the TCP header, leaves 1460. It is announced in the SYN as the maximum segment size, so each end learns what the other is prepared to receive before any data moves.
  • You have now met this arithmetic three times. W1·A3 counted what headers cost. W3·A4 showed a VLAN tag adding 4 bytes and pushing a frame to 1522. The OSPF activity showed two routers refusing to become neighbours over an MTU disagreement. Every one of those is the same 1500 bytes, seen from a different layer.
  • Note that MSS is negotiated per connection at setup, and then not revisited. A path that shrinks in the middle later — a tunnel, an extra tag — is the classic cause of a connection that opens perfectly and then hangs the moment real data flows.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Do this — watch the receiver push back
items.text:
Now make the client read slowly. --limit-rate does not slow the network; it slows the rate at which curl takes data out of its own socket, which is exactly what a busy application does.

Capture again, then:

# on CLIENT
curl --limit-rate 20k -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.12:8080/big.bin

Let it run for thirty seconds. In Wireshark, look at the Win= value on packets from CLIENT, and watch for packets Wireshark colours and labels TCP ZeroWindow and TCP Window Update.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Every acknowledgement CLIENT sends carries a window — a number saying this is how many more bytes I can accept right now. It is not a setting. It is the free space left in the receive buffer, reported on every packet.
  • As curl fell behind, that buffer filled and the advertised window shrank, packet by packet. You can watch it count down.
  • When it reached zero, CLIENT sent a ZeroWindow: stop, I have nothing left. And the server stopped — not because of an error, not because of loss, but because it was told to.
  • When curl read some more, CLIENT sent a Window Update and transmission resumed.
  • This is flow control, and the important part is who is in charge. The receiver is. The sender may be idle, the network may be empty, and the transfer still proceeds at exactly the rate the slowest participant can absorb. Nothing in the middle of the network was involved in that negotiation, and nothing in the middle even knows it happened.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Do this — the other brake
items.text:
Flow control protects the receiver. There is a second, entirely separate mechanism protecting the network, and it is easy to confuse them.

# on CLIENT — run the unlimited download again, and while it runs:
watch -n0.5 "ss -ti '( dport = :8080 )'"

Look for cwnd: and rtt: in the output.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• cwnd is the congestion window — the sender's own private limit on how much it will put in flight, which no one advertises to it. It starts small, grows while things go well, and collapses when a packet is lost.
  • So a TCP sender is limited by two numbers at once, and it obeys whichever is smaller:
Set by Protects Announced? Receive window the receiver the receiving machine yes, on every packet Congestion window the sender the network in between no — inferred from loss
  • The second one is inferred, which is worth sitting with. No router ever tells a sender to slow down. The sender guesses, from the fact that a packet went missing, that some queue somewhere overflowed, and backs off. The entire internet's stability rests on every sender voluntarily performing that guess.
  • That also explains the UDP activity's result from a new angle. UDP has neither window. It sends what the application gives it, as fast as the application gives it, and if that swamps a receiver or a link, nothing in UDP will notice or care.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Do this — starve it deliberately
items.text:
Shrink the receive buffer so the ceiling is visible in one screen:

# on CLIENT
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 8192 8192'

Repeat the unlimited download and compare the transfer rate and the Win= values with before. Then put it back:

# on CLIENT
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 131072 6291456'
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The transfer got slower, on an unchanged network, with no loss and no congestion. The receiver simply could not have as much data in flight at once.
  • This is the shape of a real and frequently misdiagnosed performance problem: a connection that cannot go fast because the window is too small for the round-trip time. On a long path the sender spends most of its time waiting for permission, and no amount of extra bandwidth helps.
  • The product of those two numbers — window size and round-trip time — is the most the connection can ever move at once. Everything else is detail.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Record
items.text:
MSS announced in the SYN, and the arithmetic behind it Where the window value appears, and how often What TCP ZeroWindow means, and who sent it What restarted the transfer Two windows, who sets each, what each protects How a router tells a sender to slow down Effect of shrinking tcp_rmem

Two sentences: a download is slow. Give one reason it might be the receiver's fault and one reason it might be the network's, and say how you would tell them apart.
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No ZeroWindow in the capture the client kept up lower --limit-rate to 10k, or shrink tcp_rmem first No MSS option in the SYN you expanded the wrong packet it is on the SYN and SYN/ACK only, never on later packets ss -ti shows no cwnd connection already finished use the 50 MB file and run watch during the transfer Window never changes window scaling makes the raw value misleading Wireshark shows the calculated value; check the scale factor in the SYN Transfer speed unchanged after tcp_rmem existing connection kept its old buffer the setting applies to new connections; start a fresh curl Speeds are unrealistically high throughout virtual links have no real bandwidth limit add tc qdisc add dev eth0 root tbf rate 10mbit burst 32kbit latency 400ms on SRV, as in W2·A6
path: Transport — The receiver sets the pace

items.title: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 PC, one OL9 Server, one Ethernet switch (or one OL9 PC + week 4's w04-base) · GNS3 project: tr-a1-handshake

The question: IP delivers packets and forgets them. TCP is described as "connection-oriented" — but no wire changes, no router is told anything, and nothing in the network remembers you. So where does the connection exist?
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Before any data is sent, how many packets cross the wire to establish a TCP connection? _
  2. Where does the connection live — in the network, or somewhere else? _
  3. You connect to a port nothing is listening on. What comes back? _
  4. Same, but a firewall is dropping it. What comes back? _
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Topology
items.text:
10.10.0.0/24

  CLIENT ─── SW1 ─── SERVER
   .10                 .20

CLIENT is an OL9 PC, SERVER an OL9 Server. Capture the CLIENT↔SW1 link for everything below.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Do this — watch a connection begin
items.text:
# on SERVER
python3 -m http.server 8080

# on CLIENT — start the capture first
curl -s -o /dev/null http://10.10.0.20:8080/

Filter the capture to tcp.port == 8080 and read the first three packets.

# Flags Seq Ack From 1 2 3
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK. Three packets, no data in any of them, before a single byte of your request moved.
  • Each side chose an initial sequence number and told the other. Each side acknowledged the other's. That is the entire ceremony: I will start counting here — understood, and I will start counting here — understood.
  • Nothing in the middle was consulted. No router was told a connection exists. The connection is two matching sets of numbers held in memory at the two ends, and nowhere else.
  • Wireshark shows relative sequence numbers by default. Turn that off (Preferences → Protocols → TCP → Relative sequence numbers) to see the real values, which are large and random — deliberately, so an outsider cannot guess them and inject data.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Do this — watch the state change
items.text:
# on CLIENT, in a second terminal
watch -n0.2 'ss -tan state all "( dport = :8080 or sport = :8080 )"'

# then, on CLIENT
curl -s -o /dev/null http://10.10.0.20:8080/

States you managed to catch: ________
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• ESTAB is the state everyone knows. The interesting ones are the ones that flash past: SYN-SENT, SYN-RECV, and after closing, FIN-WAIT, TIME-WAIT.
  • ss is reading the kernel's socket table — the same memory that is the connection. You are looking directly at the thing the network does not have.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Do this — watch it end
items.text:
Keep the capture running and let the curl finish, then look at the last four packets.

Flags on the closing packets How many packets to close Final state on CLIENT, and how long it lasts
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Closing is FIN → ACK → FIN → ACK: each direction is shut down separately, because a TCP connection is really two independent streams that happen to share a socket. One side can stop sending while still receiving.
  • The side that closes first sits in TIME-WAIT for a couple of minutes. That is not a bug and not a leak: it is the socket refusing to be reused while a delayed duplicate packet from the old connection might still arrive and be mistaken for part of a new one.
  • This is why a server you restart may report "address already in use" for a minute or two.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Do this — refused versus filtered
items.text:
# on CLIENT
curl -m5 http://10.10.0.20:9999/          # nothing listening

# on SERVER
nft add table inet f
nft add chain inet f in '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept; }'
nft add rule inet f in tcp dport 9999 drop

# on CLIENT
curl -m5 http://10.10.0.20:9999/          # dropped instead
Nothing listening Dropped What came back How long it took curl's error message

Clean up: nft flush ruleset on SERVER.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• Nothing listening → RST. The server's TCP stack answers immediately: there is no such socket here. curl fails instantly with "connection refused".
  • Dropped → nothing. curl retransmits its SYN and eventually gives up. The delay is the signal.
  • Same outcome for the user, completely different evidence for you. An instant failure means something answered; a slow failure means nothing did. That single distinction resolves a large share of real connectivity complaints, and it is the transport-layer twin of reject versus drop from W4·A6.
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Record
items.text: Packets to open a connection / to close one What each side announces in the handshake Where the connection physically exists Why initial sequence numbers are random What TIME-WAIT is protecting against Refused vs filtered: evidence and timing
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix No handshake in the capture capture started after curl start the capture first; TCP setup is over in milliseconds Sequence numbers all start at 0 Wireshark relative sequence numbers turn them off in TCP preferences ss shows nothing connection finished before watch refreshed use -n0.2, or fetch a larger file No RST for the closed port firewalld is dropping it, so you are testing the second case twice systemctl stop firewalld on SERVER TIME-WAIT not visible you watched the wrong end it appears on whichever side closed first — usually CLIENT Port 8080 refused python3 -m http.server died with its terminal restart it, background it with &
path: Transport — The three-way handshake, and what a connection actually is

items.title: Transport — UDP has no memory
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: the previous activity's topology · GNS3 project: tr-a2-udp (continue from tr-a1-handshake)

The question: TCP and UDP sit in the same place, in the same slot of the same IP header, carrying the same bytes over the same wire. Textbooks say one is "reliable" and one is not. Break the link and find out what that word actually buys you — and what it costs.

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. Send 1000 lines over TCP with 20% of packets dropped. How many arrive? _
  2. The same over UDP? _
  3. Which transfer finishes sooner? _
  4. Does the sender know, in either case? _

items.title: Do this — a baseline, both protocols
items.text:
# on SERVER
ncat -l 9000       > /tmp/tcp.out &
ncat -u -l 9000    > /tmp/udp.out &

# on CLIENT
seq 1 1000 | ncat    -w2 10.10.0.20 9000
seq 1 1000 | ncat -u -w2 10.10.0.20 9000

# on SERVER
wc -l /tmp/tcp.out /tmp/udp.out
TCP UDP Lines received

Both should arrive complete. A healthy link hides the entire difference between these protocols, which is exactly why the difference is hard to teach.

items.title: Do this — break the link
items.text:
# on SERVER — 20% of inbound packets discarded
tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 20%

Truncate the output files, then repeat both transfers.

TCP UDP Lines received Time taken Lines in order? Any error reported to the sender?

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• TCP delivered everything. Every gap was noticed by the receiver, the missing segment was retransmitted, and the application never learned any of it happened. Look at the capture: you can count the duplicate sequence numbers.
  • UDP delivered roughly 800 lines and neither end mentioned it. The sender believes it sent 1000. The receiver believes it received everything there was.
  • TCP was slower, and not by a little. Reliability is paid for in latency: every loss costs at least one round trip, and TCP also slows itself down on the assumption that loss means congestion.
  • Ordering came free with TCP and not at all with UDP. Sequence numbers are what make both retransmission and reordering possible; UDP has no such field because it has no such ambition.

items.title: Do this — where does UDP keep its state?
items.text:
# on SERVER
ss -uan
ss -tan

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The TCP socket has a state — ESTAB, TIME-WAIT, something. The UDP socket has none to show.
  • There is nothing to be in a state about. UDP has no handshake, no acknowledgement, no sequence numbers, no teardown. A UDP socket is an address the kernel will deliver datagrams to, and nothing more.
  • Which means the only thing UDP adds to bare IP is ports — the ability to have more than one conversation per host — plus an optional checksum. That is the whole protocol. Everything else you associate with "transport" is TCP's contribution, not the layer's.

items.title: Do this — why anyone chooses it
items.text:
# on SERVER
tc qdisc change dev eth0 root netem loss 5% delay 100ms

# on CLIENT — time a small exchange each way
time (echo ping | ncat    -w3 10.10.0.20 9000)
time (echo ping | ncat -u -w3 10.10.0.20 9000)

Clean up: tc qdisc del dev eth0 root on SERVER.

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• TCP paid three round trips before the first byte moved — the handshake — and pays again for every loss. UDP paid nothing and sent immediately.
  • For a voice call, a game, or a DNS lookup, a packet that arrives late is worth less than nothing: the moment it described has passed, and waiting for it delayed everything behind it. Retransmission is actively harmful there.
  • So the choice is not "reliable versus unreliable". It is who handles loss — the transport, or the application. UDP does not lack reliability; it declines to provide it, so that the application can decide what loss means.
  • That is why the newest web transport protocols are built on UDP and implement their own recovery on top. They wanted TCP's guarantees without TCP's fixed opinions about how to deliver them — and, as W4's reading describes, they wanted a shape the network would carry without asking questions.

items.title: Record
items.text: TCP / UDP lines delivered under 20% loss Which was faster, and why What the UDP sender was told about the loss What ss shows for a UDP socket, and why The only thing UDP adds to bare IP One application where retransmission is harmful

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix netem has no effect applied to the wrong node or interface it is on SERVER's eth0; tc qdisc show dev eth0 UDP delivers 1000/1000 anyway loss rule not active, or too little traffic to sample check tc qdisc show; raise to loss 40% UDP receives nothing at all ncat -u server not started, or firewalld restart it; systemctl stop firewalld TCP transfer hangs forever loss too high for recovery expected above ~40%; lower it and say why Output files keep growing previous ncat still running pkill ncat on SERVER between runs tc qdisc del errors at the end already removed harmless

items.title: DNS — One name, resolved by hand
items.text:
Time: 45 min · Needs: one OL9 Server, one OL9 PC, one Ethernet switch, Wireshark · GNS3 project: dn-a1-onename

The question: every address in this course so far has been a number you typed. Nobody types numbers. Somewhere between a name and a packet, something turns one into the other — and it is not part of IP, not part of TCP, and not built into your machine. Find out what it is and where it lives.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. You type a name into a browser. How many packets cross the wire before the first one addressed to the website? _
  2. Does your machine know any names? ☐ yes ☐ no
  3. If the name lookup fails, what does the error look like — and would you recognise it as a name problem? _
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Topology
items.text:
CLIENT ───── SW ───── SRV
     .11                 .12

An OL9 Server (SRV) and an OL9 PC (CLIENT) on one Ethernet switch. SRV will become a name server in the third activity; for now it is only somewhere to aim at. You will need dig, from the bind-utils package.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Do this — find out who your machine asks
items.text:
# on CLIENT
cat /etc/resolv.conf
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• One or more nameserver lines, each an IP address. That is the entire configuration: your machine does not resolve names, it asks someone who does, and this file is the list of who.
  • Note what is not here. There is no database of names, no list of websites, nothing downloaded. A machine's knowledge of names is close to zero and is refreshed one question at a time.
  • Note also where this came from. If the interface uses DHCP, that address arrived in the ACK alongside the IP address — go back and find it in a DHCP capture. Name resolution is one of the things DHCP exists to bootstrap, because a machine that has an address but no resolver can reach everything and find nothing.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Do this — ask one question, deliberately
items.text:
Start a capture, then:

# on CLIENT
dig example.com A

Read the output in four parts, because dig prints the response's actual structure:

Section Contains QUESTION exactly what you asked — the name, the class, the type ANSWER the records that answer it AUTHORITY which servers are responsible for that zone ADDITIONAL extra records the server thought would save you a round trip
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The question is echoed back in the reply. That is not padding: a resolver may have several queries outstanding at once over a connectionless protocol, and the echoed question plus a matching ID is how it pairs each answer with what it asked.
  • Look at the ANSWER line. It has four fields — name, TTL, class, type — and then the value. The TTL is a number of seconds, and it is the subject of the third activity.
  • In the capture: UDP, port 53, one packet out and one back. No connection, no handshake, no acknowledgement. Name resolution is the single most common thing that happens on the internet and it is done with two datagrams, because setting up a TCP connection to ask a one-line question would cost more than the question is worth.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Do this — ask for different things about the same name
items.text:
# on CLIENT
dig example.com A
dig example.com AAAA
dig example.com MX
dig example.com NS
dig +short example.com A
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The name is not a thing that has an address. It is a key with several kinds of value attached, and you have to say which kind you want:
Type Answers the question A what IPv4 address? AAAA what IPv6 address? MX where does mail for this domain go? NS which servers are authoritative for this zone? CNAME this name is really an alias for that name PTR which name belongs to this address? (the reverse direction)
  • So DNS is not "the thing that turns names into addresses". It is a general distributed lookup system that is mostly used for addresses. Mail routing, service discovery and certificate validation all ride on it.
  • +short prints only the value. Useful in scripts, and useless for learning, because everything interesting is in the parts it hides.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Do this — go behind the resolver's back
items.text:
# on CLIENT
echo '192.168.10.12 fileserver' >> /etc/hosts
dig fileserver A
ping -c1 fileserver
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• dig found nothing — and ping worked. They disagree, and the disagreement is the lesson.
  • dig speaks DNS and only DNS: it sends a query to a name server and reports what comes back. It deliberately does not consult anything local.
  • ping, like almost every normal program, does not speak DNS at all. It asks the C library to resolve a name, and the library follows /etc/nsswitch.conf, which lists sources in order — typically files dns, meaning /etc/hosts is consulted first and DNS only if that misses.
  • So there are two different resolution paths on every machine, and they can give different answers. This is the reason for a whole category of confusing incidents: "DNS is fine, I checked with dig, but the application still goes to the wrong place." Check with getent hosts <name>, which follows the same path a normal program does.
# on CLIENT
getent hosts fileserver

Remove the line from /etc/hosts when you are done.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Do this — see a failure properly
items.text:
# on CLIENT
dig doesnotexist.example.com A
curl -m5 http://doesnotexist.example.com/
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• dig reports status: NXDOMAIN — an explicit answer meaning this name does not exist, which is different from I could not reach a server (SERVFAIL) and from no answer of that type (NOERROR with an empty answer section).
  • curl says "Could not resolve host". That message is worth recognising instantly, because it tells you the failure happened before any packet was addressed to the destination — the network beyond your resolver was never involved, and testing it will waste your time.
  • The general rule this establishes: when something cannot connect, find out first whether it failed to resolve or failed to reach. Those are different problems with different causes and no overlap, and the error messages distinguish them if you read them.
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: Record
items.text:
File that lists your name servers, and where its contents came from Transport protocol and port for a DNS query The four sections of a response Three record types and what each answers Why dig and ping disagreed about fileserver Command that resolves the way a normal program does NXDOMAIN vs SERVFAIL

One sentence: an application cannot connect. What is the first thing you check, and why that first?
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: If it went wrong
items.text: Symptom Cause Fix dig: command not found bind-utils not installed dnf install bind-utils, or use host / getent hosts for most of this Every query times out no reachable resolver check /etc/resolv.conf; this lab needs egress or the local server from the third activity /etc/resolv.conf is empty interface configured statically with no DNS nmcli con modify <name> ipv4.dns 192.168.10.12 resolv.conf reverts on its own NetworkManager rewrites it from the connection change ipv4.dns on the connection, not the file dig works, applications do not different resolution paths compare with getent hosts; check /etc/nsswitch.conf No DNS in the capture the answer was cached locally queries are only sent on a cache miss; try a name you have not used
path: DNS — One name, resolved by hand

items.title: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day
items.text:
Time: 55 min · Needs: one OL9 Server, one OL9 PC, one Ethernet switch, a NAT node · GNS3 project: dn-a3-cache

The question: everyone has been told that a DNS change "takes 24 hours to propagate". Nothing propagates and nothing takes 24 hours. Serve some names yourself, then change one, and find out what that sentence is actually describing.
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: Predict first
items.text:
1. You change a record on the authoritative server. How does the old value reach anybody afterwards?
  2. What decides how long the old value keeps being served? _
  3. You are moving a service next Tuesday. When should you change anything? _
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: Topology
items.text:
CLIENT ───── SW ───── SRV ───── (NAT node, for upstream)
     .11                 .12

CLIENT is an OL9 PC, SRV an OL9 Server. SRV will run dnsmasq, which is small enough to read in one screen and does both jobs this activity needs: it can be authoritative for names you invent, and it caches everything else.

Address both by storing the configuration rather than with ip addr add. The NAT node on this wire hands out addresses, and a card with nothing stored can be handed one — which would take SRV's .12 away mid-activity, showing up as names failing to resolve rather than as an address that changed.

# on CLIENT
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name lab \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.11/24
nmcli con up lab

# on SRV
nmcli con add type ethernet ifname eth0 con-name lab \
      ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.12/24
nmcli con up lab

That distinction — a change to the running machine, versus a stored configuration NetworkManager keeps the running machine matching — is W3·A8, part 1. It also gives you the name to use where this activity says nmcli con modify <connection> later on: it is lab.
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: Do this — serve some names
items.text:
On SRV, replace /etc/dnsmasq.conf with:

# answer on this interface only
interface=eth0
bind-interfaces

# do not act as a DHCP server — that is a different activity
no-dhcp-interface=eth0

# names we are authoritative for
local=/lab.local/
address=/web.lab.local/192.168.10.20
address=/db.lab.local/192.168.10.21

# how long anyone may cache our own answers, in seconds
local-ttl=30

# where to send everything else
server=1.1.1.1

Each block is one decision:

Line The decision interface / bind-interfaces which wire this server answers on — never all of them by accident local=/lab.local/ this zone is mine — do not ask upstream about it, ever address=/…/ the records themselves local-ttl how long others may reuse our answers before asking again server= the resolver to forward everything else to 
# on SRV
systemctl restart dnsmasq
systemctl status dnsmasq

Point CLIENT at it and ask:

# on CLIENT
nmcli con modify <connection> ipv4.dns 192.168.10.12 ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes
nmcli con up <connection>

dig web.lab.local A
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• You are now the authority for a zone. local=/lab.local/ is the line that makes it so: it tells dnsmasq that questions about this zone are answered from its own configuration and never forwarded, so a name that does not exist here returns NXDOMAIN rather than being asked of the internet.
  • That "never forwarded" property is what makes an internal zone private. Without it, every internal hostname anyone looks up leaks to an upstream resolver as a question.
  • Note the TTL in the answer: 30, exactly as configured, and it does not move however many times you ask. An authoritative server states the TTL; it does not count it down.
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: Do this — watch a cache fill
items.text:
Now ask about a name you are not authoritative for, twice, and time both:

# on CLIENT
dig example.com A | grep -E 'Query time|IN\s+A'
dig example.com A | grep -E 'Query time|IN\s+A'
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
• The first query took tens or hundreds of milliseconds — SRV had to do the whole walk from the previous activity. The second took essentially zero.
  • Look at the TTL on the two answers. The first shows the full value from the authoritative server; the second shows a smaller number. Keep asking every few seconds and watch it count down.
  • That countdown is the cache. SRV stored the record along with the moment it expires, and every time it serves the record it reports the time remaining. When the number reaches zero the entry is discarded and the next question triggers a real lookup.
  • So a TTL is not a property of a record so much as a promise about how stale an answer may be. The owner of the name chooses it, and everyone else is entitled to rely on it for that long.
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: Do this — change a record and watch nothing happen
items.text:
# on SRV
sed -i 's|address=/web.lab.local/192.168.10.20|address=/web.lab.local/192.168.10.99|' /etc/dnsmasq.conf
systemctl restart dnsmasq

Immediately, on CLIENT:

# on CLIENT
dig +short web.lab.local A

Then ask again every ten seconds until it changes.
path: DNS — Run your own, and find out why changes take a day

items.title: What just happened
items.text:
